The Gap Between Description and Evaluation

There is a significant and frequently tested gap between describing a production and evaluating it. Description tells the examiner what you saw: “the performer crossed to downstage centre and the lighting faded to a single warm special.” Evaluation tells the examiner what it meant and whether it worked: “by isolating the performer downstage centre in a warm special while the ensemble faded to shadow upstage, the director communicated the character’s separation from their community at the moment of crisis — an effect that was reinforced by the audience’s collective silence.”

The 32-mark live theatre review specifically rewards substantiated evaluative judgement. That means you cannot simply state that a choice was “effective” — you must say why it was effective, with what evidence, and sometimes weigh it against moments where it was less successful.

Key Fact

A substantiated evaluative judgement has three parts: (1) a clear statement of the judgement (the choice succeeded / partially succeeded / did not achieve its intention), (2) a specific reason (the technical detail that made it work or fail), and (3) evidence (audience response, the coherence of the choice with the directorial concept, or a comparison with another moment).

What Is a Directorial Concept?

Every well-made production has a directorial concept: a central idea or question that the production is trying to explore, and which shapes every performer and design choice. When you evaluate a production, you are asking not just “did this choice work?” but “did this choice serve the directorial concept?”

For example, imagine a fictional production of a Victorian social drama at a hypothetical regional theatre in 2024 where the director set the play in a modern corporate office. In that context, every performer and design choice has a conceptual function: the sharp-edged glass and chrome set communicates the coldness of institutional power; the identical blue-grey suits worn by all characters except the protagonist suggest conformity; the sudden moment when the protagonist arrives in warm terracotta communicates her separateness before she says a word. Each of these choices succeeds if it reinforces the concept and fails if it contradicts it without purpose.

Audience Response as Evidence

One of the most powerful pieces of evidence you can use in your evaluation is the audience’s response. You were in the auditorium; you experienced the production’s effect collectively. If the audience gasped, laughed unexpectedly, fell completely silent or shifted restlessly, those are observable, real responses to specific theatrical choices.

Use this evidence explicitly: “the audience fell entirely silent for the four seconds of the blackout before the final scene, which confirmed that the director’s choice had successfully built anticipation over the preceding hour.” That sentence is evaluative, specific and evidenced. Compare it with: “the blackout was effective at the end.” The same word — “effective” — appears in both, but only the first sentence earns marks.

Imagine a fictional touring production of a Greek myth-inspired play at a hypothetical arts centre in 2024. In the final scene, the protagonist accepted their fate and knelt centre stage as the ensemble moved silently in a circle around them.

Description (no evaluation): “The protagonist knelt in the middle of the stage and the other actors walked in a circle around them. The lights went dark except for one bright light above the protagonist. The music was quiet and sad.”

Evaluation: “The director’s decision to place the protagonist kneeling at centre stage while the ensemble moved in a slow clockwise circle communicated the character’s willing surrender to forces beyond their control. The use of a high-intensity tungsten profile lantern focused from directly above — a top-light that created a perfect circle of light around the static figure — reinforced the symbolism: the character had become both the centre of the world and its prisoner simultaneously. The underscore, a sustained cello line at low volume that had been building for the previous three minutes, reached its resolution and then stopped completely as the protagonist bowed their head. The resulting silence lasted approximately six seconds before the snap blackout. The audience did not move or speak for several seconds after the lights returned, which suggests the production had succeeded in communicating the weight of the moment.”

Both paragraphs describe the same moment. Only the second one evaluates it — and only the second one earns marks in the top band.

The Language of Evaluation

Examiners are trained to look for evaluative language. Certain phrases signal that you are evaluating rather than describing. Build these into your vocabulary:

  • This succeeded in communicating… because… (names the success, names the reason)
  • This choice was particularly effective at this moment because… (links the choice to the specific moment)
  • The effect on the audience was… which suggests the director intended… (links audience response to directorial intention)
  • While this worked in the earlier scene, here it was less convincing because… (balanced evaluation, showing critical perspective)
  • The most memorable moment was… because… and this supported the overall concept of the production by… (integrates a judgement with the directorial concept)

Notice that every evaluative phrase contains “because” or “which suggests” or “by.” Evaluation always requires reasoning. A judgement without a reason is just an opinion.

Themes and Subtext

Subtext operates at every level of a production. A director who cuts a scene short, or who allows one character to remain on stage in silence after others have exited, is creating subtext through structure and staging. When you evaluate, you can acknowledge subtext as a layer of meaning: “the performer’s choice to hold the gaze of the audience for three seconds after the final line — before the blackout cut off the eye contact — communicated that the character was aware of being observed, and perhaps complicit in their own fate.”

Strong evaluative writing connects the moment to the theme: not just “this made the audience feel sad” but “this communicated the production’s central theme of inevitable loss, and the audience’s collective silence was evidence that the communication had succeeded.”

Many students believe that evaluation simply means saying “I thought it was brilliant” or “I think the director did a great job.” Unsubstantiated opinion earns the lowest marks in the top-band mark scheme.

The difference is substance: an evaluative judgement is a claim supported by specific theatrical evidence. “I thought the set was very impressive” is opinion without evidence. “The set’s decision to use a raked platform rising from stage right to upstage left forced every performer to hold themselves slightly off-balance when standing still, which communicated the physical precariousness of the characters’ social positions and was consistently effective throughout the production” is a substantiated evaluative judgement. Train yourself to follow every judgement with “because” and a specific theatrical detail.

Key Fact

A clear evaluation includes a judgement, a reason and supporting evidence. Use all three parts to make your evaluation convincing.

One Stage, Two Worlds

Blood Brothers places two families at opposite ends of the British class divide on the same stage simultaneously. The design challenge is to make those worlds legible at a glance without resorting to caricature, and to allow them to share the same physical space when the twins’ paths cross. Russell’s text does not prescribe a single staging solution, which is why Blood Brothers has been produced across a huge range of configurations — from bare-stage ensemble productions to fully realised split-set designs. Each approach makes different arguments about the play’s meaning.

Set Design: The Physical Language of Class

A split stage design for Blood Brothers divides the acting area so that the Johnstone household occupies one half and the Lyons household the other. This physical separation makes visible the class divide that the play explores thematically. The Johnstone side might feature a worn kitchen table, mismatched chairs and a damp-textured back wall — materials that suggest cramped social housing in 1960s Liverpool. The Lyons side might be signified by a polished sideboard, a pale carpet swatch and clean vertical lines, using colour and texture rather than elaborate set dressing to communicate wealth without ostentation.

Levels can reinforce the class dynamic: the Lyons household slightly elevated on a rostrum, the Johnstone household at floor level. This is not about literal geography — the Lyons family do not live upstairs — but about the visual grammar of status. An audience reads height as authority without any dialogue being necessary. The scenic transition between the two worlds, and the moments when characters cross from one side to the other, become loaded with dramatic meaning.

Key Fact

In Blood Brothers, set design is a language of class. Texture, condition and colour can communicate the difference between the Johnstone estate and the Lyons suburb without reproducing a documentary realism. A chipped enamel mug reads differently from a bone-china teacup, even in silhouette.

Lighting Design: Warm, Cold and the Space Between

Lighting designers working on Blood Brothers have a rich palette of choices for communicating the emotional contrast between the two households. The Johnstone world might use warmer gels — amber and straw tones — to evoke the cramped warmth of a full, noisy family. The Lyons world might be lit in cooler, more clinical tones: pale blue-white, clean and shadowless, suggesting order and the absence of mess. A gobo projecting the pattern of window frames could be used on the Johnstone kitchen wall, casting a grid of shadows that reads simultaneously as a domestic window and as a prison-bar motif, reinforcing the theme of entrapment without a single line of dialogue.

The lighting state shifts across the play’s time leaps are particularly important. When the action jumps from the children at seven to the teenagers at fourteen, the lighting transition should do more than simply change brightness: a shift from the high-key, primary-coloured brightness of childhood to a more complex, lower-key palette for adolescence can signal the loss of innocence without the Narrator needing to announce it. Cross-fading between states rather than using sudden blackouts preserves the dream-like, retrospective quality of Russell’s storytelling.

A very common student error is to write “I would use dark lighting to show it is sad” without specifying anything concrete. Examiners require you to name the type of lantern (profile spot, Fresnel, flood), the direction (front light, side light, top light), the colour gel, and the effect on the audience. For example: “I would use a 650W profile spot from above and slightly behind Mrs Johnstone, with a Lee 201 full CT blue gel, creating a cold top-light that isolates her in shadow when she realises the consequences of the deal. This would make the audience feel she is trapped beneath an indifferent sky.” Concrete choices, named elements, named effects — that is a design answer.

Sound Design: Contrasting Soundscapes

The soundscape for each household can be designed to reinforce class difference. The Johnstone home might carry ambient sounds of the estate: distant music from neighbouring flats, children shouting in the street, the rattle of a bus. These would be diegetic sounds that root the audience in a believable social environment. The Lyons household might be surrounded by silence, or by the faint, tasteful strains of Radio 3, suggesting a world insulated from the noise of poverty.

When the two worlds collide — in the scenes where Mickey and Edward first meet, or the teenage scenes on the bus — the sound design might blend both worlds’ sonic signatures, creating a deliberate dissonance that reflects the cultural friction of two boys who should not be in the same space. A sound designer could introduce a low, barely audible underscore whenever the Narrator appears, so the audience subconsciously associates his presence with a particular tonal texture, reinforcing his role as the play’s moral undertow.

Key Fact

Sound designers in Blood Brothers can use diegetic ambient sound to place the audience socially — the estate’s noise vs. the suburb’s silence. The contrast is not just realistic: it is a class argument made in frequency and volume rather than words.

Costume: Class on the Body

Costume design in Blood Brothers must do two jobs simultaneously: signal class instantly to the audience, and allow the cast to age convincingly across a twenty-year time span. The Johnstone children might wear clothing that is worn, hand-me-down in quality — slightly too large, slightly faded, natural fibres that have been washed too many times. The Lyons children might wear clothing that is new, well-fitted, in cleaner, more structured fabrics. The silhouette of wealth (pressed trousers, a blazer) versus the silhouette of poverty (loose-fitting, layered) communicates class before a word is spoken.

The transition from child to teenager to adult in Mickey is particularly interesting as a costume challenge. A costume transition for Mickey from the bright, layered estate-child clothing of Act One to the worn, ill-fitting adult clothing of the unemployed Mickey in Act Two should track his social decline visibly. The colours might drain from his palette — fewer primaries, more grey and brown — matching the deterioration of his circumstances and his mental state. Hair and make-up can support this: a pale, drawn face and hollow eyes for the adult Mickey contrasted with the rosy-cheeked energy of the child.

As a performer playing Mickey in the factory closure scene, you might show the moment of job loss through a sudden drop in physical energy — shoulders collapsing inward, head lowering, the chest caving as though something has been knocked out of the body. Vocally, you could shift from Mickey’s usual quick-fire Liverpudlian delivery to a slower, flatter, lower register: the energy has left his voice as it has left his body. You might stand at stage left with your back slightly turned to the audience, physically retreating from the social world represented by centre stage.

As a set and lighting designer, you might strip the set in the Johnstone area down for this scene — removing any props that suggested domestic life — so the space around Mickey is visually emptied. The lighting state could shift to a single Fresnel wash from slightly above and to one side, leaving the other half of the stage darker, so Mickey is physically isolated within the playing area. The removal of warmth from the colour palette — shifting from the straw-amber of earlier scenes to a neutral daylight white — removes the sense of shelter the Johnstone home once provided.

A Family Divided by a Coastline

Francis Turnly’s characters in The Great Wave carry the weight of a documented historical event. They are not simply dramatic constructs — they are theatrical representations of a human situation that was real for many families along Japan’s western coast in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Understanding how to perform and design these characters requires understanding both their individual psychology and their structural function in the parallel storylines. Every character exists on at least two levels: as a human being with specific desires and fears, and as an embodiment of a political relationship between two states.

Hanako: The Anchoring Figure

Hanako is 17 when she is abducted. She is the play’s central figure but also, by design, its most constrained: the physical fact of captivity means she rarely initiates action. Her dramatic arc is internal — the slow, painful accommodation to a life she did not choose, and the question of whether accommodation equals surrender or survival. A performer playing Hanako across the play’s full timeline faces one of the most demanding tasks in the GCSE set-play canon: communicating 24 years of interior change through vocal interpretation and physical evolution, without the luxury of a narrator explaining the psychological shifts.

In the early captivity scenes, a performer might play Hanako with a fast, shallow breath pattern — higher pitch, clipped phrasing, physical restlessness. She paces: she is young, frightened, disoriented. A decade later, the same performer must communicate containment without defeat. A slower pace of speech, longer pauses before responding to her captors, a more upright but very still posture — the body has learned economy, not submission. The key performance challenge is distinguishing accommodation from defeat; Hanako survives precisely because she internalises rather than breaks.

Key Fact

Hanako is the play’s emotional centre across two decades. A performer must track her ageing through specific vocal and physical changes rather than relying on costume or make-up alone: pace of speech, range of movement, and the quality of stillness are the primary tools.

Reiko: The Advocate

Reiko is Hanako’s older sister, and the last person to see Hanako before the abduction. Her arc is the inverse of Hanako’s: where Hanako is confined and controlled, Reiko becomes increasingly active, increasingly public. She refuses the easy conclusion — that Hanako drowned — and her refusal drives the Japanese storyline. A performer playing Reiko must chart a different kind of psychological journey: from grief-stricken teenager to determined adult campaigner, without losing the underlying guilt of their last argument.

In the early scenes, Reiko’s physicality might be collapsed, withdrawn, directed downward — the proxemics of grief. A performer might keep her consistently downstage right, nearer the audience but turned slightly away from the other family members — present but unreachable. In the later scenes, her energy redirects into forward motion and direct eye contact: she stands upstage centre and addresses other characters (or, in moments of direct appeal, the audience itself) with a sustained, level gaze. The posture opens, the volume increases, the pacing quickens when bureaucratic silence is confronted.

Etsuko: The Mother

Etsuko, the mother, undergoes the most visible ageing across the play. She begins as an anxious parent in middle age and ends as an elderly woman whose grief has become the shape of her life. For a costume designer, Etsuko presents an opportunity to communicate temporal change through fabric and silhouette: a domestic, practical mid-layer in the early scenes — apron, layered cottons, a dark headscarf — might give way, scene by scene, to heavier, darker fabrics that seem to weigh the body down. Hair and make-up contribute here: progressively lighter powder, more drawn lines around the eyes, slower application of movement.

For a lighting designer, Etsuko’s scenes in Japan offer the opportunity to use a warm but increasingly low-intensity lighting wash to suggest domestic space becoming emotionally colder over time. The colour temperature of the Japan sequences might shift imperceptibly from amber to a neutral white over the course of the play — so subtle that the audience feels the change before they can name it.

A common performance error for Etsuko is to play her as uniformly sad from the start. This flattens the arc. In the early scenes, Etsuko may be partly in denial — performing domestic normality — which means a performer might actually increase the pace and volume of her housekeeping activities, her insistence on routine, as a defence against grief. The breaks in this routine — the moments she stops mid-task and simply stands still — carry the greater emotional weight precisely because the activity around them has been lively. A Stanislavskian approach to Etsuko means identifying her given circumstances precisely for each scene: where is she in the emotional timeline? What does she still believe at this point? What has she been told? Has she yet seen the government’s documentation? Each answer changes what the body and voice do.

Kum-Chol and the Question of the Captor

Kum-Chol becomes Hanako’s husband in North Korea. He is one of the most demanding characters in the play to perform because Turnly resists making him simply a villain. He is complicit in a state crime, but he is also recognisably human: he has loyalties, beliefs and, perhaps, moments of doubt. A performer playing Kum-Chol must avoid the trap of playing ideological certainty as blankness. The most interesting choices for this character involve gestus — the specific way his body communicates his relationship to institutional authority. He stands a particular way when reading official orders; he moves differently when alone with Hanako. These physical contrasts are where performance becomes analysis.

Jung Sun and the Teaching Scenes

Jung Sun is a North Korean assigned to learn Japanese from Hanako. The relationship that develops between them is the play’s most nuanced portrayal of what coercion does to human bonds. She is not free either — both of them are in the grip of the same state machinery — but his situation is different. For a director, the teaching scenes are among the most choreographically rich in the play: two people sitting across a table, both pretending a neutrality neither feels, in a space that is simultaneously a classroom and a prison. The proxemics here carry enormous weight. A director might begin with the performers at maximum downstage distance from each other and have them gradually, scene by scene, reduce that distance — a physical narrative of reluctant trust.

Key Fact

The play’s character relationships are built on constrained proximity: nearly every significant pairing is between people in unequal power positions. Proxemics — the distance between performers and whether it changes — is the most direct way to communicate these power dynamics in staging.

Examiners note that students frequently describe Hanako as ‘sad’ or ‘broken’ throughout the play and treat this as a sufficient performance analysis. It is not. The specific vocal and physical journey from frightened teenager to quietly resilient adult requires different, concrete choices at different points in the timeline. ‘Sad’ is an emotion; examiners want to know how you would embody it: lowered volume, longer inhalations before speaking, a reduced gestural range, avoidance of direct eye contact with authority figures. And crucially, these choices must change across the timeline — not because Hanako becomes happy, but because her psychological strategy evolves. A student who tracks this evolution scene by scene, with specific choices, is writing at the highest level.

The Design Challenge: Three Worlds, One Stage

The Empress moves constantly between three distinct worlds — Tilbury Docks and the East End streets, the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney, and the interior of Windsor Castle. Each world carries its own class, race and power dynamic, and the designer’s task is to communicate this visually without lengthy explanatory dialogue. The fundamental design choice is about set design: does the production use a fully realistic set for each world, or a shared, flexible stylised staging concept?

Most productions of Gupta’s play favour a fluid, semi-abstract approach: a permanent architectural framework on stage that can read as a dockside, a domestic interior, or a royal chamber depending on how it is lit and populated with props. This approach allows rapid scene transitions between Rani’s world and Abdul’s without blackouts and lengthy set changes breaking the play’s momentum. The designer might use raised platforms at different levels: upstage elevated areas for Windsor Castle interiors, lower ground-level areas for the dockside — staging status literally into the geography of the stage.

Key Fact

A designer’s choices in The Empress must work politically as well as practically. The contrast between the East End’s raw materials (rope, crates, damp stone, gas lamps) and Windsor’s opulence (gilded surfaces, velvet, chandeliers) is not just period detail — it is a visual argument about imperial inequality.

Set Design: Dock, Home and Court

For the Tilbury Docks opening, a set designer might use a bare stage with a few heavy wooden crates and lengths of rope coiled on the floor. The texture is rough — raw timber, perhaps a patch of water-stained canvas. Props as symbols are powerful here: the single bag that contains everything Rani owns signals her precariousness as soon as it is placed in the performance space. Sightlines matter. In an end-on configuration, the dock could fill the full width of the stage, placing the audience in the position of spectators on the quay watching the ship arrive. In a traverse configuration, the dock becomes a corridor — the characters move through it, and the audience on both sides feel enclosed by it.

For Windsor Castle, the design language shifts completely. A gilded frame or a pair of high-backed chairs might be sufficient to signal the court. Period-detail wallpaper projected via a lighting gobo onto a plain cyclorama can transform a bare wall into an ornate Victorian interior without building a full set — and it can be removed instantly by a simple lighting cross-fade, returning the stage to neutral for the next scene in the East End.

Lighting Design: Dividing the World

Lighting is the key design tool for managing the play’s parallel storylines. A director using split staging can hold both Rani’s East End scene and Abdul’s court scene live on stage at the same time, cross-fading between them. The choice of colour temperature communicates world without words: a cool, blue-grey lighting state for the docks (suggesting overcast London skies and industrial cold), a warm amber-gold wash for Windsor (suggesting wealth, firelight, warmth used ironically given the coldness of the court politics within).

Specific lantern choices matter in an exam answer. A Fresnel flood with a half-CTO (colour temperature orange) gel gives the warm diffuse quality appropriate for the Ayahs’ Home — soft-edged, domestic, communal. A profile spot with a harder edge and a steel-blue gel, angled steeply from above, can make the dock scene feel exposed and cold. A moving light programmed to track Rani through the dock space underlines her isolation: she moves, the light follows, the rest of the stage stays dark.

Many students write “I would use period lighting to create a Victorian atmosphere.” This scores Developing at best. Period lighting is not a design choice — it is a vague intention. The examiner needs to know: what type of lantern? What gel or colour temperature? What direction? What intensity? What effect does this specific combination produce, and why does it serve this moment’s meaning? A Mastering answer names the lantern (profile, Fresnel, flood), the colour (amber, steel blue, straw), the direction (front-of-house, overhead, side), and links it explicitly to the scene’s power dynamics.

Sound Design: From Dockside to Palace

The sound cue is one of the fastest design tools for switching world. A sound designer for The Empress might build a dockside soundscape from: the low rumble of steam engines, the creak of wooden hulls, water lapping against stone, and the cries of dock workers mixing in English and Lascar languages. This can be cross-faded on a single cue into the measured formality of a string quartet minuet for the Windsor scenes — a sound transition that in itself makes an argument about the gulf between these worlds.

Indian music as underscore in Rani’s scenes and the Lascar lodging house signals cultural belonging and memory. A sound designer might use a sitar phrase or a tabla pattern, low in the mix during dialogue (non-diegetic), swelling briefly during moments of solidarity or joy, then cutting out entirely for the scenes where Rani is most isolated. The sudden silence in the middle of the dockside scene — no underscore, no ambient sound — can be more powerful than any sound cue.

Costume Design: Fabric as Political Argument

Costume in The Empress is one of the richest areas for design discussion. The visual contrast between Indian and British dress is immediately legible to the audience, but a sophisticated designer moves beyond “Indian costume versus Victorian costume”. Rani as an ayah might wear a cotton sari in a muted, washed-out colour — suggesting both Indian heritage and the fading that comes from service and poverty. The fabric drapes naturally but is worn and practical. If she is given a British-style apron or service uniform over the sari, the layering communicates her in-between status: Indian body, British domestic service.

Abdul Karim’s costume charts his change in status. Arriving in British-issued servant’s uniform, he might later be seen in embroidered Indian court dress bestowed by Victoria — but the embroidery is read differently by different characters on stage. To Victoria it is honour; to Lord Salisbury it is presumption. The designer can make this argument visible: perhaps the court figures literally look away from Abdul’s robes while Victoria leans forward. Proxemics and blocking reinforces the costume’s argument without adding a word of dialogue.

Multi-roling is a structural feature of The Empress: the British court figures and minor English characters are often doubled or trebled among the ensemble cast. A costume designer must make multi-roling legible to the audience through a clear, quick system of transformation — a tailcoat on or off, a hat changed, a wig removed. The challenge is that each transformation must read instantly from the auditorium. One approach: design the British court figures’ costumes as a single visual “kit” (black tail coat, white cravat, top hat) that can be assembled and disassembled in seconds behind a set piece, while the Indian characters’ costumes are more individual and varied — a visual argument that the British establishment are interchangeable functionaries where the Indian characters are distinct people.

Multi-roling through costume transformation

British court characters in The Empress can be designed as a matching kit — tailcoat, cravat, top hat — assembled and removed in seconds, making the establishment interchangeable while Indian characters remain visually distinct individuals.

Two Worlds, One Stage

The Great Wave by Francis Turnly spans almost a quarter of a century — from 1979 to 2003 — across two nations that share a coastline but almost nothing else. The structural challenge Turnly sets himself is formidable: how do you tell a story in which two families live through the same event from opposite sides of a border, across two decades, without ever fully knowing the same facts? His answer is a rigorously disciplined cross-cutting structure that forces the audience into the uncomfortable position of knowing more than any single character ever does.

The play is structured in two acts. The first act establishes the catastrophic event at its centre — the abduction of Hanako from the coast of Japan by North Korean agents during a storm in 1979 — and then splits into its two parallel lines: Hanako in North Korea, and her family in Japan. The second act moves deeper into adulthood, into diplomacy and silence, and towards the Pyongyang Declaration of 2002, which acknowledged for the first time that such abductions had taken place. By choosing this two-act, twin-timeline structure, Turnly gives the audience a form that mirrors its content: separation, parallel endurance, and the impossibility of reunion that looks easy from the outside.

Key Fact

The play spans 1979 to 2003 across two parallel storylines: Hanako in North Korea (abducted as a teenager) and her family in Japan (searching, grieving, advocating). The twin timelines converge emotionally but almost never physically.

The Opening Beach Scene

The play opens during a storm at the Tanaka household. The stage directions foreground the Sea of Japan: its sound, scale and menace. The storm then frames the beach sequence in which Hanako disappears. For a director, the staging of this scene is one of the most consequential choices in the whole production. Working in an in-the-round configuration, the sea becomes a surround-sound presence rather than a painted flat: waves can come from all directions, making the audience feel the disorientation of the storm. In a more traditional proscenium arch configuration, the beach might be signalled by a raked stage, a strip of projected surf at the back, and a soundscape of crashing water that gradually overwhelms the sisters’ voices.

As a performer playing Reiko in this opening moment, the choices you make about posture and proximity signal the relationship before a word is spoken. Place Reiko upstage of Hanako and have her turn away as Hanako tries to speak — the physical distance communicates the argument’s emotional temperature before either line is delivered. As a sound designer, you might begin with a low, continuous underscore of distant waves, then swell the volume as the sisters’ argument reaches its peak, so that the sea literally drowns their voices at the moment of separation — a design choice that carries the controlling metaphor of the title into the audience’s ears.

Cross-cutting means the play shifts between its two storylines in alternating scenes rather than completing one before starting the other. In The Great Wave, Turnly cuts from Hanako’s captivity in North Korea to the Tanaka family in Japan and back again, sometimes within the same act. This structure creates dramatic irony — the audience knows Hanako is alive while her family does not — and it holds both truths simultaneously rather than letting the audience forget either one.

For a director, these transitions need a clear lighting state change at each cross-cut. A common approach is a sudden blackout followed immediately by a new state — colder in North Korea, warmer in Japan — so the audience registers the geography shift through temperature and colour before any dialogue confirms it. The costume of the performers can reinforce this: subdued utility fabrics and muted earth tones in the DPRK sequences; softer domestic textures and layered clothing in the Japanese family sequences.

Time Leaps and the Ageing Body

Because the play moves across more than two decades, the performers playing Hanako and her family must communicate ageing without realistic prosthetics. Turnly’s stage directions indicate time leaps through lighting changes, sound shifts and costume alteration. A blocking strategy commonly used to communicate ageing is to give a character a progressively reduced range of movement as years accumulate — a youthful Hanako who crosses the stage in a few quick strides becomes, a decade later, a figure who moves in deliberate, contained steps, her energy disciplined by years of captivity. This is not naturalistic ageing — it is a theatrical shorthand that makes the passage of time legible in the performer’s body.

For the audience, this physical storytelling across time is more powerful than any chronological caption could be. When Etsuko, the mother, is seen in two scenes separated by a decade, a lighting designer might shift from a warmer, amber-tinted state in the earlier scene to a cooler, lower-intensity wash in the later one — signalling not just time but emotional weathering. A gobo patterned to suggest window bars or a lattice might appear in the North Korean scenes to suggest confinement without building a cell.

Key Fact

Turnly signals time leaps through lighting state changes, costume alterations and sound cues rather than captions or narration. This places the burden of storytelling on design rather than exposition, which gives the audience an active interpretive role.

Epic Structure and Documentary Roots

The structure of The Great Wave belongs to the tradition of documentary theatre — a tradition associated with the Tricycle Theatre (now Kiln Theatre), which co-produced the play’s 2018 world premiere at the National Theatre’s Dorfman, directed by Indhu Rubasingham. Documentary theatre typically presents itself as evidence rather than fiction; even though The Great Wave has invented characters, its structural discipline — the dual timeline, the diplomatic scenes, the precision of its historical markers (1979, 1983, 2002, 2003) — signals to the audience that these events are rooted in documented fact.

This epic span puts the play in company with Brechtian epic theatre structure, in which scenes function as separate episodes each carrying their own meaning, rather than as links in a single causal chain. Brecht believed that episodic structure prevented the audience from becoming lost in emotional identification; they could stand back and witness the political argument being made. In The Great Wave, the cutting between Japan and North Korea achieves a similar effect: the audience cannot fully surrender to either storyline without being reminded that another, equally real world is running parallel to it.

A common student error is to describe the play as a family drama about Japanese grief and treat the North Korean sequences as background. This misreads the structure entirely. Turnly gives roughly equal stage time to both sides; the North Korean sequences are not backdrop but a parallel central story. The examiner’s note on this is consistent: students who analyse only the Japanese family’s storyline miss the structural argument the play is making. The cross-cutting is the meaning. What the parallel structure demands of the audience is the emotional labour of holding both experiences at once — which is precisely what the abduction has denied the characters themselves.

A Play of Two Worlds

Tanika Gupta’s The Empress spans two contrasting worlds that would never ordinarily appear on the same stage: the dockside poverty of Tilbury and the gilded interiors of Windsor Castle. The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, and follows its threads across roughly a decade and a half of the late Victorian era. Its two-act structure holds two parallel storylines in tension throughout, intercutting between them so that the audience builds understanding of both simultaneously.

Rani’s Storyline: Survival in the Imperial Metropolis

The play’s invented protagonist, Rani, is a young Indian ayah who arrives at Tilbury Docks as part of a British household’s return from India. At the play’s opening, in the scene at the docks, the English family pays Rani off and leaves her without passage home. From this moment of abandonment she must navigate a London that is simultaneously the capital of the Empire she has served and a city largely hostile to her presence.

Her journey takes her into the East End, where she discovers the Lascar sailors’ community — Indian and Yemeni seafarers who have long inhabited the port districts of London — and eventually to the Ayahs’ Home, a refuge in Hackney for stranded women in her position. Gupta uses Rani’s movement through these spaces to draw a social map of the hidden Indian presence in Victorian London: domestic servants, sailors and the first tentative signs of a South Asian political community.

Key Fact

Rani’s storyline begins at Tilbury Docks when the family she worked for pays her off without a return passage. She discovers the Lascar sailors’ community in the East End and the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney — both real Victorian institutions that Gupta draws on for historical authenticity.

Abdul Karim’s Storyline: Ascent at Court

Running in parallel is the story of Abdul Karim, a historical figure who arrived at Windsor Castle in 1887 as a servant for the Golden Jubilee celebrations and rose to become Queen Victoria’s Indian secretary — her munshi. In Gupta’s dramatisation, Victoria and Abdul develop a relationship of genuine personal warmth: she learns Hindustani from him, elevates his status and protects him against the fierce hostility of the court. Lord Salisbury, the Prince of Wales and the royal household circle perceive Abdul as an inappropriate favourite and move against him repeatedly throughout the play.

The court scenes are played in sharp contrast to the East End scenes: formal, spatially rigid, visually opulent. A director might choose a proscenium arch configuration for the Windsor scenes to reinforce their theatricality and hierarchy — the court literally arranges itself for display — while the Lascar lodgings and Ayahs’ Home might be played on a thrust stage area or in a more intimate configuration to reflect communal solidarity rather than spectacle.

The Intercut Structure and Its Effect

Gupta does not tell Rani’s story to completion and then tell Abdul’s. Instead she intercuts between them scene by scene, building a pattern of parallel storylines. This structural choice carries dramaturgical weight. Every time the audience moves from a Windsor Castle scene of court conspiracy to a scene of Rani sleeping in the Ayahs’ Home, the contrast asks a question: what does the Empire mean for someone at the very top of its hierarchy, and what does it mean for someone abandoned at its edges?

The intercut structure is itself a theatrical statement. A director staging this rhythm of cuts must think carefully about transitions: how quickly do scenes change? Does music bridge the cuts? Is the set design flexible enough to shift between Windsor’s formality and the East End’s working-world warmth without a clumsy scene change? In the original RSC 2013 premiere directed by Emma Rice, ensemble multi-roling and fluid staging kept transitions fast, so that the juxtaposition landed with impact rather than interruption.

Rani is Gupta’s invented protagonist, but she is grounded in real documented history. The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney and the Lascar communities of the East End are both historically attested. Gupta has compressed and dramatised: the Ayahs’ Home opened slightly later than 1887 in reality. Examiners reward students who recognise this as dramatic history — a playwright shaping fact for theatrical impact — rather than treating the play as a documentary record. Abdul Karim and Queen Victoria are historical; Rani and her immediate world are imaginatively reconstructed from evidence of real people in similar circumstances.

The Convergence and the Ending

The two storylines draw together near the play’s close. The moment of convergence — when Rani and figures from Abdul’s world briefly occupy the same space — offers the play’s most direct statement of solidarity. Structurally, this meeting is the fulfilment of the parallel design: two streams of late-Victorian Indian experience in Britain, briefly joined. The closing tableau asks the audience to hold in mind what has survived and what has been lost: Abdul’s papers were burned after Victoria’s death; the Ayahs’ Home closed; the Lascar community was gradually displaced.

Key Fact

The parallel, intercut structure is a deliberate dramaturgical choice: placing Rani’s world and Abdul’s world in constant dialogue means the audience cannot look at Imperial wealth without simultaneously holding in mind its human cost at street level.

When a director works on the cuts between storylines in The Empress, a useful checklist includes: (1) Lighting states — a lighting state using warm amber and gold for Windsor against a cooler, more natural white wash for the East End scenes will encode the contrast in the audience’s visual memory. (2) Underscore — Hindi or Hindustani song cues between scenes can act as bridges that carry the emotional thread of the Indian characters even into the English spaces. (3) Blocking — the physical geography of Windsor scenes (courtiers fanning out upstage in hierarchical lines) versus the East End scenes (characters gathered centre stage in an impromptu circle) communicates social structure through space alone.

Themes as Staging Problems

In a Drama exam, a theme is not just an idea in the text — it is a staging problem. If Romeo and Juliet is about fate, what does fate look like on stage? If it is about the gap between young and old, how does a director communicate that gap through blocking, costume and proxemics? Every theme in this play has a physical, vocal and design equivalent that the examiner expects you to identify and discuss.

Love: Multiple Kinds, Multiple Registers

The play contains at least three distinct kinds of love and a director must stage each differently. Romeo’s early love for Rosaline is courtly love — performative, abstract, composed of borrowed poetic conventions. A performer might play Romeo in Act One with a certain theatrical self-consciousness: the postures are a little too deliberate, the sighs a little too displayed. By contrast, his love for Juliet seems to surprise him. The vocabulary changes from studied metaphor to immediate sensation. A performer must find a physical difference between these two registers: perhaps the arms are slightly spread in the Rosaline scenes, gesturing outward toward a projected image, while in the balcony scene the body inclines forward, drawn rather than posturing.

The Nurse’s love is earthy and practical: she loves Juliet like a mother but her advice is always pragmatic, never idealistic. Mercutio’s language about love is deliberately coarse, reducing it to appetite. Shakespeare gives the audience these contrasting perspectives simultaneously, and a director must think about how the design of the feast scene — where all these registers of love are present — communicates each one spatially. The Nurse might be positioned at the edge of the main action, closer to the kitchen than to the dancing, her posture practical rather than celebratory.

Key Fact

Romeo and Juliet contains at least three distinct registers of love: Romeo’s performative courtly love for Rosaline, the immediate and mutual love between Romeo and Juliet, and the Nurse’s earthy, practical affection. A director must stage each differently to communicate their contrast.

Fate and the Stars: Design Opportunities

The prologue names the lovers “star-crossed,” and the image of stars and celestial forces recurs throughout the play. For a lighting designer, this is a rich source of design language. A gobo projecting star patterns onto a cyclorama or the stage floor might appear at key moments of the lovers’ story — perhaps first softly and warmly in the balcony scene, then coolly and with harder edges in the tomb. The shift in quality of the same image — from romantic wash to cold celestial indifference — communicates the theme of fate without a single word being spoken.

But fate in this play is complicated: Shakespeare also builds in moments where free will seems possible. Friar Lawrence’s letter might have got through. Romeo might have been a moment slower. The tragedy accrues through a chain of near-misses that could, at almost any point, have been broken. A director who believes fate is the dominant force might use a lighting state that always returns to the same cold overhead quality after each moment of hope — a visual refrain that tells the audience: it was always going to end here.

Interpretation 1 — Fate is absolute: The director keeps the chorus figure visible throughout the production, seated upstage centre on a raised level, watching the action unfold without intervening. The figure’s stillness communicates the indifference of fate. The lighting keeps the chorus figure in a cool, dim wash at all times: present, watching, inevitable.

Interpretation 2 — Fate is the product of choices: The chorus figure appears only for the two prologues and does not remain to watch the action. The design uses warm, saturated lighting during the lovers’ scenes to suggest that happiness was genuinely possible — and strips that warmth away only when the irreversible choices are made. This places the weight of the tragedy on human decision rather than celestial necessity.

Both interpretations are valid and examinable. What the examiner wants is for you to choose one and justify it with specific staging evidence, not to describe both without committing.

Honour, the Feud and Inherited Rage

The feud is not just a backdrop — it is a system that characters are born into. Tybalt does not choose his rage: it is the family’s inheritance, absorbed in childhood. Romeo and Benvolio are pulled into it despite themselves. The Prince tries repeatedly to stop it from outside, but the feud is internal to both families’ identities. For a director, this means the feud should be present even when it is not explicitly being discussed: in the way Capulet servants carry themselves with contempt toward Montague servants, in the way Tybalt’s posture changes the moment he sees a Montague at the feast.

Costume is one way to externalise inherited allegiance. If both families wear clearly differentiated colour families — one cool and controlled, one warm and aggressive, or one in muted earthy tones and one in sharp contrasting solids — the audience reads the feud visually from the opening scene. The tableau of the opening brawl, frozen at the moment of maximum aggression, becomes a visual expression of inherited conflict: bodies in a pattern that has been repeated for generations.

Key Fact

The feud is a system of inherited rage, not a choice. A designer might use colour coding in costume to make the familial divide visible from the opening scene: two distinct palettes, one per family, that the audience can read at a glance throughout the production.

Youth Versus Age: The Gap That Kills

Every adult character in the play gives the young lovers advice they cannot use. The Nurse counsels pragmatic acceptance of Paris. Friar Lawrence counsels patience. Lord Capulet commands obedience. None of them understands that the lovers’ compressed timeline — their certainty, their urgency — makes none of this advice possible. The gap between youth and age is not just generational: it is a gap in temporal experience. Adults understand slow time. The lovers live only in fast time.

A director might physicalise this gap through movement vocabulary. Adult characters — the Friar, the Nurse, Capulet — move at a considered pace, cross the stage with purposeful weight, plant themselves in positions of authority. The young characters — Romeo, Juliet, Mercutio — change direction rapidly, use the full range of the stage, seem perpetually in motion. The levels between adult and young characters might reinforce this: parents and authority figures often occupy elevated positions in the Capulet household, while the lovers are most fully themselves on the same level, face to face.

Students frequently treat Romeo and Juliet as primarily a love story and underemphasise the feud, patriarchal power and the theme of fate. Examiners consistently reward answers that hold multiple themes simultaneously. A complete answer about the play’s intentions might argue that Romeo and Juliet’s love is presented as real and urgent, but that it is destroyed by systems — the feud, the patriarchal household, the misdirected letter — that have nothing to do with love. The tragedy is not that they love too much: it is that everything around them refuses to accommodate love.

For staging, this means a production should not drown the feud scenes in shadow and the love scenes in light, as if one is the “real” play and the other the obstacle. Both must be fully realised: the feud as a vivid, dangerous world, and the love as fragile within it.

The Price Family: Six Characters, Six Truths

At the centre of Things I Know to Be True are six characters whose individual arcs intersect and collide across one year. Bovell constructs each character through a combination of naturalistic characterisation and carefully placed revelation. None of the six is a simple figure. The parents have their own secrets; the children's crises are not resolved neatly. Understanding each character's motivation is essential for answering performer-focused questions and for analysing how Bovell stages the tensions between them.

Bob Price — The Father

Bob is a retired man whose identity is bound up in the rose garden. He is quietly principled and emotionally guarded: a man who loves his family but finds direct emotional expression difficult. On stage, Bob's relationship with the garden anchors his proxemics: when he is in the garden alone, he is at his most settled. When a child intrudes into that space, his physical stillness — a characteristic upright posture, hands engaged with the plants — can shift to a sudden tension in the shoulders, a hesitation before he turns. As a performer playing Bob, you would use a slower pace and lower vocal register to convey his measured, restrained quality, contrasting sharply with the moments when emotion breaks through his composure.

Bob carries a secret that is not fully revealed until winter. A performer must therefore play Bob with a layer of contained guilt or private knowledge beneath the surface of his public manner, without signalling the secret prematurely. This is classic Stanislavskian work: knowing the character's given circumstances in full, even when the audience does not yet know them.

Key Fact

Bob is emotionally guarded and principled, defined by his attachment to the rose garden. A performer must carry the weight of a concealed revelation while sustaining the surface of a loving but reserved father.

Fran Price — The Mother

Fran is a nurse: direct-spoken, pragmatic and tougher than Bob in her immediate emotional responses. She is the domestic authority of the kitchen, and Bovell frequently stages her interactions with the children in that space, where her command is physical and verbal. As a performer, Fran requires a brisk, purposeful quality: a precise, clipped delivery that can suddenly crack when she is confronted with something she is not prepared for. The contrast between her professional competence — a nurse who handles crisis daily — and her shock at her children's revelations is a key dramatic irony that a performer can exploit.

In staging terms, a lighting designer might use a warmer, directed lighting special on Fran in kitchen scenes to reinforce her as the emotional centre of this domestic space, contrasting with the more diffuse exterior quality of the garden lighting.

The Four Children

Each child is given a distinct arc and a contrasting relationship to their parents' expectations. Pip, the eldest, is leaving her marriage and her city; her revelation is about her own agency and the cost of self-determination. Her scenes with Fran carry the deepest confrontation between the women: the mother who stayed and the daughter who is leaving. A performer playing Pip must convey both the guilt of abandonment and the urgency of self-liberation — often simultaneously, in a single scene.

Mark undergoes gender transition and returns as Mia. Bovell treats this arc with careful dramatic attention. The script charts the journey across the summer season, showing how each member of the family responds differently to a transformation they may not have expected. As a performer, the challenge is to play Mark's revelation with specificity: the particular mixture of vulnerability and assertion that comes from speaking a truth about yourself to people whose acceptance matters most. Physically, the movement sequences around this arc can carry a quality of both constraint and release, as Frantic Assembly's contact work is used to express what the dialogue cannot.

Ben, the corporate financier, has been embezzling. His autumn revelation is marked by a different register: the shame of exposure in a family that values hard work and honesty. Ben's scenes with Bob carry the burden of a son seeking his father's judgement. A performer might use a tightly controlled stillness that gradually deteriorates — a tightening of the jaw, a slower and more effortful pace of speech — as the confession progresses.

Rosie, the youngest daughter, returns from Berlin heartbroken. She is the play's narrator-figure: the character who speaks directly to the audience and who appears to hold knowledge the other characters do not. Her performer–audience relationship is more openly mediated than the others'. In staging, Rosie is often placed at upstage centre or slightly apart from the family groupings when she addresses the audience, so that her dual role — participant in the family drama and witness to it — is visible in the blocking.

Examiners reward performers who answer character questions with concrete vocal and physical specificity. For the Mark / Mia arc, a strong answer avoids generalising and instead describes distinct physical and vocal choices for distinct moments. For example: in the scene where Mark speaks to the parents, a performer might use a measured vocal pace with deliberate pauses, a sustained level gaze at each parent in turn rather than looking away, and an open but grounded posture — weight through both feet, hands relaxed — to communicate both the vulnerability of the moment and the assertion of self-knowledge. This is very different from the physicality of Ben's shame-filled confession, which calls for more restricted, self-protective gestures.

The proxemic distance between Mark and each parent at this moment is itself a staging decision: how close does Bob stand? Does Fran move towards her child or remain behind the kitchen counter? These choices communicate the parents' responses before any dialogue is spoken.

Key Fact

The six Price family members each require distinct vocal and physical characterisation. Bovell builds contrast into the family's dynamics: Bob (restrained, guarded), Fran (direct, purposeful), Pip (urgent, guilty), Mark (vulnerable yet assertive), Ben (controlled, deteriorating), Rosie (narrator-witness).

Students sometimes treat Bob and Fran as a single parental bloc — two people who respond identically to their children's revelations. Bovell does not write them that way. They have different emotional registers, different relationships with each child, and, crucially, different secrets. In staging, a director might use the physical geography of the kitchen and garden to reinforce this: Fran rarely enters the garden (her territory is the kitchen), so when she does cross into Bob's space, the proxemics of that crossing signals a shift in the power dynamic between them.

Key Takeaways

  • Each of the six Price family members requires distinct vocal and physical characterisation: Bob is guarded and principled; Fran is direct and purposeful; each child is defined by the nature of their revelation and their relationship to parental expectation.
  • Mark / Mia's arc demands performer specificity at each moment of the journey; examiners reward concrete vocal and physical choices anchored to the specific point in the arc, not generalised sentiment.
  • The kitchen / garden geography gives a director a powerful proxemics language: which characters enter which space, and when, communicates shifts in power and emotional alignment before a word is spoken.

Why Context Matters for Drama Students

Understanding the social, cultural and historical context of a set play is not a separate academic exercise — it directly informs every staging and performance choice. When you know that the Lascar sailors had been settled in East London for generations by 1887, you can make a costume choice that reflects established community rather than recent arrival. When you know that Abdul Karim’s relationship with Victoria was a matter of documented record and court controversy, you can play the hostility of the English court as something felt, not invented. Context is the raw material from which staging decisions are made concrete and justified.

1887: The Golden Jubilee Year

The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee — the fiftieth anniversary of her accession. The Jubilee was a carefully managed spectacle of Imperial prestige: visiting dignitaries from across the Empire, public celebrations in London, military pageants. It was also the moment when Abdul Karim first arrived at Windsor as a young Indian man recruited to serve at the festivities. Gupta uses the Jubilee as a dramatic counterpoint: the public display of Imperial unity set against the private abandonment of women like Rani on the docks below.

For a designer, the Jubilee context opens specific aesthetic possibilities. Victorian royal ceremony had a known visual vocabulary: deep crimson and gold, military uniforms, gauze backdrops suggesting ceremonial grandeur. A director might use this vocabulary deliberately for the Windsor scenes and then undercut it: the same crimson and gold light that glamorises the Jubilee procession might, in a different scene, feel oppressive rather than celebratory when it falls on Abdul rather than on the English court.

Key Fact

1887 was the year of Victoria’s Golden Jubilee and the year Abdul Karim arrived at Windsor. Gupta uses the Jubilee as an ironic framing: the public spectacle of Empire at its height, set against the private abandonment of Rani at Tilbury Docks on the same day.

The British Raj and the Empress of India

Britain had ruled India directly since 1858, after the East India Company’s authority was dissolved following the uprising of 1857. Queen Victoria was formally declared Empress of India in 1876 — a title added at the suggestion of Benjamin Disraeli to make explicit the Imperial relationship. By 1887, India was the jewel of the Empire in official rhetoric: the source of enormous economic value, the proving ground for the British civil service, the largest territory under the Crown.

The practical human consequence of this relationship was a constant flow of Indian people into Britain: domestic servants accompanying colonial families on home leave, sailors recruited for British merchant shipping, traders and students, and eventually political figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji. The Empress stages the human texture of this flow — the real people whose arrival and often stranding in London the official Jubilee narrative had no place for.

The Ayahs and Their Home

The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney was a real institution: a hostel established by Christian missionaries to provide accommodation for Indian women stranded in London when the families they had travelled with could not or would not pay for their return. Gupta has placed the opening of the Ayahs’ Home slightly earlier than its actual documented date for dramatic compression. This is a standard technique in dramatic history: the playwright is not writing a documentary but using real institutions to give her invented characters authentic ground to stand on.

For a set designer, the Ayahs’ Home offers a richly specific environment: a Victorian terrace interior in Hackney, furnished with both English middle-class missionary taste (plain wooden furniture, Christian images) and the Indian domestic objects the women brought with them. The collision of these two aesthetics in the set dressing communicates the cultural in-between world the women inhabit — not fully at home in India because they are in England, not fully belonging to England because they are Indian.

The slight compression of the Ayahs’ Home timeline is a deliberate dramaturgical choice, not a historical error. Examiners expect students to demonstrate this understanding: Gupta is writing dramatic history, which means she shapes and compresses real events to serve the play’s dramatic and thematic needs. The play is not a history textbook and should not be judged as one. What matters is that the Ayahs’ Home was real, ayahs were really stranded in London, and the community that helped them was real — Gupta has brought these true facts onto the stage at the most dramatically compelling moment.

Lascar Sailors and the East London Community

The term “Lascar” referred broadly to Indian and South Asian sailors employed on British merchant ships. By the Victorian era, long-established Lascar communities existed in the dock districts of East London, particularly around Shadwell and the East India Dock. These communities had their own lodging houses, community networks and cultural practices. They were part of the city’s life, yet largely invisible to the official Victorian narrative of London.

As a designer staging the Lascar lodgings, the combination of maritime objects and South Asian domestic culture is the key to the scene’s atmosphere. Set design elements such as coiled rope, sea-chests, canvas and lanterns sit alongside cooking smells suggested by warm amber footlights and the sound of a Bengali folksong — a diegetic soundscape emanating from within the scene rather than externally applied.

Abdul Karim: The Historical Record

The historical Abdul Karim (c. 1863–1909) arrived at Windsor in June 1887. His relationship with Victoria is documented in her own diaries and in the diaries and letters of hostile courtiers. Victoria promoted him from personal attendant to Indian clerk to munshi; she asked to be taught Hindustani; she gave him a house and brought him to Scotland and the south of France on her travels. After her death in 1901, her son and heir Edward VII immediately had Abdul’s papers, diaries and letters burned and expelled him from Britain. The deliberate erasure of his record was itself a statement about whose history was permitted to exist.

Gupta stages this erasure as the play’s closing movement. For a lighting designer, the moment when Abdul’s world at court is systematically dismantled might use a slow fade to black for specific parts of the Windsor set while the rest of the stage remains lit — the physical erasure of his space mirroring the historical destruction of his papers.

Tanika Gupta and the RSC Commission

Tanika Gupta MBE was born in London in 1965 to parents of Bengali heritage. She has written extensively for the stage and television, and her work consistently returns to the experience of South Asian people within British history. The Empress was commissioned by the Royal Shakespeare Company for the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, and premiered there in 2013 under the direction of Emma Rice. An RSC commission is a significant artistic statement: the institution most associated with Shakespeare’s canonical English cultural heritage choosing to stage a play that recovers the Indian presence within the British story. The RSC revival in 2023 at the Lyric Hammersmith, directed by Pooja Ghai, brought the play back into public view with a second major production.

Key Fact

The Empress was commissioned by the RSC and premiered at the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, in 2013, directed by Emma Rice. The RSC’s commissioning choice was itself culturally significant: Gupta’s play brings the Indian presence in British history into the home of canonical British theatre.

Gupta is part of a tradition of Black and Asian British theatre-makers who have used the stage to recover histories excluded from mainstream cultural narrative. Her work shares ground with playwrights such as Winsome Pinnock, Roy Williams and Kwame Kwei-Armah, and with companies including the Tara Theatre and Tamasha, which have developed South Asian British theatre over several decades. Understanding this context helps students see The Empress not only as a history play but as an intervention in the question of whose history gets told on Britain’s major stages. The RSC commission brought that question to the most establishment of venues, with considerable dramaturgical intent.

A Cast Built Around Contrast

Shakespeare constructs the characters of Romeo and Juliet in deliberate pairs and oppositions. Romeo’s romantic idealism is set against Mercutio’s cynicism. Juliet’s clear-eyed decisiveness is set against the Nurse’s earthiness and eventual failure of nerve. Tybalt’s honour-driven rage is set against Benvolio’s peacemaking. These contrasts are not just character notes — they are staging opportunities. When two contrasting characters share the stage, the director must think about proxemics, levels and who controls the focus at each moment of the scene.

Romeo: Intensity and Impulsiveness

Romeo is the play’s most linguistically elaborate character — his verse is dense with antithesis and imagery — but he is also its most impulsive actor. Within hours of meeting Juliet, he proposes marriage. Within hours of Tybalt killing Mercutio, he kills Tybalt. Within minutes of entering the tomb and finding Juliet “dead,” he poisons himself. A performer playing Romeo must hold both qualities simultaneously: the poetry of his interior life and the dangerous speed of his actions.

Vocally, Romeo’s verse demands attention to iambic pentameter as physical impulse rather than recitation. Voice practitioner Cicely Berry argued that Shakespeare’s verse line acts on the body — the stress and weight of each beat pushes the actor through the speech. In Act One, Romeo’s vocal energy might be languid, self-absorbed, meandering in pace. By Act Three, the same voice needs sudden volume, a clipped pace, and the physical stillness of a man who has just done something irreversible.

Key Fact

Romeo is characterised by impulsive action and rich poetic language. A performer must translate both qualities into specific vocal and physical choices: in the early acts, a flowing pace and gestural openness; in Act Three and beyond, staccato delivery, physical tension and stillness.

Juliet: Younger Than You Think

The text states clearly that Juliet is thirteen years old. This is not incidental — it shapes every staging and design decision about her character. Modern productions face a choice: cast an adult performer and acknowledge the dissonance, or use costume, movement and playing style to suggest youth without casting an actual child. Costume might strip away the elaborate dress of a wealthy Capulet daughter and leave something simpler, less adorned. The performer might use a lower centre of gravity in movement, quicker physical reactions, less of the vocal gravitas that comes with age.

Yet Juliet is also the play’s most decisive character. When Romeo hesitates, she drives the marriage plan forward. When the Nurse fails her in Act Three, Juliet makes the potion choice alone. A performer might communicate this tension — a young girl with adult determination — through a contrast of physical openness (arms unguarded, movement quick and forward-leaning) with an increasingly still, controlled vocal delivery in the later acts as she understands the gravity of her situation.

The examiners’ most frequently noted error in questions about Juliet is treating her as an older woman or generalising her age. The text’s “not yet fourteen” is a staging constraint, not a detail to ignore.

As a designer, you might use a high-waisted chemise in white or soft cream cotton rather than heavily structured period gowns — fabric that moves easily and reads as young. By Act Four’s potion scene, a single candle lighting special from directly above, casting Juliet’s face in half-shadow, would communicate the isolation and the stakes of her decision without relying on elaborate set.

As a performer, the vocal shift from the brightness of the balcony scene to the controlled, suppressed fear of the potion soliloquy is where the character’s arc is most visible. The performer might use a lower pitch and reduced volume in the potion scene — speaking as though the words themselves are dangerous — with physical stillness that breaks only at the moment of drinking.

Mercutio, Tybalt and the World of the Feud

Mercutio is not a Montague or a Capulet — he belongs to neither family, which makes his death the clearest demonstration that the feud destroys bystanders. He is the play’s most physically energetic character: mercurial in the sense of quicksilver movement, rapid wit, an inability to stay still. A performer playing Mercutio might use the stage’s full depth and width, occupying upstage and downstage positions with equal ease, drawing focus through movement rather than stillness. His Queen Mab speech might be delivered at increasing pace until it becomes a kind of controlled hysteria — and the snap from that fantasy to pragmatic contempt when Romeo interrupts him is a moment of physical and vocal reanchoring.

Tybalt, by contrast, is all contained aggression. His posture might be upright, military, with controlled gestures — nothing wasted, nothing playful. The contrast between Mercutio’s fluid energy and Tybalt’s rigid control makes the fight between them a collision of two radically different physical languages. A choreographer designing the duel might use Mercutio’s loose, improvisational movement style against Tybalt’s precise, formal swordsmanship to communicate that these two men are fighting according to entirely different codes.

Key Fact

Mercutio is the play’s most physically energetic non-Montague non-Capulet character. Tybalt is defined by rigid, honour-driven physicality. The contrast between their performance styles in the duel communicates the clash of two incompatible codes: improvised wit versus formal aggression.

The Nurse and Friar Lawrence: Adult Guides Who Fail

The Nurse and Friar Lawrence are the play’s surrogate adults — closer to the lovers than their actual parents, and therefore more culpable when things go wrong. The Nurse uses both prose and verse. Prose often suits her comic, conversational exchanges, while her verse in the discovery scene can sharpen the force of her grief. A performer can use these shifts in form as one clue to changes in pace and emotional pressure.

Friar Lawrence’s costume is a significant design choice. The Franciscan brown habit carries authority in a Renaissance Veronese context; it might also carry a certain theatrical gravity that makes the potion plan seem credible when it is clearly reckless. A designer might consider how the habit’s bulk and covering quality communicate his function: a figure who operates in the shadows between the two families, whose anonymity is his cover. The performer-audience configuration matters here: in a theatre-in-the-round arrangement, Friar Lawrence can never fully hide — every angle of his scheming is visible.

Lord Capulet is a character who shifts register dramatically within the play. In Act One he is magnanimous, playing the generous host. By Act Three, Scene Five — when Juliet refuses to marry Paris — he becomes threatening and physically imposing. The staging of this scene is one of the play’s most significant performer challenges: the question of where Capulet stands relative to Juliet, whether he physically advances toward her, and how Lady Capulet and the Nurse position themselves (complicit, or retreating) defines the power dynamics of the Capulet household.

As a lighting designer, a shift from the warm domestic lighting wash of the bedroom to a harsher, more directional state as Capulet’s rage escalates would signal the domestic space becoming a place of threat. The designer might add a top-light on Capulet alone, leaving Juliet in softer, lower light, using the lighting geography to externalise their power relationship.

From Feeling to Technique

When a performer moves an audience to tears, the temptation is to write “they were convincingly upset.” That sentence earns no marks. The exam rewards you for explaining how the performer created that effect: the precise vocal and physical skills they deployed and the meaning those skills communicated at that specific moment.

Vocal skills and physical skills are the two categories the spec identifies. Top-mark answers always name at least one from each category, anchor them to a specific moment in the production, and explain the effect on the audience.

Key Fact

Vocal skills include: pitch, pace, pause, volume, accent, intonation, phrasing, projection and timing. Physical skills include: posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness, gait, spatial awareness and interaction with other performers.

Vocal Skills: The Language of Voice

Each vocal skill can be used to create a specific effect. Knowing which skill creates which effect is the key to strong analytical writing. Consider these:

  • Pitch: a sudden rise in pitch signals panic or excitement; a drop to the low register can convey threat, grief or resignation. The contrast between the two within a single speech is itself a technique — it shows the character’s instability.
  • Pace: rapid delivery can signal urgency or desperation; a deliberate, unhurried pace can communicate authority, menace or exhaustion. A performer who slows dramatically at the climax of a speech draws the audience in.
  • Pause: a well-placed silence is one of the most powerful tools a performer has. A three-second pause before a character’s answer can communicate internal conflict more precisely than any amount of text. Think of it as a word the playwright left blank for the performer to fill.
  • Volume: a performer who drops from normal conversational volume to near-inaudible draws the audience physically forward in their seats; a sudden shout after sustained quiet is a physical shock. Both are intentional choices.
  • Intonation and phrasing: the rising or falling melody of a sentence, and where the performer chooses to breathe and break their line, controls where the audience focuses its attention.

Physical Skills: The Language of the Body

Tableau and stillness are often more powerful than movement. When a performer freezes in the middle of chaotic action, every audience member looks at them immediately. That is focus achieved through physical discipline, not scenery.

Other physical skills to analyse include:

  • Posture: an upright, expansive posture reads as power or confidence across the room; a collapsed, inward posture reads as vulnerability or defeat. If the posture shifts within a scene, the character’s status has shifted — note exactly when it changes.
  • Gesture: gestures can be open (arms extended, palms up — invitation) or closed (arms crossed, hands pulled in — self-protection). A single raised hand can silence a stage; a pointing finger can be an accusation. Analyse the gesture, not just its name.
  • Facial expression: the micro-expressions that pass across a performer’s face in a close-focus moment are often what an audience remembers most vividly. If the performer’s expression contradicted the character’s words — a smile that didn’t reach the eyes, a flash of doubt suppressed — that subtext is gold for analysis.
  • Movement and gait: how a character crosses the stage communicates as much as what they say. A heavy, deliberate walk implies weight (emotional or literal); a light, darting movement implies anxiety or calculation.

Imagine you saw a fictional touring production of a kitchen-sink drama in 2024. In the climactic argument scene, the lead performer playing the mother confronted the adult son. Here is how you might write about that moment:

Weak version (no marks at this level): “The actress playing the mother was very emotional and you could tell she was upset. She looked like she was going to cry.”

Strong version: “In the moment when the mother finally confronted her son, the performer dropped her vocal pace to almost half its previous rate and allowed a three-beat pause after each sentence, as though each word cost her something.
