Simultaneously, her physical posture collapsed inward — shoulders drawn forward, spine curved, eyes cast downward rather than meeting his — so that despite her status as parent, she visually occupied less stage space than her adult son. This juxtaposition — a parent whose voice is measured and powerful but whose body has surrendered — communicated the complexity of her grief: she was both holding herself together and falling apart simultaneously. The audience became very still at this moment, which suggested the choice was communicating its intended meaning effectively.”

Notice: one vocal skill (pace and pause), one physical skill (posture and use of stage space), a specific moment, a named effect on the audience, and an evaluative judgement. That is the formula for a top-band paragraph.

Interaction and Ensemble

In your review, do not only write about individual performers in isolation. Ensemble moments — where the company moves, speaks or responds as a single unit — are often the most theatrically powerful. When an ensemble suddenly splits apart, or when all performers simultaneously turn to face the audience, the effect is difficult to achieve and, when it works, is deeply affecting.

Analyse the interaction between two performers as you would a single performer: what did the proxemics between them tell you? Did one performer physically diminish themselves to elevate the other? Did a brief moment of eye contact or its conspicuous absence change the mood of the scene?

A persistent error is to describe the character’s inner state rather than the performer’s external technique. Phrases like “she was angry,” “he seemed afraid” and “you could feel her sadness” describe emotions, not skills. They tell the examiner nothing about how the performer communicated the emotion.

The fix is simple: ask yourself, “what did the performer actually do with their voice or body?” Then describe that. “She was angry” becomes “her volume escalated across the scene until by the final line she was projecting at full strength from upstage right, her jaw tense and her hands forming fists at her sides.” That is performer technique, not emotional description.

Key Fact

Every time you write about a performer, you need both a vocal AND a physical choice. One alone is not enough for an 8-mark or 32-mark answer. Train yourself to pair them: “vocally she… / physically she…”

A Novel Becomes a Race Against the Clock

Jules Verne published his adventure novel in 1872, at a moment when two technologies had just made circumnavigation in eighty days theoretically possible: the Suez Canal opened in 1869 and the American transcontinental railroad was completed in the same year. Verne imagined a precise English gentleman betting £20,000 at his gentlemen's club that he could complete the journey — and the result is a breathless chase spanning India, Hong Kong, Japan, San Francisco and the Atlantic. Laura Eason's adaptation, first performed at Lookingglass Theater in Chicago in 2008 and staged at the New Vic in 2013, distils this chase into something even tighter: eight actors playing every role in the story, from Phileas Fogg himself to train conductors, customs officials, ship’s captains and a herd of elephants. Understanding the episodic structure of this adaptation is the starting point for all the staging and performance work that follows.

Key Fact

Eason’s adaptation was first performed at Lookingglass Theater in Chicago in 2008. Theresa Heskins directed the 2013 New Vic production, staged in the round with eight actors multi-roling throughout.

Episodic Structure and the Chase Narrative

Where a linear play builds one continuous action through rising and falling tension, episodic structure links a series of self-contained scenes whose energy comes from momentum — the audience is always aware of time ticking down and distance to be crossed. Eason borrows this structure directly from Verne, who organised his novel as a series of geographical episodes: London, Paris, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, Liverpool, London again. Each episode introduces new obstacles, new minor characters, and new opportunities for the eight-actor ensemble to transform themselves and the stage space. The play opens at the Reform Club opening, establishing Fogg’s precision and the terms of the wager, and closes in London with the apparent failure and then the extraordinary reveal of the international date line.

From a staging perspective, episodic structure creates specific demands. Each scene transition must be rapid — a shift of a chair, a change of costume accessory, a change of accent — and the performers and director must find ways to signal clearly to the audience that we have moved from one continent to another without slowing the pace. A director working on this play in an in-the-round space, as the original production did, must ensure that sightlines allow every audience member to see the key physical images from every angle: a tableau of the Reform Club, the arc of an elephant crossing the stage, the moment a train accelerates through the ensemble’s bodies.

A linear play (like The Crucible) builds one sustained dramatic question — will Proctor confess? — through escalating pressure in a single community. In contrast, Around the World in 80 Days has a fresh dramatic question in every new location: will Fogg catch the next departure? Will Fix succeed in detaining him? Will Passepartout survive his mishap in the Hong Kong opium-house scene? This episodic rhythm suits physical-theatre companies because each episode is essentially a self-contained performance problem: how do eight actors turn themselves into an Indian marketplace, a Japanese acrobat troupe, or a Native American war party on the transcontinental railway? The episodic form invites creativity in every transition rather than demanding sustained psychological realism in one fixed setting.

A common misconception students should avoid: episodic does not mean “random”. Every episode advances Fogg’s race against the clock, reveals character under pressure, and raises the comic and dramatic stakes. The structure is tight — the countdown creates tension across every episode, even when individual scenes are played for comedy.

Multi-Roling and the Ensemble as Engine

Multi-roling is not simply an economic decision in this play — it is the central theatrical pleasure. Eight performers play dozens of parts. One actor might be a Reform Club gentleman in the opening scene, a Suez customs officer ten minutes later, a Bombay merchant shortly after, and then a ship’s engineer in the Atlantic crossing. The audience’s delight comes partly from recognising the transformation and partly from the skill of the performer who makes each figure feel utterly distinct. For a student writing as a performer, this means that every minor character must be performed with precision: a distinct posture, a specific walk, a clear change of vocal pitch, pace or accent to mark the transition.

The eight-actor ensemble also creates the physical world of the play. Bodies become a steam engine (performers in a line, arms pumping in unison, voices creating a mechanical rhythm), an elephant (one actor as the body, others as legs, the whole image emerging from choreographed physical trust), or the heaving Atlantic (performers shifting weight in synchrony, creating a wave motion across the stage). This use of bodies-as-objects and object transformation is characteristic of companies like Complicite and Frantic Assembly, whose physical-theatre practice underpins Eason’s script.

Key Fact

The ensemble uses physical theatre to transform performers’ bodies into the world of the play — steam engines, ships, elephants, storms and crowds — making multi-roling and object transformation central staging methods rather than incidental features.

A significant student error is to treat this play as a costume drama requiring a literal, naturalistic set — a train carriage for the India scenes, a ship’s deck for the Atlantic, an Indian temple for the rescue of Aouda. In fact the play’s entire aesthetic is built on the idea that the imagination of performers and audience, not scenery, creates the world. A director who specifies a realistic Victorian set is misreading the form. Stylised staging is not a compromise here — it is the artistic intention. Chairs become railway carriages; rope becomes rigging; the ensemble’s coordinated movement becomes the ocean. Examiners reward students who understand this and who can describe how specific design choices support the transformation rather than substitute for it.

Narrated Transitions and Direct Address

Eason also employs a narration device: performers step out of the dramatic fiction to address the audience directly, setting the location, updating the countdown, and commenting on Fogg’s progress. This direct address functions similarly to Brecht’s use of a narrator in epic theatre — it frames the action, prevents the audience from losing themselves in pure empathy, and invites them to watch the storytelling as storytelling. From a design perspective, lighting transitions between dramatic scenes and narrator moments can be achieved with a sharp change of lighting state: for example, a warm, busy wash during action scenes and a tight top-light or single profile lantern on the narrator to isolate them from the rest of the stage, signalling to the audience that we have stepped outside the story.

Why Context Shapes Every Design Choice

Context is not a separate topic you bolt onto an answer about A Taste of Honey — it is the reason every staging decision means something. When a set designer chooses a damp-stained back wall, they are referencing the actual housing conditions of post-war Salford. When a director casts the jazz musicians prominently on stage, they are invoking Joan Littlewood’s Theatre Workshop practice. Understanding the contexts — social, theatrical and biographical — that surrounded the 1958 premiere is essential to understanding why the play looks and sounds the way it does, and what any 21st-century production is in conversation with.

Salford 1958: Social and Economic Reality

Salford in the late 1950s was a distinct industrial city — not, as students sometimes write, part of Manchester. It had its own economy, its own dialect, its own social geography of mills, dockyards and terraced streets. Post-war Britain was a country still managing the aftermath of the Second World War: rationing had only ended in 1954, the welfare state was newly built but unevenly experienced, and for working-class communities in the industrial north, austerity remained a daily reality. The kitchen-sink drama movement was a direct response to this: a generation of writers insisting that the ordinary lives of people like Helen and Jo deserved to be on stage.

For a designer, the social context of 1958 Salford informs every material choice. A costume designer researching the period would find: working women in second-hand utility fashion, coats worn long past their best, aspirational details (a fake pearl earring, a bright headscarf) signalling the gap between the life a woman wanted and the one she could afford. A sound designer might use diegetic sounds from off-stage — the ship’s horn, the fairground’s distant music, the trams — to locate the play in its physical world without changing the single-set staging. A diegetic sound design of 1950s Salford industrial noise keeps the world of poverty present even when the flat feels briefly warm.

Key Fact

Salford is a separate city from Manchester with its own distinct industrial identity. This matters for the play because Delaney’s voice is specifically Salford — the dialect, the geography, the particular kind of working-class pride and poverty she depicts. A director who conflates Salford with a generic “northern city” loses the specific social texture Delaney is working with.

Theatre Workshop and Joan Littlewood

Theatre Workshop was the company Joan Littlewood had built at Theatre Royal Stratford East in East London. Its methods were deeply influenced by Bertolt Brecht: collective creation, rehearsal as research and play, physical and vocal precision, and a commitment to staging work that spoke to and about working-class audiences rather than the West End establishment. When Shelagh Delaney sent her script to Littlewood — having written it at 19 — Theatre Workshop did not simply produce it: they workshopped it, devised elements of it, and added the live jazz musicians that are now inseparable from the play’s identity.

For a student answering questions about the play’s form, this matters because some of the play’s most distinctive features are Theatre Workshop’s additions, not Delaney’s original intentions. The live music, the direct address, the tonal swings between comedy and pathos — these are products of a devised ensemble practice as much as a single writer’s vision. An examiner will reward a student who can discuss the collaborative origin of the play’s form.

Theatre Workshop was explicitly influenced by Bertolt Brecht’s epic theatre, in which the audience is prevented from fully losing themselves in the story and encouraged to think critically about what they are watching. The live jazz musicians in A Taste of Honey function as a Brechtian device: they sit on stage visibly, they comment on the action, and they remind the audience that this is a constructed performance rather than a slice of real life. The moments of direct address to the audience — when characters speak out of the fiction and acknowledge the watchers — work in the same way.

A 21st-century director staging the play might reinforce this Brechtian quality through design. A theatre in the round configuration would make the musicians’ presence even more exposed and commenting. A minimalist set — a few pieces of furniture rather than a fully rendered flat — would prevent the audience from the complete illusion of naturalism, keeping them slightly at a Brechtian distance. Both choices would honour the Theatre Workshop aesthetic while making it speak to a contemporary audience.

Shelagh Delaney: The Teenage Outsider

Shelagh Delaney was born in Salford in 1938 and left school at seventeen. She wrote A Taste of Honey at nineteen, reportedly after seeing a play she felt patronised working-class women. The script was not the polished product of a drama school education — it was written quickly, from inside the world it describes. This gives it a quality that critics noticed immediately: a freshness of voice, a refusal of sentimentality about poverty, and a lack of the middle-class mediation that characterised most plays about working-class life at the time.

Delaney’s outsider status — young, female, northern, working-class — is also the play’s subject. The play premiered on 27 May 1958 to reviews that were frequently condescending about Delaney’s age and background even as they recognised the play’s power. The Lord Chamberlain’s office required edits to the script before performance — a system of pre-censorship that remained in place until 1968. Despite this, the play reached the stage substantially intact.

Key Fact

Shelagh Delaney was 19 when she wrote A Taste of Honey. It premiered on 27 May 1958 at Theatre Royal Stratford East, directed by Joan Littlewood. These biographical and production facts are frequently tested in context questions.

The kitchen-sink movement is sometimes described as the “Angry Young Men” generation, named after John Osborne’s 1956 play Look Back in Anger. But A Taste of Honey complicates this framing: its central characters are women, its anger is quieter and more structural, and its playwright was a teenager from Salford rather than a product of the English literary establishment. Delaney’s play broadened the kitchen-sink canon in ways that are historically significant — it was one of the first mainstream British plays to centre a working-class girl’s experience, an interracial relationship and a sympathetically drawn queer character simultaneously. A student who can discuss what A Taste of Honey adds to — and where it diverges from — the kitchen-sink tradition will produce more nuanced context answers than one who simply calls it “a kitchen-sink play.”

A Hybrid Form

Things I Know to Be True is one of very few GCSE set plays that is genuinely hybrid in its theatrical form: it was written to be performed using two distinct and historically separate performance traditions in the same production. The naturalistic family scenes draw on Stanislavskian acting principles. The movement sequences were developed in collaboration with Frantic Assembly and draw on physical theatre practice. Understanding both traditions and — crucially — how they interact in this play is the foundation of the practitioner-application question for this unit.

This is not a case of two traditions accidentally colliding. Bovell wrote the play specifically with Scott Graham of Frantic Assembly as a creative partner; the movement sequences are not added after the fact but are built into the dramatic structure. The result is a form where the transitions between registers — from dialogue to movement, from naturalism to physical abstraction — carry meaning in themselves. Understanding when and why those transitions happen is as important as understanding each tradition in isolation.

Key Fact

Things I Know to Be True uses two traditions deliberately: Stanislavskian emotional truth for the naturalistic dialogue scenes, and Frantic Assembly physical theatre for the movement sequences. Both are structural, not decorative. A student who treats the movement as ‘extra’ misses half the play’s theatrical language.

Stanislavski and the Price Family

Konstantin Stanislavski (1863–1938) developed a systematic approach to actor training that changed the way realistic drama is performed. His central insight was that truthful acting comes from the actor understanding the character’s inner life: their history, desires, relationships, and the specific circumstances of the scene. He called this the given circumstances. For a performer playing any member of the Price family, the given circumstances are richly specified by Bovell: each character’s profession, their history with each other, the year they are having, the specific weight they carry into each scene.

Stanislavski also asked actors to pursue an objective in every scene — a specific, playable goal that the character is trying to achieve. For Bob in the garden scenes, his objective might be simply “to keep this world intact” — to maintain the order and beauty of the space as a counterweight to the disorder his children keep introducing. For Fran in the kitchen confrontations, her objective might be “to make my child tell me the truth” or “to protect this family from what is coming.” When a performer anchors their choices to a clear objective, every physical and vocal decision becomes purposeful: it is always in the service of getting what the character wants.

For the performer playing Mark, whose arc moves towards his identity as Mia, Stanislavski’s given circumstances are particularly important. The examiner rewards sensitive, specific choices that are grounded in who this character is in relation to this family. The given circumstances include: Mark’s relationship with his parents (the particular emotional dynamic of each parent); his sense of what the revelation will mean for the family; the specific setting (the kitchen or the garden, indoors or out, the season); and the circumstances that immediately precede the scene. A Stanislavskian performer does not play a generalised “coming out scene” — they play this character, in this moment, with these specific people. The choices that come from that specificity are always more compelling, and more mark-worthy, than the generic ones.

Frantic Assembly: Physical Theatre as Emotional Language

Frantic Assembly was founded in 1994 by Scott Graham, Steven Hoggett and Vicki Middleton. The company’s physical theatre practice is distinctive in that it is not primarily dance: it grows from everyday movement — the physicality of ordinary people — and heightens it into something expressive. Their key techniques include round-by-through-under sequences, contact lifts, and chair duets. Scott Graham was the co-director of the original production with Geordie Brookman, contributing movement direction specifically shaped around the Price family’s emotional dynamics.

What makes Frantic Assembly’s approach relevant to Things I Know to Be True specifically is their philosophical starting point: movement should communicate what words cannot. In the context of this play, this translates directly to the moments of greatest emotional intensity. When Bob and a child cannot speak to each other directly about what is happening, Bovell gives them a movement sequence instead. The sequence does not illustrate the conversation; it replaces it with something more honest. A chair duet between Bob and Rosie, for instance, might communicate across several minutes of movement everything that a two-page conversation between them could not.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly’s key techniques in this play: chair duets (two performers using chairs as contact-improvisation props, expressing relationship through shared weight and negotiated movement); lifts (one performer carrying or lifting another, expressing both protection and the effort of love); and round-by-through-under sequences (continuous, flowing movement through each other’s bodies, suggesting emotional entanglement). None of these are decorative; all are structurally placed to replace dialogue at the point where dialogue fails.

The Moment of Transition: Moving Between Registers

The most interesting theatrical moments in Things I Know to Be True are the transitions: the point where naturalistic dialogue ends and a movement sequence begins, or where a movement sequence dissolves back into dialogue. How does a company signal to the audience that the register is changing? And how does a designer support those transitions?

In production, these transitions are typically managed through a combination of sound, lighting and the performers’ own physical approach to stillness. The dialogue scene reaches its emotional peak — a phrase, a silence, a look — and then the movement begins, often initiated by a single performer before the others join. A sound designer might cue a shift in the soundscape: the domestic acoustic of the kitchen falls away and a non-diegetic, texturally abstract underscore takes its place. A lighting designer might allow the lighting state to shift slightly: the movement sequences often benefit from a reduction in overall intensity, with one or two moving lights following the performers, so that the space feels different — more interior, more subjective — than it does during the dialogue scenes. When the movement ends and dialogue resumes, the lighting returns, the soundscape resolves, and the audience is brought back to the domestic world they were in before.

Stanislavski’s system asks: what does this character want? What are their given circumstances? How does their past shape this moment? It starts from the inside — from the character’s inner life — and works outward to the physical expression of that inner life. The result, when it works, is a performance that appears effortlessly truthful: the words and the body seem to arise from the same source.

Frantic Assembly’s approach asks: what does this body do? How do two bodies relate to each other in space? What does shared weight communicate that words cannot? It starts from the outside — from physical contact and spatial relationship — and works inward. The performers are not asked to “feel something and show it”; they are asked to execute a precise physical task, and the feeling arises from the task. This is in some ways the inverse of Stanislavski’s method, yet in Things I Know to Be True the two approaches are placed alongside each other in the same production and the same family, and they reinforce rather than contradict each other. The Stanislavskian given circumstances of the Price family give the Frantic Assembly movement sequences their specific emotional charge; the movement sequences, in turn, reveal the subterranean emotional life that Stanislavskian truth keeps below the surface of the dialogue.

A Play That Speaks to Its Audience

One of the most striking features of A Taste of Honey is that it refuses to stay locked behind an invisible wall. From the opening moments, characters turn outwards and acknowledge the audience directly. This technique, known as direct address, signals immediately that the play will not simply present a slice of Salford life and let the audience watch from a comfortable distance. Instead, it invites them in — as witnesses, as confidants, sometimes as a kind of jury judging the characters’ choices.

This blending of naturalistic domestic drama with outward-facing presentational moments is central to what makes the play theatrically distinctive. The fourth wall — the imaginary invisible barrier between performers and audience in a conventional proscenium arch production — is repeatedly breached. In staging terms, a director must decide how and when to lean into these moments: does a performer step downstage to address the front rows? Do they freeze mid-scene while one character speaks out? The blocking choices around direct address shape how complicit the audience feels in what they witness.

Key Fact

Direct address breaks the fourth wall and invites the audience into the characters’ world. In A Taste of Honey, it allows Jo and Helen to share their inner thoughts with the audience even when they cannot or will not share them with each other — creating dramatic irony and emotional intimacy simultaneously.

The Jazz Musicians: Brecht on the Salford Stage

The most audacious theatrical element in the original 1958 production was not scripted by Shelagh Delaney at all: it was Joan Littlewood and Theatre Workshop who placed live jazz musicians on stage, visible to the audience throughout. This device draws directly on the thinking of epic theatre. When a jazz trio sits at the edge of the stage in full view, playing between scenes and sometimes underscoring the action, the audience is reminded that they are watching a performance — not peeping through a keyhole at a real family. This is a deliberate alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt).

For a sound designer working on a contemporary revival, this tradition opens rich decisions. The jazz score is not merely decoration. A muted trumpet playing a slow, bluesy phrase as Helen sweeps out in Peter’s car can comment ironically on her exit — undercutting her cheerfulness with the hint of loss she refuses to acknowledge. Alternatively, a brighter, faster tune in a major key can heighten the play’s moments of unexpected comedy. The musicians can be used as a soundscape — a tram bell, a foghorn, the distant Salford industrial hum — building the world just beyond the flat’s walls without any elaborate set.

A common student error is to describe the jazz as “background music to set the mood.” Examiners reward much more specific answers. The music’s function shifts throughout the play — from ironic commentary to emotional underscore to diegetic sound (music that exists in the world of the play, heard by the characters). A strong answer names the instrument (trumpet, double bass, piano), the quality of the playing (muted, up-tempo, staccato), whether it is live or recorded, and the specific effect on the audience at that moment. “Sad jazz” is generic; “a muted trumpet playing a falling phrase as Geof leaves” is specific. The distinction between diegetic sound and non-diegetic underscore is worth knowing and applying.

Tonal Swings: Comedy That Hurts

One of Delaney’s most powerful dramatic methods is her ability to pivot between comedy and pain within the same exchange. A sharp piece of banter between Jo and Helen can shift, within seconds, into something that reveals genuine wound or grief. This tonal instability is not accidental — it mirrors the precariousness of these characters’ lives. The comedy protects them: it is the armour both Jo and Helen wear against vulnerability.

For a performer, these tonal swings require precise timing and a strong sense of sub-text. Jo’s wit is not delivered from a place of security; it comes from a teenager who has learned that laughter keeps her mother engaged and keeps pain at arm’s length. A performer playing Jo might choose to let the laugh die just a fraction too quickly in certain scenes, giving the audience a glimpse of what lies beneath before the next quip arrives. The pace of delivery — quick, clipped Salford vowels, a slight catch on a word that matters — can do extraordinary work.

Key Fact

The play’s tonal swings between comedy and pain are a deliberate dramatic method, not just local colour. They reflect the characters’ use of humour as a defence mechanism and keep the audience off-balance — laughing one moment, unsettled the next. This makes the emotional blows land harder when they come.

Staging the Hybrid Form

Directors and designers approaching a revival face a central question: how naturalistic should the staging be? A fully naturalistic set — peeling wallpaper, a real gas ring, period kitchen furniture — signals to the audience that this is a slice-of-life play. But if the jazz musicians sit in full view on a thrust or end-on stage, or if characters step forward into a spotlight for direct address, the production announces its hybrid character: it is both kitchen-sink realism and Brechtian theatre event.

Lighting can reinforce or counterpoint these shifts. For the naturalistic scenes inside the flat, a warm, slightly dim lighting wash from above and the sides might evoke the bare-bulb gloom of the flat. But when Jo breaks the fourth wall and speaks directly to the audience, a single forward-facing lighting special can separate her from the domestic scene behind her — placing her momentarily outside the story, in direct communion with the auditorium.

A director staging A Taste of Honey must decide how openly they will signal the play’s Brechtian elements. One option is to commit fully to kitchen-sink naturalism everywhere except in the jazz interludes — making the musicians feel almost intrusive, jarring the audience out of a domestic reverie. Another option is to stylise the staging throughout: sparse set, visible lighting rig, musicians integrated as a constant presence rather than a surprise. Both choices are defensible, but a student explaining their directorial intention should name which approach they are choosing and justify why it serves the play’s themes of performance, mask, and honesty.

In costume, the contrast between Helen’s fur coat (aspirational, borrowed glamour) and Jo’s more functional dress already carries the play’s class tensions without a word being spoken. A designer choosing 1950s period costume signals historical context immediately to the audience. Alternatively, a director choosing to update the setting — keeping the emotional dynamics but placing the characters in a contemporary context — would need to find equivalent costume signals for the same tensions. The choice of period is itself an interpretive decision, not a given.

The Performer’s Task in The Crucible

Every performer in The Crucible faces the same fundamental challenge: Miller’s characters are under enormous pressure and yet must speak in a controlled, formal idiom that resists direct emotional expression. The drama lives in the gap between what the characters feel and what the language permits them to say. A performer’s job is not to “be” the emotion but to make that gap visible — through vocal restraint, through physical containment that hints at what is held back, through the choice of where and how to move. This is what separates a drama answer from a literary one: you must translate the interior life into concrete, observable choices that an audience can read across a theatre.

The exam rewards specificity. Saying “I would play Proctor angrily” earns almost nothing. Saying “at the moment Proctor demands the court hear Mary Warren’s recantation, I would stand downstage centre, spine straight, feet planted wide apart, weight evenly distributed — a stillness that communicates controlled fury more powerfully than movement would” demonstrates that you understand how performance communicates meaning.

Playing John Proctor: Controlled Force and Moral Weight

Proctor is a physically large man in his mid-thirties — Miller’s stage directions emphasise his power — but the play consistently asks him to contain that power rather than release it. In the linen scene with Elizabeth, a performer might play the opening with deliberate physical neutrality: slow, deliberate movements as Proctor tastes the stew; a slight pause before he comments on the seasoning; a careful proxemics that keeps him on the opposite side of the central table from Elizabeth, the furniture a physical sign of the emotional distance between them. The vocal tone might be low and measured — a pitch that is artificially flattened to avoid the argument both characters are circling.

In the courtroom scene in Act 3, the physical vocabulary shifts. As Proctor presents Mary Warren’s deposition to Danforth, the performer might use advancing movement — stepping forward and upstage towards where Danforth sits at the raised table — each step communicating increasing urgency. The voice might rise in pitch and pace as Proctor’s composure begins to crack, before the confession of adultery drops the voice suddenly to a flat, almost mechanical delivery: the sound of a man dismantling himself in public. Then silence — a full three-count pause — before the next word.

Key Fact

For Proctor, the most powerful choice is often stillness, not movement. A performer who understands that tableau — a completely still pose — focuses audience attention more powerfully than restless movement will reach the Mastering band. Know when your character stops moving and why.

Playing Abigail Williams: Performance Within Performance

Abigail is the most challenging performance role in the play because she is always performing — even when she appears most sincere. In the courtroom scene, her “possession” is not supernatural affliction but theatre: she is directing the other girls, managing an audience and controlling a narrative. A performer playing Abigail must therefore build two layers of performance simultaneously — the public display of distress and, visible underneath it to the audience if not to the court, the calculation that drives every gesture.

For the moment when Abigail turns the courtroom against Mary Warren, a performer might place Abigail at upstage right, controlling the sightlines of the other girls. Her physical choices could include a slow turn to face Mary Warren, a long held gaze before the voice drops to a flat, controlled tone — the stillness of a predator rather than the trembling of a victim. Then, when she launches the full performance of possession, the contrast in vocal pitch and physical energy is maximised: the calculated stillness makes the apparent explosion feel more threatening rather than more sincere.

As a performer, here is a concrete sequence for the moment Abigail redirects the courtroom’s attention from Proctor to Mary Warren. Abigail is upstage right, initially appearing absorbed in her own distress. As Proctor’s challenge to her credibility becomes clear, she turns her head slowly towards Mary Warren — a slow rotation of the head only, body remaining still, communicating the deliberate, unhurried quality of someone who knows exactly what she is about to do.

Her voice drops: low pitch, slow pace, a long pause before the first word she addresses to Mary. The other girls begin to echo her movements — Abigail controls them through a slight tilt of her chin towards them, a near-invisible gestus of leadership. Then, as the girls begin their chorus of mimicry, Abigail’s own physical performance escalates: raised arms, gaze directed upwards and away, a trembling that increases in frequency but never loses its internal control. The effect is of a performance that only the audience can see as performance — and the dramatic irony makes it devastating.

Playing Elizabeth Proctor: Restraint as Resistance

Elizabeth Proctor is often misread as cold or passive. In fact, her restraint is a form of moral courage: she inhabits a society where a woman’s testimony has almost no power, and yet she holds herself upright, controls every word, and maintains an emotional dignity that the play presents as heroic. A performer playing Elizabeth should understand that her silence and stillness carry at least as much dramatic weight as Proctor’s outbursts.

In the moment when Elizabeth is brought to court and asked about her husband’s relationship with Abigail, a performer might place her centre stage, physically isolated — no furniture near her, no other figure close enough to offer support — in a levels arrangement where every court figure is above her. Her vocal delivery might be quiet and controlled, with only the slightest catch before she speaks the lie: a single brief pause, a downward look, then the answer delivered without eye contact. The audience, knowing the truth, experiences the full weight of what she is sacrificing to protect John.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s lie is delivered with physical and vocal restraint, not with melodrama — and that restraint is what makes it heartbreaking. A performer who shows the audience the cost of self-control (the single pause, the downward gaze, the slight flattening of the voice) will communicate more than one who plays the moment too big. Examiners reward this kind of physical specificity.

The most common error in 8-mark performer questions is naming an emotional state rather than translating it into physical and vocal specifics. “I would play Proctor angrily to show his frustration” is an Emerging-band answer. It describes the feeling but not the performance.

A Mastering-band answer translates that feeling: “At the moment Proctor challenges Danforth’s decision to proceed, I would stand with my weight forward on my front foot, hands pressed flat on the court table, invading the judge’s personal space from below. My voice would be at a lower pitch than natural — a deliberate suppression of the emotional register, which communicates that Proctor is choosing to control himself even at the edge of losing control. The effect on the audience is that they can feel the effort of the restraint, which is more frightening than an outburst would be.”

Two Worlds on One Stage

The design challenge of The Great Wave is fundamental: how do you put Japan and North Korea on the same stage without either location feeling vague? Turnly’s play demands a design language that can differentiate between two politically and emotionally distinct worlds, often within the same scene transition. The solution most productions reach for is not naturalistic scene-painting but a split staging strategy: a stage divided so that the Japanese household and the North Korean compound can each claim a permanent location, with lighting doing the work of telling the audience where they are.

For a staging configuration, an end-on or thrust stage both offer advantages for this play. A thrust configuration brings the audience close to both worlds simultaneously, collapsing any comfortable distance between spectator and the injustice they are watching — a Brechtian effect even in a predominantly naturalistic production.

Key Fact

The two locations demand contrasting design vocabularies: Japan evokes domestic warmth and coastal openness — natural light, timber, the blue-grey of the sea. North Korea evokes state control — flat, harsh overhead light, institutional walls, the absence of the natural world. Every design choice should be readable as belonging to one or the other.

Lighting Design: From Coastal Softness to State Searchlight

The Japan scenes can be lit with a warm amber-tinted lighting wash that evokes domestic interior light and coastal afternoon. For the North Korean compound, the design logic shifts entirely. A harsh overhead rig — profile lanterns angled steeply downward, producing sharp shadows — communicates institutional control without a single piece of dialogue. Hanako is surveilled; the light does not flatter or warm, it locates and exposes.

The “searchlight” image referred to in the play’s design history extends this logic: a tight lighting special that picks out a performer centre stage, surrounded by darkness, functions as both interrogation lighting and a visual metaphor for isolation. A gobo patterned with a window-frame or horizontal bars, projected across Hanako’s body, makes her captivity legible without any set-piece prison construction.

A common student error is to write: “I would use cold blue lighting for the North Korea scenes to show it is cold and unfriendly.” Examiners need much more than this. Specify: which lantern type (profile spots for hard-edged shadows; Fresnels for a softer, more diffused chill), what intensity (70% rather than full, so the actors are readable but the environment feels leached of warmth), what colour gel (a Lee 201 “Full C.T. Blue” or similar cold wash), and what directional angle (steep top-light creates institutional surveillance rather than the enveloping cold of a side or front wash). Each specific choice carries meaning; a generic description carries none.

Sound Design: Waves and Propaganda

The play’s soundscape moves between two very different audio environments. The Japan scenes carry the sound of the sea — waves that begin as natural beach noise and gradually, across the play, become something the family has to choose to hear or not. A sound designer might position the sea sound binaurally (from the sides of the auditorium) in early scenes, then bring it to a mono centre speaker in later scenes, as if the sea has retreated into memory.

The North Korean compound scenes can be underscored by institutional sound — a low, steady drone that belongs to the building, not to nature; or, more specifically, by occasional fragments of state propaganda broadcast — distant music, an announcer’s voice — that arrive not as dramatic set-pieces but as background texture, as ordinary as traffic. This is the sound of a system that does not need to shout because it is simply the air you breathe. A soundscape underscore of this kind is more unsettling than a dramatic sound cue precisely because it feels unremarkable.

Key Fact

The sea functions as a controlling sound motif: it begins the play (the beach storm where Hanako disappears) and it is always available to the sound designer as a marker of the original loss. In the North Korean scenes, the absence of the sea — or its replacement by state sound — measures how far Hanako has been taken from herself.

Set Design: Minimalism Across Decades

Because the play covers 24 years and two countries, a realistic naturalistic set would require constant scene changes and would slow the play’s momentum fatally. Turnly’s play calls for a minimalist set: a stage that holds both locations simultaneously, with a handful of key elements that can be rearranged or relit to signal transitions. A low platform levels structure can separate the domestic Japanese household at one depth from the clinical compound surfaces at another, without a scene change.

Projections on the cyclorama can carry the sea without requiring a physical construction: a rolling ocean image projected behind the Japan scenes gives way to a blank institutional wall in the North Korean compound sequences. This also allows the projection to evolve — the sea becoming stormier or calmer — in response to the emotional arc of the family’s scenes.

Costume: Decade, Culture, Coercion

Costume in The Great Wave carries enormous narrative load because it must show the passage of decades (1979 to 2003) and the erasure of Hanako’s Japanese identity within the North Korean state. The design must signal two things simultaneously: the historical period (1980s Japanese civilian clothing moves through decades) and the institutional pressure on identity (Hanako’s costume in North Korea becoming less her own over time — more muted, more uniform, less personal).

For the Japanese family scenes, costume colour and silhouette can reflect period fashion while also tracking emotional states: Etsuko’s palette might grow greyer as the years pass, her costume gradually losing the bright accent colours of the early scenes. For Hanako in captivity, a DPRK-inflected institutional grey or khaki — plain fabric, functional cut — replaces the personal clothing of the beach scene. The contrast between what she wore at 17 and what she wears a decade later can be read by the audience as the visual measure of what she has lost.

Design choices only work if the performer engages with them. A performer playing Hanako in the compound scenes can use proxemics to reinforce the costume’s meaning: keeping a formal, controlled distance from officials, never allowing her body to claim the space as her own — the body contained within the uniform rather than inhabiting it. When Hanako has a rare private moment, a small physical release — dropping the shoulders, letting the hands open — can signal the self that still exists underneath the institutional costume. These micro-choices are what separate a performance that merely wears the costume from one that lives in it.

Performing a Family Under Pressure

The Price family in Things I Know to Be True are ordinary people in an extraordinary year. Each character carries a different kind of pressure, and a performer’s job is to hold that pressure truthfully across the entire arc of the play — not only in the big revelatory scenes but in the domestic moments in between. Andrew Bovell’s naturalistic dialogue gives performers rich material: overlapping thoughts, sentences that stop before they finish, the particular shorthand of a family that has been talking to each other for decades. Understanding how to use vocal interpretation and physical interpretation for each character is the foundation of every performance answer in the exam.

This lesson focuses on Bob, Fran, and the four children at the play’s most charged moments: Bob’s stoicism in the face of his children’s revelations; Fran’s directness and toughness; Mark’s reveal scene; Pip’s departure; and the ensemble physicality of the play’s ending tableau. In each case, the performer must balance what the character says with what the character cannot say — the subtext that Bovell builds into every scene.

Key Fact

For every performance question, you must name both vocal AND physical choices, anchored to a specific named moment. Saying “I would act sad” is not enough. Name the tool: slower pace, a drop in volume, a held pause; or a stillness in the body, a lowered gaze, hands released to the sides. The more specific you are, the higher the mark.

Bob: Stoicism and the Weight of What Is Unsaid

Bob Price is a study in restraint. He tends his roses, maintains a sense of order, and responds to each of his children’s revelations with a quietness that the audience must learn to read. His silence is not emptiness; it is full of suppressed feeling. A performer playing Bob must understand this as the central technical challenge of the role: how to communicate emotional depth through stillness and economy rather than through display.

In the garden scenes, Bob’s physicality can be rooted in a specific task — he is pruning, or turning soil, or standing with his hands at his sides among the plants. Proxemics matter enormously for this character: when a child approaches him in the garden, the way Bob adjusts his position — whether he turns fully to face them, or continues his task with his body angled slightly away, or holds himself very still — communicates volumes before a word is spoken. Vocally, Bob speaks measured, unhurried. A slower pace than the other characters; pauses before significant responses; a volume that does not rise even under pressure. When he receives a revelation that shocks him, the most powerful choice is often to lower the volume still further: a near-whisper that forces the audience to lean in.

The winter scene in which Mark tells his parents that he is transitioning to Mia is one of the play’s most complex performance challenges. For the performer playing Mark, the approach must be grounded in the character’s specific circumstances: this is not a generalised coming-out scene but a particular person, in a particular family, telling two particular parents something that has cost him an enormous amount to hold back. The given circumstances — who Bob is, who Fran is, how the family communicates — shape every choice.

Vocally, the performer playing Mark might begin the scene with a pace that is slightly faster than usual — the energy of something that must be said before the courage runs out — and then slow significantly once the words are out, allowing the silence of the parents’ response to land. Physically, Mark might begin the scene at a measured distance from his parents — neither close nor far, a neutral proxemics — and during the most difficult part of the speech take a step towards them rather than away, communicating that the revelation is an act of trust rather than an exit. A small, specific gesture — the hands open, facing upward, at the sides, as if offering something — can communicate vulnerability without overplaying the emotional register. Examiners reward specificity: not “I would look scared” but “I would hold my body very still from the waist down while allowing a slight tremor in the hands, so that the effort of physical control is visible to the audience.”

Fran: Directness Under Pressure

Where Bob retreats into stillness, Fran advances. She is the more direct of the two parents — a nurse by profession, accustomed to saying difficult things plainly. A performer playing Fran must resist the temptation to play her as simply hard. Her directness is a form of love: she speaks truth because she believes her children deserve it. The challenge is to hold both qualities in the body at once: the toughness and the vulnerability beneath it.

In the kitchen confrontation scenes, Fran’s physicality is active: she might be at the kitchen counter or the table, engaged in a practical task, and she continues that task for longer than is comfortable while a conversation is beginning around her. This use of physical business — the act of doing something with the hands while a difficult emotional conversation unfolds — is a classic Stanislavskian approach to grounding a scene in physical reality. When Fran finally stops and turns to face the person she is speaking with, the stillness of that turn communicates that something significant is now happening.

Key Fact

Fran’s directness is grounded in physical business: she works with her hands while conversations unfold around her, and the moment she stops signals to the audience that something real is now being said. As a performer, using and then releasing physical business is a precise technique for controlling the rhythm of a scene.

The Ensemble and the Ending Tableau

The play’s final image is a tableau — the whole family gathered in a configuration that carries the weight of everything the year has delivered. In the Frantic Assembly co-production tradition, this moment may be embedded within or arrived at through a movement sequence: the family assembling themselves physically, finding their spatial relationship to each other and to Bob at the centre, so that the final image is not simply “they stand together” but a precisely constructed statement about love, damage, truth and endurance.

As a director working with the ensemble for this moment, the key decisions are about blocking and spatial hierarchy. Who is closest to Bob? Who is furthest away? Who makes physical contact with another character, and who is isolated? Does the tableau face the audience directly, or is it angled so that some characters have their backs to us, creating a sense of privacy or enclosure? Each of these decisions changes the meaning of the final image and must be justified in relation to the revelations the play has delivered across the year. The lighting state for the final tableau should be considered: a slow fade rather than a blackout, perhaps, so that the audience holds the image for longer — both literally and emotionally.

A common exam error in performance-interpretation answers is to describe what the character is feeling (“I would show that Bob is devastated”) rather than describing the specific vocal and physical choices that communicate that feeling without naming it. Audiences do not need to be told what a character feels; they need to be shown it through concrete theatrical means. Think of this as the difference between illustrating an emotion and communicating a thought. The character is not “performing sadness”; the character is pursuing a specific action (trying to hold themselves together, trying not to let a child see the damage their words have done), and it is that pursuit — the effort of it — that the audience reads as feeling. Always ask: what is this character doing, physically and vocally, in this moment? Start there, not with the emotion label.

The Four Major Characters

Around the World in 80 Days has a small core company at its dramatic centre, surrounded by the dozens of minor characters produced by the eight-actor ensemble. Understanding each major character’s function — and the precise physical and vocal choices a performer might make — is essential for the extended-response questions you will encounter in the exam. Let’s take them in turn.

Phileas Fogg: the Still Centre

Fogg is one of the most unusual protagonists in the set-play list. Where most leads carry the play through visible emotional change — Proctor's moral disintegration, Mickey's rage-filled final scene — Fogg’s dramatic function is almost the opposite. His stillness is the comic engine. Every obstacle that throws Passepartout into comic crisis simply registers on Fogg as a minor inconvenience to be noted in his schedule. A performer playing Fogg should resist the temptation to play him as broadly comic. Instead, the performance choices are rooted in understatement: an upright posture, precise and unhurried movement, a measured vocal delivery with minimal variation in pitch — and then, in the moments that matter (the rescue of Aouda, the final London revelation), a tiny shift of vocal warmth or physical openness that carries enormous weight precisely because of the stillness that surrounds it.

From a design perspective, Fogg’s visual identity is equally precise. A costume designer might use a dark Victorian frock coat, waistcoat and pocket watch as the anchoring constant — the one costume that never changes throughout the journey while everything around him transforms. This contrast between Fogg’s fixed costume and the constantly shifting proxemics of the ensemble around him gives the audience a visual anchor in every new location.

Key Fact

Fogg’s stillness and emotional restraint are his defining performance quality. The comedy arises from the gap between his unflustered calm and the chaos erupting around him — and this gap is entirely dependent on Passepartout’s energy as contrast.

Jean Passepartout: the Audience's Way In

If Fogg is the still centre, Passepartout is the kinetic perimeter. The French valet functions as the audience’s emotional guide through the journey: he worries when we worry, panics when the plan threatens to unravel, and celebrates when the adventure turns in their favour. A performer playing Passepartout has much greater physical and vocal range to work with than the performer playing Fogg. Blocking choices for Passepartout should be energetic and reactive — he might move frequently across the stage, use larger gestures, speak with more variation in pitch and pace, and respond visibly in his body to each new development. His relationship to the audience can include moments of direct comedy: a wide-eyed look to the audience when Fogg announces the next leg of the journey, a physical double-take, a sudden stillness of comic alarm.

Crucially, examiners reward students who understand that Passepartout and Fogg’s comedy is entirely dependent on their contrast. If a performer plays Fogg as energetic, the play loses its engine. If a performer plays Passepartout as restrained, the comic double-act collapses. The proxemics between them — Fogg typically upstage centre or slightly elevated, Passepartout closer to the audience at downstage centre — reinforces the status difference while keeping Passepartout as the audience’s primary point of identification.

Consider the moment in the play when Fogg announces each new leg of the journey after an obstacle has threatened to derail the schedule. As a performer playing Fogg: hold an upright posture, speak the announcement in a measured pace with a level pitch, and allow a brief pause before delivering the key line — the pause creates audience anticipation. As a performer playing Passepartout in the same moment: stand in contrast — slightly hunched from exertion or anxiety, reacting visibly in the shoulders and face. When Fogg delivers his line, allow a beat of stunned stillness followed by a physical release of breath that communicates relief or disbelief. This is the double-act mechanism at work: Fogg’s understatement amplifies Passepartout’s reaction, and Passepartout’s reaction amplifies the comedy of Fogg’s stillness.

Inspector Fix: the Pursuing Antagonist

Fix is a Scotland Yard detective who is convinced Fogg is the perpetrator of a bank robbery. He pursues the party from the Suez Canal onwards, attempting to delay Fogg at each stop so that a warrant can catch up with him. Fix creates dramatic irony: the audience knows Fogg is innocent, Fix does not, and this gap generates comedy as well as tension. A performer playing Fix must walk a line between genuine threat (he has the legal power to detain Fogg) and comic obsession (his certainty is transparently wrong, and increasingly desperate). Vocally, Fix might employ a slightly faster pace than Fogg — suggesting agitation beneath a professional exterior — and physical choices that place him in the gaps between the main party: always slightly upstage, slightly to one side, watching from upstage in a way that signals surveillance without interrupting the main action.

Aouda: from Rescued to Active

Aouda is the young Indian woman rescued by Fogg from a dangerous situation in India. Students often under-write her, treating her as a passive figure — rescued, grateful, silent. This is a significant misconception. While Verne’s original novel is a product of its time in its portrayal of Indian women, Eason’s adaptation (and the performance traditions that have grown around it) understand Aouda as someone whose arc moves from shock and vulnerability in her first scenes to active participation in the company as the journey continues. By the final London scenes she is part of the decision-making group, not simply an observer. A performer playing Aouda should track this arc physically: an initial containedness — quieter movement, closer proximity to Fogg as her protector — gradually opening into a more assured spatial presence, with more confident eye contact with both other characters and the audience, as her trust in the company grows.

Key Fact

Aouda moves from a rescued, vulnerable figure in the India scenes to an active member of Fogg’s company by the London ending. A performer should track this arc through changes in posture, spatial confidence and eye contact across the play.

The Multi-Roled Ensemble: Character Through Transformation

Beyond the four core characters, the eight-actor ensemble plays every other role in the play — the Reform Club wager-makers, the Suez customs official, the Bombay merchant, ship captains, train conductors, Native American warriors, Yokohama acrobats, and more. Each transformation requires the performer to signal a new character quickly and clearly. The technique is not naturalistic psychology — there is no time for a Stanislavskian interior journey into each minor character’s backstory. Instead, the physical-theatre vocabulary of the play demands clear gestus — a posture or gesture that instantly communicates the character’s social function and status. The Suez customs official stands with an officious squared-up posture, arms slightly out to signal authority; the Yokohama acrobat drops into a low centre of gravity with loose, ready limbs. These images are legible to the whole audience in an in-the-round configuration because they read from every angle.

A common student error is to describe minor characters as “the same performers in different costumes.” In Eason’s play, the theatrical pleasure of multi-roling comes from the distinctiveness of each transformation. The skill is in the precision of the gestus — how fully and quickly a performer can inhabit a completely different physical and vocal register. When writing as a performer for the exam, always specify what changes: the posture, the pace of movement, the pitch or accent of the voice. “The performer would act differently” scores no marks; “the performer would shift from Passepartout’s loose, reactive physicality to a squared, authoritative stillness and a more clipped English accent for the Reform Club gentleman” scores well.

Three Interlocking Themes

Around the World in 80 Days asks three related questions that operate simultaneously: what does time mean? What does the British Empire mean? And what is adventure? These are not separate compartments in the play — they are woven together in every scene. Fogg’s obsession with the schedule is inseparable from the Victorian culture of industrial precision that made British imperialism possible. The places Fogg travels through — India, Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, America — are the map of British and European colonial reach in 1872. And the sense of adventure that Verne’s novel celebrates is, in a modern production, always in dialogue with the question of whose world is being adventured through. A post-colonial reading of the play does not require abandoning the adventure — it requires understanding what the adventure was for.

Time, Schedule and Victorian Punctuality

The wager itself — £20,000 on an eighty-day circumnavigation — is a meditation on industrial time. The Suez Canal and the transcontinental railroad had made the journey mathematically possible; Fogg tests this possibility against the precision of timetables, departure slots and scheduled connections. For a Victorian audience, this celebration of schedule was a celebration of modernity itself: steam, rail, and the telegraph had compressed the world into measurable units. From a staging perspective, the theme of time can be physicalised in many ways. A sound designer might create a soundscape in which a ticking clock is woven underneath every scene — barely audible at the start but gradually louder as the eighty days compress. The rhythm of the ensemble’s physical work — the mechanical precision of the steam engine sequence, the synchronised tick of the Reform Club gentlemen consulting their watches — gives the theme physical form.

Key Fact

The theme of time is not just a narrative fact — it is a design opportunity. A ticking clock soundscape, growing in volume as the eighty days diminish, physicalises the countdown and creates cumulative tension for the audience regardless of which scene they are watching.

The British Empire and the Colonial Gaze

Verne’s novel is a product of the imperial imagination: the world outside Europe exists primarily as backdrop for Fogg’s determination and Passepartout’s comedy. The Indian characters are largely incidental; Aouda is defined initially by her need to be rescued; the Native American attack on the transcontinental railroad is a thrilling obstacle rather than a historically contextualised act of resistance. A 21st-century production cannot present this material uncritically without becoming uncomfortable in ways that serve neither the play nor the students watching it. Eason’s script and the production tradition around it find a range of ways to address this: the ensemble’s awareness of each new location can be performed with genuine curiosity rather than condescension; Aouda’s arc gives an Indian woman agency in the second half of the play; and design choices about costume and soundscape can represent the cultures Fogg passes through with specificity and respect rather than as a generic “exotic.”

Examiners reward students who acknowledge this tension and engage with it as a production question rather than a moral verdict. The question is not “is this play racist?” but “how would you, as a director or designer, stage the Indian marketplace scene so that the audience engages with India as a real, complex place rather than a colourful backdrop for Fogg’s journey?” This is a staging and design question, and it has specific, assessable answers.

Consider three specific design approaches a modern director might take. First, in soundscape: a sound designer could build the Indian marketplace scene from authentic Indian musical textures — a tabla rhythm, a specific raga mode played on sitar — rather than a generic “Eastern” musical cliché. This communicates that the production has engaged with the real culture rather than Verne’s impression of it. Second, in costume: ensemble members playing Indian characters might have specific, researched costume elements — a particular fabric, a specific garment form — that communicate cultural identity with precision. Third, in performance: the ensemble members might play Indian characters with the same specificity and gestus care they bring to the Reform Club gentlemen, resisting the temptation to use Indian scenes as pure physical spectacle. None of these choices requires rewriting the play; all of them require careful, thoughtful production design.

Adventure, Comedy and the Audience

The third major theme — adventure — is the play’s most immediate emotional register. Audiences come to have fun, to follow a chase, to laugh at Passepartout and admire Fogg. The adventure genre has specific theatrical vocabulary: pace, physical spectacle, comic reversal, the near-miss. Eason honours this by keeping every episode moving, by using the tableau sparingly for high-impact moments (the rescue of Aouda, the final reveal), and by placing the ensemble’s physical virtuosity at the centre of each new location. A director working on this play must balance the adventure’s energy with the moments of stillness that give the themes weight. The London ending — in which Fogg believes he has failed, then discovers through the international date line that he has succeeded — requires a complete tonal shift: from the silence of apparent defeat to the joy of unexpected victory. Blackout followed by an entirely different lighting state can serve this tonal pivot: a deep silence and near-darkness for the apparent failure, then a warmth of light and sound flooding back in as the date line is revealed.

Key Fact

The London ending demands a tonal pivot: Fogg’s apparent failure followed by the date line revelation. A blackout and silence mark the low point; a warm lighting wash and sound flooding back in mark the turn — a simple but powerful staging choice that communicates the emotional reversal.

Students sometimes feel that the “correct” answer to colonial themes is to stage the play as a critique of Fogg or Verne. This is too simple. The play’s joy and energy come from the adventure; a production that turns the comedy into a lecture about imperialism will lose its audience. The more sophisticated production approach — and the one examiners reward — is to use design and performance choices to add depth and specificity to the non-European characters and locations, so that the world Fogg travels through feels genuinely inhabited by real people with their own dignity, rather than as a backdrop. This does not require condemning Fogg; it requires the production to be aware of what Verne’s novel couldn’t see, and to quietly, visually correct that blind spot through skilled design.

Key Takeaways

  • The three major themes — time, empire and adventure — are inseparable: Fogg’s schedule-obsession, the colonial geography of the journey, and the adventure genre’s energy all operate together in every scene.
  • The colonial theme is a production and design question: examiners reward students who describe specific staging choices that give the cultures Fogg passes through dignity and specificity, not students who simply note that Verne was writing in the Victorian era.
  • The London ending’s tonal pivot from failure to joy is a lighting and sound design opportunity: blackout and silence for the low point, a warm wash and returning sound for the revelation — a simple choice that communicates emotional reversal.

A Tragedy Measured in Days, Not Years

Most tragedies unfold over months or years. Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet compresses its entire arc — courtship, marriage, exile, death — into roughly five days. That compression is not an accident of storytelling: it is a deliberate structural choice that makes every action feel irreversible and every delay feel fatal. When you think about staging this play, the structure itself becomes a design and performance challenge: how do you signal the passage of time, the change of day from night, the acceleration toward catastrophe?

Key Fact

Romeo and Juliet is structured in five acts and takes place over approximately five days. The lovers meet on Sunday evening, marry on Monday, Romeo is banished on Tuesday, Juliet drinks the potion on Wednesday night, and the tragedy concludes in the early hours of Thursday.

The Prologue: Telling the Audience the Ending

Before a single character speaks, a prologue chorus tells the audience everything: two families in conflict, two “star-crossed lovers,” and their deaths. This is a remarkable structural decision. Shakespeare is not interested in suspense about whether the lovers will die — he is interested in the audience watching how and why it happens, knowing all along that it cannot be stopped.

For a designer, the prologue presents an immediate staging question: who speaks it, and from where? In a thrust stage arrangement, the chorus figure might stand at the very tip of the stage, addressing the front rows directly as if confiding in each spectator individually. In a proscenium arch configuration, the figure might stand in a single tight lighting special, downstage centre, while the rest of the stage remains in darkness. Either choice communicates the same message: this figure stands outside the story, seeing it whole.

As a performer: the chorus figure might deliver the prologue in a slow, measured pace with a low, even pitch — almost ceremonial — to signal that what follows is already decided. A long pause after “star-crossed lovers” lets the weight of the word “star-crossed” settle. Physical stillness throughout, arms at the sides, direct eye contact with the audience: the body should not betray emotion that the lines themselves withhold.

As a designer: the lighting state for the prologue might be a single cool-white profile lantern hitting the chorus figure from a steep downstage angle, with the rest of the stage at zero. The sound design might include a low ambient drone — a non-diegetic soundscape — that fades as the first scene of street violence begins, replaced by natural city sounds.

Act by Act: The Shape of the Tragedy

Act One functions as exposition: it establishes the feud, introduces Romeo’s lovesickness for Rosaline, and ends with the meeting of Romeo and Juliet at the Capulet feast. The shared sonnet at that first meeting — fourteen lines of verse split between the two characters in an exchange that moves from formality to first kiss — is itself a structural signal. Two people who have never met construct a perfect poetic form together. Proxemics are crucial here: the director must make choices about how close the performers begin, how the distance closes through the fourteen lines, and whether the surrounding party guests physically frame the encounter.

Act Two contains the play’s most famous scene — the balcony scene — and the secret marriage. The pace accelerates: within twenty-four hours of meeting, the lovers are wed. This haste is thematic, not careless; Shakespeare wants the audience to feel how quickly the joy comes and, by Act Three, how quickly it shatters.

Act Three is the structural turning point. The deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, Romeo’s banishment, and the Capulet ultimatum to Juliet happen in rapid succession. If Act One is light and Act Five is dark, Act Three is where the light goes out. A director must think about how the design registers this shift: a costume palette that darkens, a lighting palette that loses its warm tones, a soundscape that moves from festive to foreboding.

Key Fact

Act Three, Scene One is the structural pivot of the play. Mercutio is killed by Tybalt; Romeo kills Tybalt in revenge; the Prince banishes Romeo from Verona. This single afternoon destroys the marriage, separates the lovers, and sets the tragedy in motion.

Act Four belongs almost entirely to Juliet. She faces the ultimatum to marry Paris, seeks Friar Lawrence’s help, and takes the sleeping potion alone on stage in a soliloquy that asks her to perform a sequence of emotions — terror, resolve, dread, courage — in rapid succession. The designer’s challenge is to build a staging for that bedroom scene: isolated lighting on Juliet, perhaps a bare stage with a single bed as a raised level, the surrounding darkness suggesting the void she is about to enter.

Act Five compresses the final catastrophe. Romeo learns of Juliet’s apparent death, races to Verona, kills Paris at the tomb, and poisons himself beside Juliet’s body. Juliet wakes shortly afterwards. The multi-roling and ensemble movement in the tomb sequence — how the bodies are arranged, whether Paris’s corpse remains visible throughout, where the Prince and families stand when they arrive — are design decisions that shape the audience’s reading of the final moments.

Students often describe the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt in Act Three as the play’s climax. In structural terms, Act Three is the turning point (or peripeteia in Aristotelian tragedy) — the moment when fortune reverses. The true dramatic climax, where the highest stakes are resolved, is the tomb scene in Act Five. Examiners reward students who hold both ideas: Act Three as the pivot that makes tragedy inevitable, Act Five as the point where that inevitability is fulfilled. For a designer, this means the design choices must build across all five acts, not peak in Act Three.

Pace, Rhythm and the Compressed Timeline as a Staging Problem

The compressed timeline creates pace as a structural feature. Directors have responded to this in contrasting ways: some accelerate the whole production (playing the full text in under two hours with no interval), some slow the lovers’ scenes to make their brevity ache, some stage the party scene with frenetic ensemble choreography that deliberately exhausts the audience before the quiet of the balcony. There is no single right answer — but every choice should be shaped by an awareness that Shakespeare has built urgency into the architecture of the play.

As a performer, you must calibrate your energy to the arc. Romeo in Act One is languid, performance-ready with a poem for Rosaline; Romeo in Act Three, Scene One is reactive and explosive. The blocking in Act One might be spacious and unhurried; in Act Three it becomes compressed and colliding.

Two Worlds, One Journey

Around the World in 80 Days exists in two historical moments simultaneously. Jules Verne’s story first appeared in 1872, feeding a Victorian appetite for global adventure at the precise moment when industrial technology had made such adventure feasible. The New Vic staged Eason’s adaptation in 2013 in the north of England, for a 21st-century audience well aware of what empire had meant and where the “adventure” of Victorian global reach had led. Understanding both contexts is essential not because examiners will ask you to reproduce biographical facts, but because context shapes every staging choice a modern production might make — from the style of the physical theatre to the way the ensemble performs the non-European characters. Both Verne’s world and Eason’s inform what happens on stage.

Jules Verne and the Victorian Moment

Jules Verne (1828–1905) was a French novelist and one of the founders of adventure fiction as a genre. He was fascinated by science and technology, and his novels are populated by engineers, explorers, submarines and balloons — the machines of a world in which human ingenuity was transforming the possible. Around the World in 80 Days first appeared serially in a French newspaper in 1872, before being published as a book in 1873. It arrived at a specific historical junction: the Suez Canal had opened in 1869, dramatically shortening the sea journey between Europe and India; the American transcontinental railroad, also completed in 1869, had linked the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. Together these two engineering achievements made Verne’s premise credible — a journey that would have taken six months was now theoretically achievable in eighty days.

The novel’s popularity was also driven by a specifically Victorian cultural obsession with time. The Great Exhibition of 1851 had celebrated industrial progress and the mastery of nature through technology; by the 1870s, standardised railway time was replacing local time across Britain, the telegraph was sending messages faster than any human traveller, and the world was being divided into predictable time zones. Fogg’s devotion to his schedule is not a character quirk — it is a satirical portrait of Victorian industrial modernity, where the precision of the timetable had become a cultural value.

Key Fact

Verne wrote his novel in 1872, shortly after the Suez Canal (1869) and the transcontinental railroad (1869) made circumnavigation in 80 days theoretically possible. The Victorian obsession with time, schedules and industrial progress gave Fogg’s character its cultural meaning.

The Novel's Colonial Assumptions

Verne’s novel is a product of French and European imperial culture. The world outside Europe functions as spectacular terrain for Fogg’s determination. India, China, Japan and America appear as a series of exotic episodes, each offering a different flavour of drama or comedy. Verne writes with genuine curiosity about these places, but his gaze is consistently that of the European traveller: the cultures he describes are observed from the outside. This is not a unique failing of Verne — it was the dominant mode of 19th-century travel writing, in which the world was divided into the civilised (European) traveller and the colourful (non-European) spectacle. A modern student reading the novel will notice this immediately; a modern director staging the play must decide how to handle it.
