Victorian adventure fiction as a genre typically features: a Western (usually British or French) protagonist whose ingenuity and stoicism are tested by the world; a loyal, comic companion who provides the audience’s emotional reaction; a series of exotic locations each with its own distinctive “character”; and a resolution that confirms the protagonist’s superiority through success. Verne’s novel fits this template closely, which is why Eason’s adaptation can engage with both the pleasure of the genre and the questions a modern audience brings to it. The physical-theatre form Eason writes for — eight actors explicitly constructing the world — is itself a kind of comment on the genre: by making the construction visible, the production invites the audience to watch the storytelling as storytelling, rather than being absorbed unquestioningly into the colonial adventure. This is the same principle as alienation effect in epic theatre: the ensemble’s visible transformations remind the audience that they are watching a story, not experiencing reality.

Laura Eason and the 2013 New Vic Production

Laura Eason is an American playwright. Her adaptation had its world premiere at Lookingglass Theater in Chicago in 2008; Theresa Heskins directed the New Vic production in 2013. This matters for staging: an in-the-round space requires a very different approach from a proscenium arch. There is no “upstage” as a place of exit or hiding; there is no wing space for surprise entrances; every costume change, every physical transformation, every blocking choice must work from every angle. The 2013 New Vic production used the space’s demands: the episodic multi-roling structure, physical-theatre vocabulary, minimal set and performer ingenuity made the world visible from all sides.

Eason’s adaptation is firmly in the tradition of physical theatre. The influence of companies like Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994) is visible in the script’s demands: performers are asked to become not just multiple characters but multiple objects and environments. This ensemble physical-theatre tradition sits comfortably alongside the Brechtian concept of the visible storyteller — the performer who steps out to narrate, to comment, to address the audience directly, making the theatrical fiction visible rather than concealing it behind a naturalistic fourth wall.

Key Fact

Eason’s script draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994), whose ensemble work — object transformation, bodies-as-environments, ensemble storytelling — underpins the play’s staging demands.

A student who understands both historical contexts can answer a context question with precision. For example: a 12-mark practice question asking how historical context shapes a director’s choices for the India scenes might draw on three facts — (1) Verne wrote these scenes from a colonial gaze; (2) Eason adapted the play for a post-colonial 21st-century audience; (3) the physical-theatre form (visible transformation, ensemble storytelling) allows a modern production to handle this material critically without pausing the adventure. The directorial choice that follows from this context might be: the ensemble perform Indian characters with specific, researched gestus — a particular posture, a specific movement quality — that communicates genuine cultural specificity, not a tourist’s impression. This is a contextually informed staging choice.

Why Practitioners Matter in This Play

When applying a practitioner’s ideas to a set play, do not give a biography of Brecht or Stanislavski. Instead ask: how do specific techniques from a practitioner’s practice shape the way the play is performed and designed? In The Empress, Gupta draws on two distinct theatrical traditions that pull in different directions — and understanding why she uses both is the key to a sophisticated answer.

Bertolt Brecht developed what he called epic theatre, a mode in which the audience is reminded that they are watching a constructed event, not reality. The purpose was political: Brecht wanted audiences to reflect on social systems and imagine alternatives, rather than losing themselves in emotional identification with characters. His techniques include direct address, songs that interrupt the action, narrative captions, ensemble multi-roling, and gestus — physical actions that reveal social roles rather than psychological interiority.

Key Fact

Gupta’s stated aim in writing The Empress was to bring hidden histories to the stage — to make visible the Indian people who lived in Victorian Britain but whose presence was written out of the official record. This is a Brechtian project: the audience’s role is to witness and recognise, not just to watch and feel.

Brechtian Techniques in The Empress

The play’s use of direct address is openly Brechtian. When Rani steps forward and speaks to the audience, she is functioning as a narrator of her own story as much as a character within it. Brecht called this the alienation effect (or Verfremdungseffekt): the audience is pulled out of emotional absorption and asked to process what they are seeing as a witness rather than as a participant. A director staging these moments of direct address can reinforce the Brechtian signal through design: lights shift to a cool, even lighting wash rather than an intimate special, breaking the illusion of the scene’s naturalistic world.

The Hindi songs serve a similar function. Brecht used songs in his plays not to advance the plot emotionally but to comment on the action and interrupt the audience’s feeling with a moment of reflection. When a Hindi song rises in The Empress, the naturalistic drama pauses. The audience is given space to think about what the song’s presence means: this is not just Rani’s private world — it is a culture, a community, a history that predates the Empire and refuses to be absorbed by it. A sound designer staging the songs as fully amplified, theatrically lit events (perhaps with a sudden change in the lighting state, a bright full-stage wash without shadow) underlines the Brechtian rupture.

Brecht’s concept of gestus is particularly useful for the British court figures in The Empress. A director using a Brechtian approach might instruct the performers playing Lord Salisbury, Bertie and the household to adopt a set of repeated, recognisable gestures that expose their social role rather than creating rounded psychological characters: a slight backward lean when confronted with anything un-English, hands clasped behind the back in a posture of proprietary authority, a collective turning of backs towards Abdul. These gestural choices would be deliberately stylised rather than naturalistic — almost choreographic in their coordination — so that the audience sees the court as a social institution rather than a collection of individuals. The multi-roling of these figures reinforces this: if one performer plays three different court functionaries, the gestus must be consistent across all three, making the point that the faces change but the power structure does not.

Stanislavski: Individual Truth

Constantin Stanislavski developed a practice centred on psychological realism: the performer finds the inner motivation of the character, builds a belief in the character’s past, and allows genuine emotion to surface through that interior work. Where Brecht wanted the audience to think, Stanislavski wanted them to feel. A Stanislavskian approach to Rani asks the performer to develop a full interior life for the character: her memories of home, her relationships before the voyage, her private fear and her private determination. None of this is stated in the text; it is held internally and filters through every choice the performer makes.

Gupta’s play needs Stanislavski most where it needs the audience to care deeply about a specific person rather than a historical category. If Rani is only the political argument — the symbol of the abandoned ayah — the play risks becoming a lecture. It is the specificity of her individual responses (her particular humour in the Lascar lodging house, her particular stubbornness in refusing to perform gratitude to Mrs Wormwood) that makes the political argument land emotionally. The Stanislavskian craft of the performer creates the individual life; the Brechtian structure of the play places that individual life within a historical argument.

Students sometimes argue that because Brecht rejected Stanislavski, no play can use both. This is historically and practically wrong. Brecht’s theoretical objection was to emotional indulgence that stopped the audience thinking; in practice, his own productions used deeply specific, truthful performers. In The Empress and in many contemporary productions of historically engaged plays, the two approaches operate at different levels: Brecht shapes the structure (how scenes are framed for the audience, what songs and direct address do) while Stanislavski shapes the individual performance (what this specific character wants in this specific moment). Examiners reward students who can hold both without collapsing them.

Design as Political Comment

A Brechtian design approach for The Empress would resist visual illusion in favour of theatrical visibility. Rather than a realistic Victorian dock, a Brechtian designer might use a stylised set: bare stage with a few key props that acquire symbolic weight (a single piece of rope, a single crate, a single chair that becomes both a dock bench and a throne depending on who sits in it and where). The lighting rig would be visible — not hidden in the flies — reminding the audience that they are in a theatre making meaning together. Projection might be used to display historical captions: “London, 1887” or “There were over 100 ayahs stranded in London each year” — Brechtian titles that comment on the scene rather than delivering it.

Costume in a Brechtian production might use a deliberately non-naturalistic approach for the multi-roled British court figures while keeping the Indian characters’ costumes specific and individually realised — a visual argument that the Empire’s functionaries are interchangeable while the Indian characters it categorises are distinct people. The blocking of the ensemble in court scenes might be semi-choreographed, almost mechanical, contrasting with the organic, varied blocking of the scenes in the Ayahs’ Home — proxemics deployed as a consistent design language throughout.

Key Fact

The best practitioner answers for The Empress do not simply apply Brecht or Stanislavski separately — they show where the two approaches operate at different levels of the same production, and why Gupta’s project of bringing hidden histories to the stage requires both the Brechtian witness-frame and the Stanislavskian individual life.

How Theme Works in Drama

Themes in a play are not abstract ideas floating above the action: they are embodied in staging choices, costume decisions, lighting states and the physical relationships between performers. When Gupta writes about Empire in The Empress, she is writing about something that manifests in where people stand, how they speak, what fabric they wear and who holds the lantern above the scene. Your job as a performer or designer is to ask: how do I make this theme visible in the specific moment I am working on?

Theme 1: Empire as Lived Experience

The British Empire in The Empress is not a political slogan but an environment in which every character lives. For Rani, it is the system that carried her to Britain as domestic labour and left her stranded. For Abdul Karim, it is the framework within which an extraordinary personal ascent is possible — and ultimately the power that erases his legacy. For Queen Victoria, it is the vast dominion over which she feels personal pride and responsibility, without always seeing its human cost. Gupta’s dramaturgical intention is to make all three perspectives visible simultaneously, so that the audience cannot hold a single, simple view of what the Empire was.

A designer staging the Empire theme might consider: in the Windsor scenes, a lighting wash in deep gold and warm amber, with heavy draped set pieces suggesting the material weight of Imperial wealth. In contrast, the docks and the East End scenes lit with a cooler, harsher white or a pale blue-grey — the light of labour, of weather, of London’s working waterfront. The contrast is not just aesthetic: it makes the inequality legible at a glance.

Key Fact

The Empire theme in The Empress is made concrete through contrasting staging: Windsor’s opulence against the East End’s austerity. Examiners reward designers who can specify the exact lighting state, colour, fabric or set element and explain what it communicates about power.

Theme 2: Race and Racial Hierarchy

Late Victorian Britain had its own articulated racial hierarchy, in which the British ruling class considered themselves at the apex. This theme enters the play most forcefully through the court’s reaction to Abdul Karim: their hostility to him is not merely snobbery but a specific racial refusal to accept an Indian man as a close intimate of the queen. For a performer playing Lord Salisbury or Bertie, the challenge is to embody this worldview without caricature — to show how a system of racial superiority felt, from the inside, like natural order.

Sightlines and focus are useful tools here. A director might block the court conspiracy scenes so that the English characters are placed in a closed circle from which Abdul is spatially excluded: the staging itself enacts the racial hierarchy without needing dialogue to explain it. When Abdul is then admitted to Victoria’s private space, the open blocking — the two characters facing each other across a more intimate distance — represents a rupture in the spatial logic of the court.

Theme 3: Domestic Servitude and the Hidden Labour Force

The ayahs and Lascar sailors of the play represent what historians sometimes call the Empire’s ‘shadow economy’: the Indian domestic and maritime labour that made the British way of life possible but was rendered largely invisible in the official record. Gupta makes them visible. As a designer, the Ayahs’ Home scenes offer an opportunity to stage this community with care and specificity: the domestic objects that fill the space (worn saris, cooking vessels, children’s toys brought from India) become props as symbols. A cracked teacup might have been carried from Calcutta to London; it is simultaneously an ordinary object and an emblem of displacement.

Gupta’s approach is more theatrically interesting than simple editorialising. She presents characters on all sides of the Imperial divide with specificity and interior life. Victoria is genuinely warm; Salisbury genuinely believes in order; Rani genuinely survives. The play’s argument about Empire emerges from the juxtaposition of these experiences, not from any character becoming a mouthpiece. Examiners reward students who can analyse Gupta’s dramatic method rather than simply labelling the play’s politics.

Theme 4: Language, Identity and Power

Language in The Empress is not neutral. The play features bilingual exchanges in English, Bengali and Hindustani, and the choice of which language a character speaks in any given scene is a political act. When Victoria asks Abdul to teach her Hindustani, she is crossing a cultural threshold that her court considers improper — the Queen of England learning the language of a colony. When Rani speaks Bengali in the Ayahs’ Home, she is reclaiming a private self that she suppressed in English domestic service.

For a sound designer, the bilingual texture of the play opens possibilities. Hindustani songs might be underscored beneath Abdul’s scenes with Victoria, creating a soundscape that insists the Indian world is present even in Windsor. The decision of when to hear the underscore and when to remove it can track the power dynamics of each scene: is India welcome in this space, or suppressed?

Theme 5: Solidarity and Community in the Diaspora

Against the play’s theme of Imperial exploitation, Gupta places an equally important counter-theme: solidarity. The Lascar sailors who take Rani in, the ayah community of Hackney, the early Indian political networks around Hari — these are not passive victims. They are people building community, mutual support and a shared identity in a country that official culture treats as foreign. This theme reaches its theatrical culmination in the moment of convergence near the play’s end, when Rani’s storyline and the world of Abdul and Hari briefly meet.

Key Fact

Gupta places the theme of solidarity at the same dramatic weight as the theme of Imperial exploitation. The Ayahs’ Home and Lascar community scenes must be staged with warmth and specificity — not as scenes of suffering, but as scenes of survival and community-building.

As a performer in the Ayahs’ Home scenes: Rani’s physical transformation from the contracted, isolated posture of the docks scene to an open, relaxed body in shared space is one of the play’s most important character moments. You might mark this with a deliberate unclenching of the hands, a deepening of the breath, a willingness to make eye contact across the room. Vocally, the shift from the guarded English register she uses with Mrs Wormwood to the Bengali and Hindi of the home community could be marked with a change in pitch, a faster pace and a genuine rise in volume: the sound of someone speaking in their own voice for the first time in the play.

As a designer for the same scenes: a low, warm Fresnel wash in amber-gold (echoing, at lower intensity, the Windsor palette) could suggest warmth and belonging without irony — this is not the Empire’s gold but domestic lamplight. The set might be arranged with performers in a circle at centre stage, using the in-the-round configuration (or a modified thrust) to make the audience feel included in the community rather than observing it from outside.

Two Countries, One Stage

Francis Turnly’s The Great Wave takes place across two countries and 24 years. To hold those two worlds simultaneously, Turnly relies on a single structural engine: cross-cutting. Scenes in Japan and North Korea alternate in quick succession, so the audience is never allowed to settle entirely into one world before the other pulls them back. This is not accidental restlessness — it is Turnly’s way of insisting that both lives are happening at the same time, that Hanako’s captivity and her family’s grief are not separate stories but a single wound.

Key Fact

Cross-cutting in The Great Wave creates parallel time: the audience watches Hanako adapting to life in North Korea at exactly the same moment that Reiko and Etsuko in Japan are refusing to accept she is dead. The two timelines are always in tension.

Stage Directions and the Sea

Turnly’s stage directions do far more than describe the set. They specify the sound of the sea as a recurring presence — waves are not decorative background noise but a reminder of the beach where Hanako disappeared. A director staging the play must decide how to realise this: a soundscape of waves can fade in and out to mark every transition between storylines, functioning as an audible signal that the two worlds are connected by that same sea. The stage direction does not merely set the scene — it instructs the entire company about the play’s emotional geography.

For a designer, realising the sea means a choice between approaches. A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey across the cyclorama can evoke the sea’s restlessness without requiring literal scenic waves. Some productions have used gobos to throw fragmented light patterns suggesting water moving across the floor — so even the North Korean compound scenes carry a visual trace of the sea the captive cannot reach.

Because the play spans 1979 to 2003, transitions between scenes must carry not just geographical shift (Japan to North Korea) but also temporal shift — sometimes several years pass in a single cut. Turnly’s stage directions use a combination of signals: a change in lighting state, a costume change visible to the audience, and a change in the physical bearing of the performers. A character who was upright and defiant in the preceding scene may enter the next one carrying the weight of another two years in their posture and pace.

For the director and designer this means agreeing a consistent vocabulary for transitions. If a blackout followed by a surge of wave sound means “time has passed,” that convention must be established early and held consistently — otherwise the audience loses its bearings across the play’s long arc. The blocking at the start of each new scene can itself signal time: a performer moving quickly to a new position suggests arrival in a new moment, while stillness as the lights rise signals that this scene begins mid-thought.

Code-Switching and Language as Subtext

One of Turnly’s most striking dramatic methods is the use of language as a marker of identity and coercion. The play uses English alongside phonetic Japanese and Korean. In several scenes, dialogue begins in Japanese or Korean before returning to English so the audience can follow it. This code-switching can make identity and power audible: Hanako teaches Japanese to Jung Sun while living under coercion in North Korea.

For a performer playing Hanako, the challenge is to carry the weight of that language shift in the body as well as the voice. A shift to Korean might be accompanied by a slight change in posture — a contained stillness, proxemics that keep her at a formal distance from the officials around her — so that the audience reads the language change as a kind of performance within performance, Hanako surviving by playing a role.

Key Fact

The play is based on real abduction cases, which Turnly researched for six months. Its dramatic methods can make the historical context feel immediate without turning the fictional characters into documentary evidence.

The Wave as Structural Metaphor

The play’s title is not set dressing. A wave is something that cannot be stopped once it begins; it moves people without asking permission; it appears to recede but leaves a changed landscape behind. Turnly uses this image structurally: the cross-cutting itself moves like a wave — rising in intensity as diplomatic events accelerate in the play’s second half, and finally cresting in the scenes around the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration. A director staging the play needs to feel and shape this rhythmic architecture, using the pace of scene transitions to build that wave towards its final breaking point.

Students sometimes describe cross-cutting as though it were simply a way to “keep the story moving.” Examiners reward much more than this. Cross-cutting in The Great Wave is a political act: by refusing to let the audience follow only Hanako’s story or only the family’s story, Turnly forces us to hold both in mind simultaneously — to feel the injustice of the gap between a family waiting for news and a daughter alive but unreachable. The technique creates dramatic irony and moral pressure on the audience, not just narrative variety.

When you discuss cross-cutting in an extended-response question, always explain its effect on the audience’s emotions and understanding, not just its technical description. Ask yourself: what does the audience know in this scene that the characters on stage do not? How does that knowledge create tension or grief?

Why Watching Is Not Enough

Most people leave a theatre humming the music or remembering the big emotional moments. For your live theatre review, that is not enough. The exam rewards you for being able to pinpoint specific choices — a performer's exact vocal quality at a named moment, the intensity and colour of a lighting state, the texture of a costume fabric — and then judge whether those choices successfully communicated meaning to the audience.

That level of detail requires a different kind of watching: critical spectatorship. This lesson gives you a framework for doing exactly that, both in the theatre and in the notes you write immediately afterwards.

Key Fact

The exam rewards specific technical detail, not general impressions. “The lighting was dark” earns no credit; “a single Fresnel special focused downstage centre, producing a cold blue wash at low intensity” can earn top marks.

The What / How / Why Framework

Before you enter the theatre, memorise this three-part scaffold. It structures every paragraph you will write in the exam:

  • What was the choice? Name it precisely: a sharp blackout, a sudden drop in the performer's vocal pitch, a costume change carried out in view of the audience.
  • How was it executed? Add technical detail: a Fresnel lantern at 20% intensity, a downward pitch shift of half an octave, a black linen coat replaced by a cream silk dress in full stage lighting.
  • Why did it work (or not)? Evaluate: what did the audience feel as a result? What meaning did the director intend to communicate? Did it succeed, and why?

This scaffold applies whether you are writing about a performer, a designer or the directorial concept. The key shift is from describing to evaluating.

Taking Notes in the Theatre

You cannot write full sentences in the dark, but you can capture trigger words that unlock memory later. Keep a small notepad and pencil. During the performance, note:

  • Performer moments: write the character's name, a one-word description of what the performer did, and a physical cue (e.g. “Mira — freeze — USL, turns away”). This helps you reconstruct the blocking later.
  • Design moments: note colour, direction and quality of the lighting state; any abrupt sound cues; unusual set elements. Even “blue wash — cold — interval end” is useful.
  • Audience reaction: if the audience gasped, laughed or fell silent at a particular moment, write it down. Audience response is evidence that a choice worked.
  • Stage configuration: sketch the stage layout in the margin — whether it is theatre in the round, a proscenium arch, or a thrust stage. This affects how proxemics read for the audience.

The interval is gold. Use the first five minutes to expand your shorthand notes while the first act is fresh. Ask yourself: what was the single most striking performer choice so far? What design element most affected my mood as an audience member? What do I think the director wants me to think about this production’s themes?

Write answers to these three questions in full sentences. You may use them almost verbatim in your exam. At the end of the second act, sit for two minutes before leaving — identify your most striking moment from the whole production before the crowd noise and adrenaline erase it.

Post-Show Notes: The Production Log

Write your production log within 24 hours of seeing the production. After that, specific sensory memories fade fast. Structure your log under four headings that match the exam’s focus:

  1. Production context: title, company, venue, date, stage configuration, approximate running time.
  2. Performer analysis: for each performer you plan to write about, record one vocal choice and one physical choice for a named moment, plus the effect on you as an audience member.
  3. Design analysis: one lighting example with technical details; one sound example; one set or costume observation. For each, note the specific moment and the audience effect.
  4. Directorial concept: in two or three sentences, state what you believe the director’s central intention was and give one piece of evidence for it.

Many students write a plot summary in their review — they retell what happened scene by scene. This earns little credit because the exam is asking you to analyse how meaning was communicated, not what the story was.

Think of the examiner as someone who also saw the production. They already know the plot. What they want to read is your analytical voice: why did a particular lighting state succeed in creating unease? Why did a performer’s sudden stillness communicate power more effectively than movement could have? That analytical perspective only comes from the What / How / Why scaffold, not from scene-by-scene summary.

Key Fact

Your course must include a live performance of at least 50 minutes, with at least two actors, dialogue and a range of production values. You may use a digital or streamed production in the exam. You may not write about your set play in the live theatre question.

Why Practitioners Matter for This Play

When examiners ask students to apply a practitioner’s techniques to a set play, they are not asking for a biography. They want to see students understand how a specific working method — a way of creating scenes, rehearsing the ensemble, constructing images or relating to the audience — could shape the choices a modern company makes when staging this text. For Around the World in 80 Days, three practitioner traditions are directly relevant and practically applicable: Frantic Assembly, Complicite, and the music-hall and circus tradition that the play’s comic form echoes.

Key Fact

The three most relevant practitioner traditions are: Frantic Assembly (ensemble physical theatre, contact work, collaborative image-making), Complicite (object transformation, storytelling ensemble, narrator-led staging) and the music-hall/circus tradition (direct audience address, comic precision, shared theatrical pleasure).

Frantic Assembly: Bodies as Storytelling Instruments

Frantic Assembly, founded in 1994 by Scott Graham, Steven Hoggett and Vicki Middleton, built its reputation on a form of physical theatre in which the body is not decorative but dramaturgical — the body’s movement tells the story and creates the emotional world of the play. Their signature vocabulary includes round-by-through exercises, chair duets and contact choreography, and lifts that serve narrative rather than spectacle.

In Around the World in 80 Days, Frantic Assembly’s influence is most visible in the sequences where the company must become a single creature or vehicle. The elephant sequence, the train sequence, the ship — all require the same principle Frantic Assembly built their method on: the whole is more than the sum of its parts, and the audience reads a collective physical decision as a single image. A director working from Frantic Assembly’s approach would develop these sequences in rehearsal through physical improvisation, allowing the company to find the movement together rather than having it choreographed from outside.

As a performer working in a Frantic Assembly-influenced rehearsal for the elephant sequence, you might begin the devising process with a round-by-through exercise in which two performers in physical contact with each other explore the rhythm and weight of a large, slow-moving creature. The goal is not to mime an elephant — it is to find the weight and rhythm in your own body so the physical choice becomes instinctive. Your vocal contribution in this scene is silence: the physical precision carries the full dramatic load.

As a lighting designer for a Frantic Assembly-influenced staging of this sequence, you would trust the physical storytelling and resist the temptation to overilluminate. A warm amber wash from a high angle (suggesting the Indian sun), perhaps a dim state with a gobo of leaf-shadow patterns projected onto the floor — giving the ensemble’s bodies maximum visual impact against a subtly textured background — would be the Frantic Assembly aesthetic: clean, powerful, serving the movement without competing with it.

Complicite: Object Transformation and the Narrator

Complicite (founded 1983, still directed by Simon McBurney) built a different but equally relevant tradition. Where Frantic Assembly’s strength is in the physical ensemble, Complicite’s signature is in object transformation and in the figure of the storytelling narrator. In Complicite’s productions, company members regularly step in and out of the fiction to address the audience directly, to handle and transform objects, and to remind the audience that they are watching a story being told, not a reality being reproduced.

This is exactly the theatrical mode Eason’s script requires. The Complicite-influenced director would pay close attention to the way objects change meaning during the play: a chair is never just a chair once the ensemble has trained itself to use it as a carriage; a rope is never just a rope once it has been ship rigging. The discipline is that the transformation must be total and committed — there is no half-way position where the audience is uncertain whether this is a chair or a carriage. Complicite’s training method emphasises that the object’s transformation is effected entirely by the performer’s physical relationship to it.

Key Fact

Complicite’s core principle: the object’s meaning is entirely created by the performer’s physical use of it. A chair becomes a train carriage the moment the performer sits in it as if in a moving carriage — not because the chair looks like a carriage, but because the body’s logic makes it one.

Brechtian Elements: The Narrator and the Episodic Frame

Bertolt Brecht’s theatrical principles also have limited but specific relevance here. Brecht’s Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) — using narration, direct address and visible theatricality to remind the audience they are watching a construction — is built into Eason’s structure. Every time a company member steps forward to narrate the passage of days or comment on Fogg’s progress, they perform a Brechtian function: the story is held at arm’s length so the audience can observe it.

The episodic structure — short scenes in clearly labelled locations, no attempt at continuous realistic time — is also Brechtian in spirit. Brecht’s epic theatre avoided the seamless illusion of naturalism in favour of a structure that acknowledged each scene as a discrete unit. However, important to note: Around the World in 80 Days is not a Brechtian play in the full sense — it does not make political-didactic demands on its audience in the way The Caucasian Chalk Circle does. The Brechtian elements are structural tools within a comedy-of-adventure, not an ideological programme.

Victorian music hall — the variety entertainment tradition that was the dominant popular theatre form when Verne’s novel was published — operated on principles that resonate strongly with Eason’s play. Direct audience address was the norm; performers acknowledged the presence of the audience and played to them explicitly. Comic precision — the exact timing of a pratfall, the perfectly judged pause before a punchline — was a highly valued craft skill. Songs, physical spectacle, and an awareness that the audience’s pleasure was the goal rather than their passive observation were all central.

Some productions of this play interpolate live music — a piano onstage, a percussionist tracking the journey — that explicitly invokes this tradition. A director drawing on music-hall principles would coach Passepartout in particular on the shared, audience-aware quality of his comedy: the moment when he turns to the audience with an expression of disbelief, or when he makes an aside directly to the front row, is the music-hall gesture surviving into 21st-century ensemble theatre. In terms of performer-audience relationship, this play operates much closer to the music-hall end of the spectrum than to the fourth-wall naturalism of Stanislavski.

The Age Leap: Performance’s Central Challenge

Blood Brothers spans roughly twenty years and demands that its principal performers age convincingly from children of seven to adults in their mid-twenties within a single production, often with minimal costume change. This is one of the play’s most significant performance challenges. The solution is not cosmetic — it is physical and vocal. A performer who plays Mickey at seven through voice alone — speaking in a slightly higher pitch, perhaps — will be marked as Developing. The examiner wants to see that you understand how a child inhabits their body differently from an adult.

Playing Mickey at Seven: Physical and Vocal Choices

At seven, Mickey is physically impulsive, centrifugal and low. His energy radiates outward from his body rather than being held in. A performer playing this version of Mickey should work with: a lower centre of gravity (knees slightly bent, weight forward onto the balls of the feet, ready to run); loose, uncontrolled arm movements that express the whole thought rather than a controlled portion of it; a physical curiosity that turns the head quickly and often; and an inability to sustain stillness for more than a few beats. These choices signal “child” to an audience without relying on a squeaky voice or exaggerated naivety.

Proxemics matter particularly for the seven-year-old Mickey. Children are not yet fully socialised into adult rules about personal space — Mickey might lean in too close to Edward, touch his arm without permission, press his face very near to examine the new arrival. This invasion of personal space characterises a child who does not yet know how to regulate proximity. An adult audience will recognise it instantly.

Key Fact

Playing a child in drama is a physical skill, not just a vocal one. A lower centre of gravity, outward-radiating energy, impulsive movement and an absence of social proxemics rules are the tools that make an audience believe in the seven-year-old Mickey. Examiners reward performers who can articulate these choices specifically.

Playing Mickey at Twenty-Five: The Body Under Pressure

The adult Mickey — unemployed, dependent on prescription drugs, hollowed out by his circumstances — is almost the physical inverse of the child. Where the child was centrifugal and restless, the adult Mickey is centripetal: his energy collapses inward. A performer should consider: a higher, contracted posture (shoulders forward, chest concave, arms close to the body); a slower, heavier gait that carries the weight of his circumstances in every step; a reduced range of gesture; and a vacancy behind the eyes that can be communicated through a tendency to not quite focus on the person being addressed.

Vocally, the adult Mickey’s pace slows drastically from his childhood delivery. Where the child Mickey fired words out in quick, staccato bursts, the adult speaks with long pauses, incomplete sentences and a lower, flatter pitch that has lost the musicality of his youth. The Liverpudlian accent remains — it is a constant identity marker — but the warmth has drained from it. A vocal coach would work with a performer on this transition, ensuring that the voice reflects the psychological collapse without simply sounding drugged or monotone: there should be occasional flares of the old Mickey, moments where the child resurfaces briefly in a gesture or a laugh, before sinking back under the weight of the adult’s reality.

Students often write “I would use a higher-pitched voice to show Mickey is seven years old.” This is a partial answer that stays in the lower bands because it only addresses one vocal parameter and ignores the physical dimension entirely. Examiners reward answers that articulate physical choices (centre of gravity, movement energy, proxemics) alongside vocal choices (pace, pause pattern, inflection, accent). A squeaky voice without the physical vocabulary of childhood is unconvincing on stage; the two must work together to create a believable age portrayal.

Playing Edward: The Body of Privilege

Edward’s physical and vocal world is the mirror of Mickey’s: contained where Mickey is impulsive, precise where Mickey is loose, and marked by the received pronunciation that signals his class background and private education. A performer playing Edward at seven can show a child who has already begun to internalise the rules of polite behaviour — standing straight, reaching out a hand for a formal greeting, speaking in complete sentences. The comedy of the early scenes between Mickey and Edward depends partly on this contrast: one child who has been taught manners and one who has not.

As adult Edward, the performer faces the challenge of showing a man who genuinely loves Mickey but exists inside a body and accent that marks him as untouchable. Edward’s vocal delivery as a councillor — clear, measured, authoritative — is the very thing that makes Mickey feel excluded and patronised, even when Edward means only warmth. A subtle physical choice for adult Edward might be a very slight distance he instinctively maintains in social situations — a courteous but marked proxemic boundary that has been cultivated by a middle-class upbringing — in contrast to Mickey’s old habit of physical closeness.

Mrs Johnstone: Exhaustion as Physical Vocabulary

Mrs Johnstone is on stage for much of the play, and her physical arc across twenty years is one of the most demanding in British musical theatre. She begins as a young mother — stretched thin but still upright, still animated by the energy of multiple children and the remnants of the “Marilyn Monroe” self-image she carries. As the play progresses, the physical vocabulary of exhaustion should accumulate: a slower gait, a deeper tiredness in the eyes, a tendency to lower her weight onto the nearest surface rather than remain standing. Her voice should age too: a little rougher at the edges, the consonants a little more effortful, the warmth never gone but increasingly hard-won.

In the final scene, the performer playing Mrs Johnstone must find the physical language of a woman who has always known, on some level, that this moment was coming. Her posture in the closing tableau might return briefly to the upright bearing of the prologue, as though the worst has finally happened and something that was braced against it has been released. This is a choice with enormous effect on the audience: grief, but also the terrible completion of a story that was always going to end this way.

At seven: lower centre of gravity, weight on balls of feet, outward-radiating energy, impulsive movement, close proxemics, fast staccato vocal delivery, high inflection at end of phrases, wide expressive eyes.
At fourteen: the body is lengthening and becoming self-conscious; physical choices should show an adolescent awkwardness — longer limbs that seem difficult to manage, a slight slouch that is different from the child’s low-set energy, a voice that has dropped but is not yet settled, moments of swaggering confidence alternating with sudden shyness, particularly around Linda.
At twenty-five: contracted, inward-facing posture; shoulders rolled forward; slower, heavier gait; reduced gesture range; flat vocal delivery with long pauses; a flattening of the Liverpudlian music; eyes that do not quite focus; the physical vocabulary of a person whose hope has been used up.

The collapsed body of Mickey at twenty-five

A performer playing Mickey at twenty-five should use rolled-forward shoulders, a heavy, slow gait and flat vocal delivery with long pauses — the physical vocabulary of exhausted hope.

The Challenge of Playing Time

A performer playing Hanako in The Great Wave faces one of the most demanding tasks in any of the nine set plays: she must show a journey from a defiant 17-year-old arguing on a storm-swept beach in 1979 to a woman in her late thirties who has survived captivity, forced re-education, and the slow erosion of her original self. She does this without the aid of sophisticated prosthetics or years of naturalistic preparation — she does it through the precision of vocal and physical choices, scene by scene, across the play’s 24-year arc.

This is not simply about playing “older.” Playing older is a surface effect (slowed movement, deeper voice). What the play requires is something more specific: tracking how Hanako’s relationship to proxemics, to space, to silence, changes as she learns to survive inside a system designed to contain her. The body that moves freely and claims space on the beach is not the same body ten years into captivity. The difference is not just age — it is accommodation.

Key Fact

Playing Hanako across time requires a performer to track three layers simultaneously: age (physical changes in posture, pace, breath); accommodation (how the body learns to move within a system of surveillance); and internal resistance (the private moments where the self underneath the performance emerges). All three must be visible at different moments of the play.

Hanako: Physical Containment and Release

In the beach scene — Hanako’s last moment of freedom — a performer can play her in full ownership of her body: wide stance, blocking that cuts across the stage diagonally, gestures that reach outward. The argument with Reiko in the storm can use full vocal range — high pitch on challenge, fast pace as the argument escalates, volume that competes with the implied sound of the wind. This is a young woman who has not yet learned that her body can be owned by someone else.

The contrast in the first captivity scenes should be stark. Now, the performer might begin reducing the size of every gesture: arms held closer to the body, movements that do not claim more space than strictly necessary, eye-contact that is carefully managed — not downcast (that would signal defeat too early) but controlled, the eye-contact of someone learning when it is safe to look and when it is not. The voice becomes more contained: lower register, measured pace, pauses that are not emotional hesitation but strategic hesitation — calculating what to say rather than feeling unable to say it.

The “release moments” — private scenes where Hanako is not under official observation — give the performer the opportunity to show what is still alive underneath the accommodation. A sudden small physical release (letting the hands open, a brief change in spine alignment) can communicate volumes. These moments should be very short — the accommodation has become second nature, the release is a flash — and they function as a kind of dramatic punctuation, reminding the audience that Hanako is not the role the state has written for her.

The interrogation scenes are some of the play’s most demanding. Hanako is being asked to confirm or deny an identity — to accept a new name, a new history. A performer who plays these scenes by trying to “look scared” misses the point entirely. The more interesting and more truthful choice is stillness: absolute stillness, placed centre stage under a harsh overhead light, with the minimum of facial expression. This choice tells the audience that Hanako is conserving herself — spending as little energy as possible, giving as little as possible, preserving something inside that the system cannot reach.

Vocally, the same principle applies. A flat, even delivery in the interrogation scenes — not dead, but carefully neutral — communicates the same conservation of self. The voice is not the character’s private voice; it is the voice produced for the officials. The distinction between this voice and the rare private voice (warmer, perhaps slightly faster) is something the audience begins to read as the play goes on, so that a shift in vocal register becomes a signal of private self re-emerging.

Reiko: Grief That Does Not Resolve

The performer playing Reiko faces a different temporal challenge: not the gradual accommodation of captivity but the gradual hardening of unresolved grief into something that looks like certainty. Reiko spends the play refusing to accept that Hanako is dead. In the early scenes this refusal is raw — it can be played with a vocal tension that sits high in the chest, a physical restlessness, hands that cannot settle. In the middle scenes, the grief has been lived with long enough that it has taken on structure — it has become a project, an advocacy position. The proxemic patterns change: Reiko moves toward people, demanding to be taken seriously, whereas early-grief Reiko might move away, closing off.

For a performer, the key is never to play the same version of Reiko twice. Each scene must show the accumulation of years. A simple physical marker — the way she holds herself when addressing officials, a very slight brittleness in the voice that was not there at the beginning — communicates the weight of two decades without requiring the performer to play every moment at full emotional intensity.

Etsuko: Resignation That Is Not Defeat

The mother, Etsuko, ages the most visibly of the three central women across the play’s timeline. But the danger in playing her is to reduce her ageing to physical signifiers only (slower movement, quieter voice) without tracking her interior journey. Etsuko’s trajectory is from active maternal grief to something that examiners often describe as “resignation” — but a performer who plays resignation as a collapse misses the point. Etsuko’s silence in the later scenes is not weakness; it is the outcome of having waited so long that the waiting has become her identity. A performer might express this through very deliberate, economical physicality — each movement purposeful, nothing wasted — and a vocal quality that is low and steady, suggesting not defeat but endurance.

Key Fact

All three central performers must show change over time: this is the play’s deepest requirement. Not a single fixed characterisation but a performance in which the audience can feel the weight of 24 years accumulating in the body and voice. Examiners reward answers that track specific changes — not just “she becomes sadder” but “in the early scenes her voice is in the upper register with rapid pace; by the final act the pace is slower and the pitch lower, suggesting the energy of grief has become the quiet weight of endurance.”

A very common performance-interpretation error is to reduce Hanako’s 24-year journey to a single emotional note: sadness, or alternatively resilience. Both are too simple. Hanako’s journey includes defiance, survival, accommodation, moments of real connection (with Jung Sun), moments of private resistance, and eventually the confirmation that her family has known she was alive — a discovery that is not straightforwardly joyful. A performer who has made a specific, evolving set of physical and vocal choices throughout the play will be able to land that final complexity in a way that a performer playing a single emotion cannot. “I would play her as sad” scores at Developing. “In the teaching scenes I would allow a small warmth to enter the voice when addressing Jung Sun — a slightly raised pitch, a fractionally faster pace — as the only moment where the accommodation shows a crack in its surface” scores at Mastering.

A Play Rooted in Documented Events

Understanding The Great Wave as political theatre requires knowing the history it is built on. Between 1977 and 1983, North Korean agents abducted Japanese citizens in Japan and overseas. The Japanese government has officially confirmed 17 cases; campaigning organisations and some academics put the number higher. These citizens were taken to North Korea and used as language teachers — teaching Japanese to North Korean operatives — and as identity sources for undercover agents operating abroad. The operation was a documented function of state policy, not an aberration.

The most widely known case is that of Megumi Yokota, who was 13 years old when she was abducted in 1977. Her case became the public face of the abduction issue in Japan and internationally: her parents spent decades campaigning for her return, and her story was documented in books, films and parliamentary hearings before and after the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration. The Great Wave is not a biographical account of Megumi Yokota or any single individual, but its research roots in these documented cases are central to how the play functions theatrically. When a director stages the abduction scene, they are staging something the audience knows — or should know — was real. This is the basic condition of documentary theatre: the audience’s knowledge of the real events is part of the theatrical experience.

Key Fact

Between 1977 and 1983, North Korea abducted at least 17 Japanese citizens (Japanese government count) for use as language teachers and identity sources. The 2002 Pyongyang Declaration was the first official acknowledgement that these abductions had taken place.

Cold War East Asia: The Political Context

The abductions took place within a specific Cold War geopolitical context. North Korea in the late 1970s and early 1980s was a tightly closed state with no diplomatic relations with Japan, operating under the leadership of Kim Il-sung. Japan, an American ally with a functioning democracy and a rapidly expanding economy, was the regional contrast: open, prosperous, constitutionally pacifist. The Sea of Japan — the body of water that separates the two countries — was the border through which the abductions were conducted, using small, fast boats on dark nights near isolated beaches.

For a set designer, the political geography of the play can be communicated through the stage itself. A traverse or traverse configuration might represent the two countries as occupying opposite ends of the stage, with the sea — the border — as the acting space between them. A director working in this configuration would be making a staging argument: that the two worlds of the play are literally separated by water, and that every cross-cut transition is a crossing of that divide. A thrust stage might bring the Japanese family sequences close to the audience, making their grief immediate, while the North Korean sequences are played at the farthest reach of the stage.

Japan in the 1980s and 1990s: The Domestic Context

The Japanese family sequences of The Great Wave take place against a backdrop of significant social change. Japan experienced a major asset bubble in the late 1980s; after it burst in the early 1990s, the economy entered a period of stagnation. The families of the abductees spent these decades campaigning in a Japan that did not always want to hear about the abductions — official relations with North Korea were diplomatically awkward, and the Japanese government’s response to the abduction cases was slow and, many families felt, inadequate. A costume designer staging the Japanese family scenes might use the distinctive civilian clothing of 1980s and 1990s Japan — subdued professional wear, practical domestic layers — to ground the audience in the specific social world of families living alongside an unresolved national trauma.

The contrast with the North Korean sequences is a design opportunity. If Japan is warm, domestic and textured — layers of fabric, ambient household sounds, the soft pool of a domestic lamp — then North Korea can be its visual opposite: a world of institutional uniformity, flat surfaces, and the cold geometry of controlled space. A lighting colour palette that reserves amber and warm white for Japan and uses cool blue or neutral white for North Korea is a simple, legible visual grammar that reinforces the play’s structural argument every time a scene changes.

In September 2002, North Korean leader Kim Jong-il met Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi in Pyongyang and acknowledged that North Korean operatives had abducted Japanese citizens. Five surviving abductees were permitted to return to Japan; others, including Megumi Yokota, were declared dead by North Korea. Her family and the Japanese government contested this. The Pyongyang Declaration was a rare moment of official acknowledgement that the abductions had occurred, but it resolved almost nothing for most families. In the play, this event is a structural hinge: it is the moment the audience has been waiting for, and Turnly stages the family’s receipt of this information as a dramatic climax whose resolution is partial at best. A director staging this scene must resist the temptation to treat it as a happy ending: what the Declaration gives the family is confirmation, not return.

Francis Turnly and the Playwright’s Context

Francis Turnly is a Northern Irish playwright of Japanese-Irish heritage. His father, a Northern Irish journalist, met Turnly’s Japanese mother while teaching English in Tokyo. Turnly spent six months researching the abductions and consulted language advisers. The Great Wave had its world premiere at the National Theatre’s Dorfman in 2018, in a co-production with the Tricycle Theatre (now Kiln), directed by Indhu Rubasingham. The Tricycle/Kiln Theatre has a long association with political documentary theatre — producing work that holds institutions to account through theatrical investigation — and this context shapes the production values and staging conventions that Turnly writes within.

For students, the playwright’s dual heritage and personal connection to Japan matter because they explain the emotional register of the play. Turnly is not a journalist reporting on a foreign case; he is a playwright with personal ties to the culture he is writing about. This gives the play a quality of given circumstances-level specificity — the domestic details of Japanese family life, the precise cultural weight of certain kinds of silence, the specific texture of grief across decades — that a more distanced political play might lack.

Key Fact

The play had its world premiere at the National Theatre’s Dorfman in 2018, in a co-production with the Tricycle (now Kiln), directed by Indhu Rubasingham. The Tricycle’s documentary theatre tradition shapes the production’s staging conventions: factual precision, minimal theatrical artifice, the audience as witness.

Examiners note that students who treat The Great Wave as a family drama loosely set during political events miss the central analytical opportunity. The play’s documentary roots are not background: they are the reason the staging choices carry the weight they do. When a director signals the Pyongyang Declaration through a change in lighting state and the sound of a radio broadcast, the audience’s knowledge that this event actually happened amplifies the emotional impact beyond anything a purely fictional story could achieve. A student who answers context questions by describing ‘the difficult political situation between Japan and North Korea’ without naming the abductions, Megumi Yokota or the 2002 Declaration is unlikely to reach the highest marks. Specific historical knowledge, correctly applied to a discussion of staging or performance, is what distinguishes the strongest answers.

A Play Between Two Traditions

Any production of The Great Wave must make a fundamental directorial decision: how much does it lean into its documentary theatre roots, and how much does it employ Brechtian distance? These are not mutually exclusive — in practice, the most powerful productions of the play hold both simultaneously. But understanding each tradition separately helps a director and designer make deliberate, informed choices rather than accidental ones.

Francis Turnly spent six months researching the DPRK abductions. This research heritage means that the play carries what documentary theatre scholars call an ethical obligation to the real: the events depicted happened to identifiable people. At the same time, Turnly is a dramatist, not a journalist, and The Great Wave is not a verbatim play. It uses the tools of dramatic art — composite characters, shaped scenes, theatrical climax — to communicate the truth of the abductions in a way that a simple documentary record cannot.

Key Fact

Documentary theatre (including verbatim theatre at its purest) uses the actual words, documents, or testimonies of real people. The Great Wave is not verbatim — Turnly has shaped and fictionalised — but its documentary roots give it the weight of the real: examiners reward students who understand that the play engages with documented historical events (the DPRK abductions, the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration) rather than treating it as pure fiction.

Brecht: The Audience as Witness

Bertolt Brecht’s approach to political theatre rested on a fundamental conviction: audiences who are lost in emotional identification with characters on stage are not thinking. He developed a range of techniques designed to interrupt this identification and return the audience to critical awareness. His term for the distancing effect produced by these techniques was the Verfremdungseffekt, often translated as the “alienation effect” or “estrangement effect.”

For The Great Wave, the Brechtian frame is powerful because the play is about a political crime: the DPRK abductions are not a private tragedy but a state act, and Turnly wants the audience to understand them as such. A director who applies Brechtian thinking might use direct address at key structural moments — a scene might pause, a character might step out of the fiction to address the audience as though they are witnesses rather than spectators. Projected titles (dates, locations, the number of confirmed abductees) can interrupt scenes to insist that this is not just a story but a documented event.

Brecht’s concept of gestus is directly applicable to the power dynamics of The Great Wave. The officials who oversee Hanako’s captivity can be staged with a gestus that makes their social role unmistakable: a particular upright bearing, a way of occupying the stage that signals authority without requiring it to be stated. Kum-Chol, Hanako’s husband in North Korea, is a character Turnly renders as recognisably human — but a Brechtian directorial choice might use gestus to ensure the audience always reads the role he plays in the system, even in his most sympathetic moments.

While Brechtian techniques work powerfully for the play’s political argument, the role of Hanako cannot be reduced to a gestus. Her 24-year journey demands what Stanislavski’s method offers: a detailed understanding of the character’s given circumstances (what has been taken from her, what she still has), her objectives at each moment (to survive, to preserve herself, to find some form of connection), and her relationship to the other characters as real psychological encounters rather than symbolic positions.

The teaching scenes with Jung Sun are the clearest example. These scenes depend on the audience sensing a genuine emotional shift in Hanako — something approaching warmth, however provisional — even within captivity. A Brechtian approach alone would flatten this. Stanislavski’s attention to given circumstances (what does Hanako know, what does she need, what is the emotional history between these two people?) gives the performer the tools to make that warmth specific and earned. The result is a production that can be politically clear (Brechtian) and emotionally true (Stanislavskian) at the same time.

The Ethical Dimension: Staging Real Victims

Because The Great Wave is based on real people’s experiences, any production carries an ethical responsibility that a fully invented play does not. A Brechtian directorial approach can honour this: rather than asking the audience to live through Hanako’s captivity as a fully immersive emotional experience (which would place us in the centre of her story), the Brechtian frame positions us as witnesses. We are asked to see clearly, to think, to judge — and perhaps to act. This is the didactic intent of political theatre: not to make audiences cry and go home, but to make them understand something they could choose to act on.

Key Fact

The most successful productions of The Great Wave use both practitioners: Stanislavski for the private emotional truth of Hanako and the family (so the audience cares); Brecht for the political frame (so the audience thinks and understands the systemic cause). The two approaches do not cancel each other out — they produce the complexity the play requires.

The Tanaka Household: Where Documentary Meets Domestic

The Japan scenes — the Tanaka family — offer a design and performance zone where the documentary and domestic meet. The design can be naturalistic enough to feel real (a Japanese domestic interior, period detail from the 1980s onwards) while the blocking and spatial arrangement reflect the Brechtian idea that every domestic arrangement is also a political one: who sits at the table, who stands, who approaches the officials. A tableau at a key moment — the family receiving news from the officials, frozen in the light — can function as both a Brechtian quotation mark (“look at this image”) and a moment of Stanislavskian emotional weight.

Many students believe that applying Brecht means the audience must not feel anything — that emotional engagement is the enemy of political thinking. This is a misreading of Brecht’s own practice. Brecht wanted audiences to feel; he wanted them to not be incapacitated by feeling. His techniques interrupt total identification at key moments — they do not prohibit warmth, sympathy or even grief. In The Great Wave, a production that generates no emotional response to Hanako’s situation will fail to communicate why the abductions are an injustice worth caring about. The Brechtian frame asks the audience to understand the systemic cause of their emotional response — not to switch it off.

Why Performer Skills Matter

A performer communicates character, emotion, and intention entirely through what they do with their voice and body. The audience cannot read the performer’s mind — they can only see and hear what the performer gives them. This means every choice — whether to speak quickly or slowly, whether to stand tall or collapse inward, whether to move toward another character or retreat — must be deliberate, repeatable, and truthful to the character’s situation. The specification separates performer skills into two categories: vocal skills and physical skills. In the exam you will often be asked to write “as a performer” — which means naming specific skills from both categories and anchoring them to a named moment of the play.

Vocal Skills: Terms Named in the Specification

The specification gives nine examples of performers’ vocal interpretation of character: accent, volume, pitch, timing, pace, intonation, phrasing, emotional range and delivery of lines. Use them to explain how a performer communicates character.

Intonation is a subtler skill than volume or pace, but it is the one that determines how a line is understood. The same words can mean entirely different things depending on how they are inflected. A character saying a simple farewell can, through intonation, communicate resignation, contempt, grief, or barely suppressed rage — without changing a single word. Projection is the ability to be heard clearly from the back of the auditorium; it is not simply about being loud, but about placing the voice forward, using breath support and resonance.

Key Fact

A pause is not an accident — it is a deliberate choice. A long pause before answering a question can communicate guilt, calculation, fear, or contempt. A short, clipped pause mid-sentence can signal suppressed emotion. In exam answers, when you name “pause” as a vocal skill, you must explain what the pause communicates at that specific moment — not just that it “creates tension”.

Physical Skills: Voice with the Body

The specification gives examples of performers’ physical interpretation of character: build, age, height, facial features, movement, posture, gesture and facial expression. Posture is perhaps the most immediate physical signal: a character who stands with their shoulders back and chin level reads as confident or authoritative; a character who hunches forward, pulls their shoulders inward, and lowers their gaze reads as cowed, tired, or defeated. Status in theatre is communicated more through posture than through any other single physical tool.

Gesture must be precise and intentional. An aimless wave of the hand is not a gesture — it is a habit. A clenched fist rising slowly to the chest and then stopping tells a very specific story about suppressed emotion. Gesture and speech should either reinforce each other (congruent) or contradict each other (incongruent) — incongruent gesture and speech is a powerful tool for showing a character saying one thing while feeling another. The examiner wants to know not just that you would gesture, but exactly what gesture, at what moment, and to what effect on the audience.

Stillness is the absence of unnecessary movement, used at a moment of intensity so that the audience’s focus sharpens. A performer who has been moving constantly through a scene and then suddenly becomes completely still draws the audience’s eye with great force — the stillness signals that something of significance is happening. Used at a moment of realisation, confrontation, or grief, stillness amplifies emotional impact in ways that movement cannot.

Timing is not just about comedy (though comedy depends on it entirely). Timing is the performer’s ability to land a line, a gesture, or a movement at precisely the right moment relative to what has come before and what will come after. A reaction that arrives a beat too late can read as distracted; a reaction that arrives a beat too early can deflate a moment. Timing requires the performer to listen — to their scene partner, to the sound design, to the rhythm of the scene — and respond within it.

Proxemics: Using the Space

Proxemics — the use of physical distance and spatial relationships on stage — is how a performer communicates the quality of a relationship without words. Characters who are in close proximity signal intimacy, trust, vulnerability, or threat, depending on the context. Characters kept at opposite ends of the stage — one upstage left, one downstage right — communicate distance, estrangement, or reluctance. As a performer, the choice of where to stand relative to another character, and how that distance changes through a scene, is a form of choreography — it maps the emotional journey of the relationship.

The direction of the performer’s body also matters: facing front (full front) is open and available to the audience; in profile (three-quarter turn) suggests the performer is engaged with another character rather than with the audience; back to the audience (full back) is rare in proscenium staging and usually signals a powerful dramatic moment of withdrawal or concealment.

Key Fact

The most common exam error in performer questions is writing “I would say it angrily” or “I would look scared”. These score in the Emerging band because they do not specify a skill. Always translate emotion into craft: “I would lower my pitch and reduce my pace to almost nothing, allowing a three-second pause before the final word, while keeping my body completely still with my gaze lowered to the floor, so the audience sees the character’s grief as something he cannot speak.”

Imagine a scene where a young character finally confronts an older authority figure who has wronged them. As a performer playing the young character, you might begin the speech with a raised pitch and rapid pace — the voice tight and high from adrenaline — then let it slow and drop in pitch as the character finds their authority, ending the speech in a low, measured register with a deliberate pause after the final accusation. Physically, you might start the scene in profile, angled away from the authority figure, then rotate by increments through the speech until you are full-front to both the authority figure and the audience, signalling full confrontation. Your proxemics might move from upstage, close to the exit, toward downstage centre, closing the distance between yourself and the authority figure with each step.

As a lighting designer for that same moment, you might design the opening of the speech in a warm, low-intensity side-light that keeps the young character partially in shadow, signalling their uncertainty. As the character gains courage, you slowly bring up a front-of-house profile lantern in a neutral white, increasing in intensity through the speech, so that by the final accusation the young character is in full, clear, unambiguous light — exposed and resolute. The authority figure, meanwhile, is allowed to drop fractionally in intensity, as though the balance of power is visibly shifting.

A Year in the Price Garden

Andrew Bovell's Things I Know to Be True is structured around the four seasons of a single year. Each season belongs primarily to one of the four adult Price children — Pip in spring, Mark in summer, Ben in autumn, Rosie in winter — and each season delivers a revelation that unsettles the suburban family. This seasonal frame is not decorative. It is the play's dramatic structure: four interlocking acts of unequal emotional weight, building cumulatively towards a shock at the play's close that retrospectively re-orders what the audience believed they understood.

The structure is broadly chronological, moving through a calendar year. Yet within each season, time is not always linear. Bovell inserts direct address monologue passages, particularly through the voice of Rosie, who acts as a narrator-figure. These moments allow characters to speak from a future perspective, as if looking back on what the season revealed, creating a layer of dramatic irony that gives the audience information slightly ahead of the other characters.

Key Fact

The four seasons map onto four children: spring (Pip), summer (Mark), autumn (Ben), winter (Rosie). Each season brings a revelation that tests the Price family's sense of who they are and what holds them together.

The Kitchen and the Garden as Twin Centres

The action takes place primarily in two spaces: the Price family kitchen and the suburban rose garden Bob tends throughout the year. The garden is both a literal and symbolic space. As a symbol, it holds Bob's emotional life: his sense of order, control and beauty in a world where his children's revelations keep threatening to undermine the certainties he has built. On stage, the garden can be established simply — a few rose bushes, a soil patch, a garden chair — and the blocking often places Bob alone there before another character arrives to disturb his peace.

The kitchen, meanwhile, is the domestic centre: Fran's territory, associated with food, practicality and direct speech. In production, the two spaces can coexist on stage simultaneously, so that a director's choice about proxemics between characters moving between kitchen and garden becomes itself a staging language. When a child crosses from the kitchen to join Bob in the garden, the move marks a shift in emotional register.

A common student error is to retell the four revelations as plot summary. Examiners reward analysis of why Bovell chose this structure. Consider what the seasonal frame achieves: each revelation lands at a different emotional temperature. Spring carries the energy of new beginnings; Pip's departure is therefore against the grain of hope. Autumn's association with decay and harvest perfectly frames Ben's arrest. Winter's coldness amplifies the shock of the play's ending.

The structural symmetry also allows Bovell to make each child's season resonate against the others. The audience accumulates information across the year, so by winter they carry the emotional weight of every previous season. As a designer, you might reflect this accumulation through a gradually changing lighting palette — brighter, warmer in spring, progressively more stripped and cool by winter — creating a visual arc that reinforces the structural one.

Frantic Assembly Movement Within the Seasonal Frame

The play was co-developed with Frantic Assembly, the British physical theatre company, and their influence shapes where moments of stylised movement are inserted into the seasonal structure. At emotional peaks — moments too large for naturalistic dialogue — the characters enter Frantic Assembly movement sequences: chair duets, contact lifts and round-by-through-under partner work. These sequences do not replace the dialogue; they abstracted the emotion that dialogue cannot fully express.

In structural terms, these movement passages function like the heightened soliloquies in classical drama: they signal that the play is stepping outside its naturalistic register to allow the audience to feel rather than analyse. As a performer, you must understand where you are in the seasonal structure when one of these sequences begins — the physical demands of a spring chair duet carry a different emotional charge from a winter one.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly movement sequences interrupt the naturalistic dialogue at moments of heightened emotion. They are structural devices, not decoration: they show what characters feel but cannot say.

The Shock Ending: Dramatic Irony in Retrospect

Bovell builds a late-play revelation about Bob — a revelation that casts new light on everything that has preceded it. This is a structural device Bovell uses across his work: the thing you think you know is retrospectively undone. The audience carries their understanding of Bob through all four seasons and then, in winter, discovers they have been watching with incomplete information.

For a director, the challenge is to stage the ending so that the tableau at the play's close resonates with every earlier tableau the audience has seen. The ending must feel both surprising and, in retrospect, inevitable — the hallmark of precisely engineered dramatic structure. In production, designers often use a sudden, stark shift in the lighting state to mark the revelation: a wash that was warm and amber throughout the summer season becomes a cold, bare white or a near-blackout, so that the structural shock is felt as a physical change in the space.

Students sometimes treat the direct-address passages as straightforward narration — information delivery. In fact, they are structurally complex. Rosie's monologues are spoken from a temporal perspective that is partly ahead of where the action has reached. This means the audience is in a state of partial dramatic irony: they sense that things will go wrong before they go wrong. As a performer playing Rosie, the challenge is to hold both timeframes in your body: the innocence of the present tense and the knowledge of the future. Physically, this might mean a stillness that contrasts with the movement of the scenes around her, positioning her slightly apart — at upstage centre, separated from the family activity downstage — to suggest her dual temporal position.

Designing a World Without a Set

The 2013 New Vic production used theatre in the round at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme. That configuration shapes its design decisions: there is no back wall to hang flats on, no single “front” to place a painted landscape. Everything must work from all angles. This forces the production into a minimalist aesthetic where objects, light and bodies carry the entire scenic burden — and that turns out to be the production’s greatest creative asset.

For a GCSE Drama student, this unit is a masterclass in how minimal scenography can actually communicate more than a fully realised naturalistic set. When the audience watches the company convert four chairs into a railway carriage, they are not passive observers — they are actively co-creating the fiction. The designer’s job is to give them just enough information so that their imagination completes the picture.

Key Fact
