The production typically uses chairs as railway carriages, rope as ship rigging and canes as multiple tools — each transformation is achieved through precise physical use by the performer, not through visual trickery.

Set Design: The Empty Space as Possibility

The set designer’s first decision is stage configuration and levels. A production of this play that uses a central raised platform for the Reform Club gives Fogg an immediate visual authority: he is literally above the world he is about to conquer. When Passepartout operates at floor level, the contrast in levels communicates their relationship instantly, before a word is spoken.

Across the episodic structure, the only constants are a table and a set of chairs that can be reconfigured per scene. A row of chairs placed upstage and angled slightly can become the viewing gallery of the Reform Club; the same chairs rotated and placed downstage become a train carriage hurtling across America. The speed of these reconfigurations is part of the show’s theatrical language — an audience that sees chairs moved quickly learns to read those moves as scene changes and accepts the new location immediately.

A persistent student misconception is to suggest a large scenic elephant as the design solution for the India sequence. This misses the form the play is written for. Productions use puppet elephants or pure physical theatre (ensemble bodies) precisely because the play’s style is anti-naturalistic. Suggesting a painted or mechanised elephant in an exam answer signals that you have misread the genre. Examiners reward students who suggest stylised physical solutions consistent with the ensemble aesthetic — for example, a puppet elephant built collaboratively by the company using poles, fabric and collective movement, or pure ensemble mime.

Lighting Design: Painting the Globe

Because the set is minimal, the lighting designer carries enormous scenic responsibility. Each new location must be painted in light. A warm amber wash from a high angle creates the heat of India; a cold blue wash from the sides suggests the Atlantic crossing in winter; a neutral, slightly grey top light places us in foggy London. Lighting wash choices are the quickest way to transport an audience across continents.

More specific effects come from lantern choices. A profile lantern can be used to throw a hard-edged spotlight onto Fogg at the moment of the wager — isolating him from the Reform Club chatter as if the rest of the world has receded. A gobo of moving water patterns projected from above transforms the bare stage floor into the surface of the ocean for the Atlantic crossing. These specific design choices communicate location and mood simultaneously without a single piece of scenery being added.

Key Fact

Lighting transitions replace scene changes in this production. The move from a warm amber wash (India) to a cold blue wash (the Atlantic) is a design shorthand that takes less than ten seconds and instantly relocates the audience without a single piece of furniture being moved.

Sound Design: A Soundscape Around the World

The soundscape is equally important. Train whistles, steam hiss, ship bells, the call to prayer from a minaret, Yokohama street noise and the rhythmic clatter of railway track can all be designed into the production’s score. The sound designer has two main tools: diegetic sounds (those the characters would hear — the steam engine’s release of pressure) and non-diegetic underscore (a rising orchestral phrase as Fogg’s train accelerates, unheard by Fogg but felt by the audience).

Some productions interpolate live music — a pianist in the corner, a percussionist tracking the journey — which adds the additional layer of music-hall theatricality that the play’s comic tradition invites. The sound of a music-hall piano underscoring a chase sequence immediately signals that the play is aware of its own genre and inviting the audience to enjoy the theatricality, not just the story.

Costume Design: Identity in an Accessory

Costume design in this production must solve the multi-roling problem: one performer will play many roles, so each role must be instantly readable from a limited set of accessories. The base layer — typically a neutral Victorian-inflected suit in grey or cream — stays constant. Over it, a pith helmet signals India; a captain’s peaked cap and a slightly maritime posture signals the ship; a sheepskin hat and heavier coat signals the American West.

Signifier costume strategy means the designer must choose accessories that read clearly from every audience sightline (critical in in-the-round staging) and that can be donned and shed in seconds. The choice of colour is also important for character identity: Fogg’s costume is typically a consistent, precise dark grey or navy — the visual equivalent of his personality. Passepartout, by contrast, might have a slightly more bohemian base layer and brighter accessories to signal his continental exuberance.

As a lighting designer for the moment when the company begins burning the ship’s wooden deck for fuel, you might build from a cool steel-blue wash (open Atlantic, night-time) and introduce a warm orange-red flicker from below stage level — using floor-level lanterns or footlights — to suggest the growing fire. The juxtaposition of cold blue above and warm orange below creates a visual instability that mirrors the desperation of the moment. A slow, pulsing rhythm to the flicker (rather than a frantic strobe) keeps the audience in the drama rather than pulling them into a safety-concern.

As a sound designer, you might layer a low, continuous drone beneath the scene — representing the ship’s engines slowing — with the distant crack and hiss of timber burning. Non-diegetic underscore could begin quietly here: a single, sustained string note that rises very gradually in pitch as the fire takes hold, cueing the audience that something important is at stake without spelling it out.

A Play Built Around One Room

A Taste of Honey takes place almost entirely in a single rented flat in Salford — damp walls, sparse furniture, a view of nothing in particular. This single-setting approach is one of Shelagh Delaney’s most powerful structural choices. The world beyond the flat is real but unreachable: Peter’s car, the canal, the fairground, the docks where the Boy’s ship is moored — all of it exists only as something characters come from or disappear to. As a designer, you might use a set design that makes the flat feel cramped and trapped: low ceilings implied by low borders, a single practical window through which light changes with the seasons, peeling wallpaper as a visual symbol of neglect.

Key Fact

The play is set entirely in a rented flat in Salford, Lancashire, in the late 1950s. The single, unchanging location keeps the audience focused on relationships and traps Jo and Helen in their circumstances — escape is something that only happens off-stage.

The Two-Act Structure

The play divides into two acts separated by the passage of roughly six months. Act One takes place in winter: Helen and Jo arrive at the flat, Helen departs with Peter, and Jo begins her brief relationship with the Boy before he sails away. Act Two takes place in spring and summer: Jo is pregnant, Geof moves in to help her, and eventually Helen returns and Geof is forced out. The structure is symmetrical in a bleak way — the play begins with a departure (Helen leaves Jo for Peter) and ends with a departure (Geof leaves Jo for good), leaving Jo and Helen alone together just as they began.

This circularity is Delaney’s signal to the audience that nothing has fundamentally changed. Jo has not escaped the cycle her mother modelled. A director staging this structural irony might use identical blocking at the opening and the close — Jo in the same position by the window, light at the same low winter angle — so the audience recognises the echo visually.

Kitchen-sink drama is a movement that emerged in British theatre in 1956–1959, placing working-class characters in domestic spaces at the centre of the action. Before this shift, the mainstream British stage was dominated by drawing-room comedies and upper-middle-class settings. John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) and A Taste of Honey (1958) were its two landmark texts.

For a designer, the kitchen-sink aesthetic demands authentic poverty: crockery that is chipped rather than matched, a gas ring rather than a full cooker, curtains that don’t quite reach. Props become symbols of economic reality. Costume choices reinforce class position: Jo’s school coat worn past the point of childhood, Helen’s attempts at glamour with second-hand accessories. A prop as symbol — such as the cheap ring the Boy gives Jo — communicates both affection and precarity in a single moment.

The Role of the Jazz Musicians

One of the most distinctive structural devices in A Taste of Honey is the presence of live jazz musicians on stage throughout the performance. This was added by Joan Littlewood’s Theatre Workshop during rehearsal — it was not in Delaney’s original script — and it draws directly on Brechtian practice. The musicians comment on the action, punctuate scene transitions and prevent the audience from ever fully forgetting that they are in a theatre watching a play. This breaks the fourth wall and creates a presentational quality sitting alongside the naturalistic domestic content.

Key Fact

Live jazz musicians on stage was a Theatre Workshop addition, not in Delaney’s original script. They comment on the action, mark transitions between scenes and create a Brechtian distance that prevents the play from becoming pure naturalism.

Staging Configuration and Space

The original premiere at Theatre Royal Stratford East used a proscenium arch configuration. For a 21st-century production, directors have choices that alter meaning. A thrust or in-the-round configuration would place the audience in closer proximity to Jo’s cramped flat, making the poverty and intimacy of the scenes between Jo and Geof intensely felt. Positioning the jazz musicians upstage in a proscenium staging keeps them visible but separate, emphasising their role as commentators rather than participants. In a thrust configuration, musicians placed to the side could feel more embedded in the world of the play, blurring their Brechtian function.

A common mistake is to describe A Taste of Honey as a purely naturalistic play. The domestic setting, dialect speech and psychological truth of the characters are naturalistic, but the jazz musicians, the moments of direct address to the audience, and the tonal swings from comedy into pathos are all presentational or Brechtian in character. Examiners reward students who identify this hybrid form and discuss how the two modes create meaning together.

A designer staging the hybrid form might keep the set itself firmly realistic — a literally rendered damp flat — while using lighting states that become stylised at key moments: a cool blue wash for the scene by the canal, a harsh white special on Jo when she realises she is pregnant, warmth flooding the stage only during the few scenes when Geof and Jo are at peace together. This contrast between naturalistic set and expressive lighting communicates the emotional temperature to the audience without changing a single piece of furniture.

The Performer's Job: Translating Text into Body

Every character in Romeo and Juliet presents a specific set of performance challenges. A performer must not simply feel the emotion of a scene — they must make choices about vocal interpretation and physical interpretation that communicate those feelings to an audience in the back row. Saying “I would play Romeo as passionate” is not a performance choice. Saying “I would enter the balcony scene at a run from upstage left, my voice breathless and high, slowing to stillness as I see Juliet above me, my volume dropping to near-whisper and my gaze fixed upward” is a performance choice. This lesson works through the key scenes with that level of specificity.

Romeo at the Balcony Scene

When Romeo discovers Juliet on the balcony in Act 2 Scene 2, a performer faces an immediate staging question: where is he? In most productions he is downstage, in shadow, while Juliet is elevated. The physical relationship — him below, her above — is already a staging argument about the terms of their love: she is the fixed point and he is the one reaching upward.

Vocally, a performer playing Romeo at this moment has several strong choices. He has just come from the feast, from the noise and heat of the Capulet party. His speech opens with wonder — the famous lines about the sun are an act of private worship, not a declaration to Juliet herself. A performer might choose to speak them quietly, almost to themselves, the pace slow and hushed, as if articulating something almost too private to say aloud. Proxemics here are crucial: if he comes too far downstage and too close to the audience, the speech becomes a set piece; if he remains mid-stage in partial shadow, the audience feels they are watching something private, something stolen.

Key Fact

Romeo’s youth and impulsiveness are not just character traits — they are physical habits. A good performer communicates his haste through short, forward movements that stop abruptly; his intensity through stillness at key moments, as if the body has caught up with the feeling. The contrast between physical rush and sudden arrested stillness is what makes the character visible.

Juliet: Watchful, Not Passive

A common mistake in staging Juliet in the balcony scene is to place her as an object of Romeo’s gaze — passive, waiting to be addressed. The text gives Juliet her own complex inner life in this scene: she is thinking, questioning, testing the speed of this encounter. A performer should resist the temptation to play Juliet as rapturous from the first moment. Instead, her physical language might begin guarded — arms partially wrapped around herself, a slight turn of the body away from full exposure — and open gradually as the exchange deepens.

Vocally, Juliet’s lines in the balcony scene move between lyrical verse and rapid questioning. A performer can use pace to distinguish these registers: the lyrical moments slower and more openly pitched, the questioning moments faster and at a slightly higher pitch, leaning forward across the balcony railing. The physical lean forward over the balcony is itself a choice: it closes the physical distance that the staging has imposed, making visible her desire to breach the social and physical separation that the design has built.

Mercutio’s Queen Mab speech in Act 1 is one of the most demanding extended speeches in the play for a performer. It begins as playful mockery of Romeo’s romantic idealism, but shifts midway into something darker and more feverish. A performer must negotiate this tonal arc physically: the opening of the speech might be delivered on the move, circling Romeo, voice bright and pace quick — the performance of a man who controls the room. As the speech escalates, the physical energy might become less controlled: larger gestures, a wider path around the stage, the voice pushing into a higher register, the pace accelerating until Romeo’s interruption is almost an act of physical rescue.

For a director, where Mercutio ends the Queen Mab speech — and what his physical state is — is a choice about how to read the character. Is his fever the sign of a man who is already at the edge? A director might use a lighting state change during the speech — a subtle tightening of the beam around Mercutio, the other characters slightly darker — to isolate his internal world from the social space around him, making visible what Romeo cannot yet see.

Tybalt and the Duel: Physical Theatre

Tybalt’s defining quality is controlled, cold aggression. A performer making choices for Tybalt’s scenes in Act 3 Scene 1 must resist the temptation to play him as simply angry. Tybalt’s rage is disciplined — it has the shape of emotional memory directed through precise physical training. A still, upright posture with contained hands signals danger more effectively than wild movement. The performer might choose to keep Tybalt’s voice consistently low and measured, the pitch barely rising even in the heat of the confrontation — the contrast between his stillness and the chaos around him making him more frightening, not less.

The choreography of the duel itself is a design question as much as a performance question. A director drawing on physical theatre approaches — as Frantic Assembly did in their 2008 Othello — though that technique translates directly to Romeo and Juliet — might stage the fight as a sequence of highly stylised lifts, falls and slow-motion impacts rather than a realistic sword fight. This approach makes visible the emotional weight of each hit: Mercutio’s death might be staged as a moment of sudden, terrible stillness — a tableau of the body in mid-fall — before the action resumes.

The tomb scene in Act 5 is the most demanding sequence for both Romeo and Juliet performers. Romeo enters believing Juliet is dead; the performer must communicate the quality of grief that has moved beyond ordinary feeling into a kind of cold clarity. Vocally, Romeo’s speech in the tomb might be delivered at a lower pitch than earlier in the play, pace steady and deliberate, as if each sentence is being chosen with great care — the language of a man who has decided. The physical language changes too: where the earlier Romeo moved impulsively and quickly, this Romeo might move with the deliberate slowness of the bereaved, touching the stone, touching Juliet’s hand, placing himself beside her with a precision that feels final.

When Juliet wakes to find Romeo dead, the performer has a completely different task: she moves from the confusion of waking to understanding to action in the space of a few lines. A director must choreograph this arc. The waking might be staged slowly — gradual, the body reasserting itself — then snapping into urgency when she sees Romeo. Her final speech should not be played at speed: the verse is short-lined and decisive, and a performer who slows down and lowers the volume, speaking as if into a silence the audience must lean into, will hold the house more completely than one who rushes the ending.

Key Fact

Examiner feedback consistently identifies the same gap in performer answers: students describe the emotion but not the physical action. A strong answer always names a body part (hands, gaze, posture, feet), a spatial choice (proxemics to another character or to the set) and a vocal quality (pace, pitch, volume, pause) — all three anchored to a specific named moment.

The Challenge: One World, Eight Actors

Laura Eason’s stage adaptation of Jules Verne’s novel asks a small ensemble to create an entire planet. Fogg’s journey crosses three continents, dozens of locations, and involves dozens of incidental characters — customs officials, ship’s captains, train conductors, Yokohama acrobats and one very large elephant. With a cast of typically eight, every performer must be skilled in multi-roling: stepping out of a minor part, shedding an accent or a hat, and stepping instantly into another. The play’s pleasure lies in watching this transformation happen live, in front of the audience, with no apology and no disguise.

Understanding these dramatic methods is essential for exam-style questions. Examiners want to see that you recognise why Eason chose this form, not just that the cast is small. The form makes the world feel vast and the journey feel kinetic — qualities a naturalistic production with a large cast and scene-changes could never achieve.

Key Fact

Eason’s adaptation uses multi-roling, mime, direct address narration, object transformation and ensemble physical theatre as its core dramatic methods. Together they let eight actors tell a story that spans the globe.

Narration and Direct Address

One of the production’s most important tools is direct address. Company members step forward to narrate transitions between scenes, update the audience on the days remaining, or comment on Fogg’s progress. This has two effects: it keeps the racing pace alive (no long scene-change during which energy drains away), and it recruits the audience as fellow travellers tracking the wager in real time.

Narration here is not passive. A performer narrating a train journey is also simultaneously performing it — their voice creates the soundscape while their body mimes the carriage, so the boundaries between “telling” and “showing” dissolve. This is ensemble storytelling at its most efficient. The technique owes a debt to practitioners such as Complicite, whose work since the 1980s has made the narrator—performer a central figure in physical theatre.

A common student error is to treat Eason’s ensemble form as a practical limitation — “there aren’t enough actors for a big cast.” This misses the point entirely. Eason chose this form deliberately because the experience of watching actors transform — from a train conductor to an elephant’s front legs to a Reform Club gentleman — creates theatrical energy that a naturalistic production cannot. The rapid role-switching mirrors the dizzying speed of Fogg’s journey. Examiners reward students who understand that the form is the meaning.

Mime and Physical Theatre

Mime is the engine of the production’s scene-setting. Where a naturalistic production would build a set, this company uses bodies. In the journey through India on elephant-back, the ensemble arranges itself to suggest the rhythm and sway of a large animal — one or two performers may form the front legs, others the haunches, while Fogg and Passepartout “ride” on top. The physical precision demanded of the company is equivalent to that of a dance piece.

Similarly, the crossing of the snowy American plains by train sees the ensemble arranged in rows of chairs, collectively swaying as the “carriage” accelerates. A performer at the front enacts the engine’s motion. The audience reads these configurations instantly. The vocabulary draws on the physical theatre tradition associated with Frantic Assembly and Complicite: the body is a flexible instrument capable of representing any object or environment with the right training and ensemble trust.

Key Fact

In this play, mime is not a fallback for missing props — it is the primary visual language. The audience’s imagination is recruited as a co-creator: they read a row of sway-and-jostle bodies as a train because the physical rhythm is unmistakably right.

Object Transformation

Object transformation is the third pillar of this production’s method. Chairs become railway carriages or the pews of a Reform Club; a length of rope becomes the rigging of a ship; a cane becomes a walking stick and then a conductor’s baton and then a rifle. The audience learns to interpret these transformations rapidly, partly because the physical use of the object teaches them what it “is” at any given moment.

This technique demands that performers commit fully. A chair is only a railway carriage if the performer sitting in it behaves exactly as they would in a moving train. The physical life — the sway, the grip on an imaginary armrest, the gaze out of an invisible window — persuades the audience. Break the physical logic and the fiction collapses. This requirement for total physical commitment is a core principle of physical theatre.

As a performer playing one of the ensemble in the elephant sequence, you might hold a low-to-the-ground posture, knees slightly bent, arms loose at the sides to suggest bulk. Your rhythm would synchronise with the other “legs” of the elephant — a slow, deliberate, four-count sway. Vocally, you would be silent: the physical work carries the scene. Your proxemics to the other ensemble members are tight — within touching distance — to suggest you are one creature rather than separate performers.

As a lighting designer, you might use a warm amber lighting special from a high angle to suggest the heat of the Indian sun. A gobo projecting dappled leaf-shadow patterns could suggest jungle canopy without a single physical piece of set. The warm wash would contrast with the cooler, greyer light used in London, immediately orientating the audience in a different part of the world.

Fast Costume Changes and Comic Timing

Multi-roling also demands a distinctive costume strategy. The production typically uses a base layer for each performer — a neutral Victorian suit or simple rehearsal costume — onto which accessories are layered rapidly: a hat, a badge, an accent, a way of walking. The base layer plus accessories system means a change from Reform Club gentleman to Indian customs official takes seconds rather than minutes.

Alongside this runs one of the production’s most important performance demands: comic timing. The play’s humour depends on the contrast between Fogg’s absolute stillness — his refusal to be rattled by any obstacle — and Passepartout’s physical and emotional expressiveness. Fogg’s stillness is the comic engine: it sets up a straight line against which Passepartout’s energy lands. Examiners reward students who understand that Fogg’s restraint is as much a performance choice as Passepartout’s flamboyance.

Key Takeaways

  • Multi-roling, mime, direct address narration and object transformation are Eason’s core dramatic methods — they allow eight performers to create a globe-spanning world and are central to the play’s theatrical identity.
  • Narration collapses the boundary between telling and showing: the narrating performer is simultaneously performing the action, keeping pace alive and recruiting the audience as fellow travellers.
  • Comic timing — particularly the contrast between Fogg’s stillness and Passepartout’s energy — is a performance choice, not an accident; examiners reward students who analyse it as a deliberate method with a specific effect on the audience.
