A Cast of Arrivals and Departures

Every character in A Taste of Honey either arrives and leaves, or is left behind. Shelagh Delaney’s five-character study maps a world in which no relationship is secure and every connection is temporary. As a performer or director, understanding each character’s function in this structure of departure is essential to every staging decision. The way characters move through space — proxemics — tells the audience about power and need before a single line is spoken.

Jo

Jo is a teenager, sharp-tongued and quietly terrified. She has literary ambitions — she notices the wallpaper, she reads, she wants to become an art student — but she is surrounded by a world that does not accommodate that ambition. As a performer playing Jo, you are balancing two registers simultaneously: a caustic wit that Jo deploys as self-protection, and an underlying fear and longing she rarely allows the audience to see directly. In the early scenes with Helen, Jo keeps physical distance — rarely upstage of her mother, often crossing to the window or the door as if planning an exit. In the scenes with the Boy, the performer might gradually reduce that distance: a tentative step closer, a hand movement that almost reaches out, the body language of someone discovering trust for the first time.

Vocally, Jo uses pace and pitch as armour. A performer might deliver her sharpest lines at speed, running the words together to prevent silence — and then allow a sudden stillness, a lowered volume, when something genuine escapes. Contrast between those two registers, anchored to specific moments, is what makes Jo's character legible across the play’s emotional range. A costume designer might keep Jo in the same school coat throughout Act One — slightly too small, buttons straining — as a visual signal that childhood is ending whether Jo is ready or not.

Key Fact

Jo operates on two registers: defensive wit (fast pace, raised pitch, movement away from other characters) and suppressed vulnerability (stillness, lowered volume, reduced proxemic distance). A skilled performer must make the audience feel both even when Jo herself is suppressing one of them.

Helen

Helen is Jo’s mother — semi-alcoholic, restless, charismatic, and largely absent in every sense that matters. She has made her own choices for survival in post-war Salford and those choices have not included being the mother Jo needed. Delaney asks us not to condemn Helen but to understand her: she is a woman shaped by limited options, not a villain. A performer playing Helen must resist the temptation to make her cruel. She loves Jo in the way she is capable of loving — intermittently, distractedly, warmly when she remembers to be. Physically, Helen takes up space: she moves with an ease and confidence that Jo does not have, occupying downstage centre as if it belongs to her.

When Helen returns in Act Two, a director might use her positioning relative to Geof to communicate the power shift that her arrival represents. Helen and Geof never really share the stage comfortably — a director might use tableau moments when the three of them are present to make the tension in that triangle spatial and visible. Helen’s costume might contrast with Jo’s: brighter colour, more embellishment, a deliberate performance of femininity that echoes and ironises Jo’s situation.

Peter is Helen’s boyfriend and then husband: older, wealthier, given to cruelty. His function in the play is partly structural — he takes Helen away from Jo — and partly thematic: he embodies the economic and sexual power that men of his class and age exercised over women like Helen. A performer playing Peter might use physical bulk and slow, deliberate movement to communicate his dominance, occupying space in the flat as if he already owns it before Helen has agreed to his proposal.

Peter is not on stage for large portions of the play, which means his appearances should feel imposing and slightly alien in a world that is primarily Jo and Helen’s. A lighting designer might use a cooler, harder lighting special during Peter’s scenes to contrast with the warmer domestic light of the flat’s other moments — a subtle signal to the audience that his presence changes the atmosphere.

Geof

Geof is a young queer art student who befriends Jo and moves in to look after her during her pregnancy. He is the play’s moral centre: caring, patient, domestic in the best sense. In 1958 Britain, homosexuality was a criminal offence — a fact that makes Geof’s vulnerability and courage explicit for the audience. He risks a great deal by the simple act of building a life in that flat with Jo. A performer playing Geof might communicate this through a physical watchfulness — a slight self-containment in public scenes, a contrasting ease and openness in the private scenes between him and Jo. The tenderness of the scenes when Jo and Geof make a home together is the play’s warmest section, and a director should stage this warmth carefully: close proxemics, gentle overlapping movement, the actors working in parallel rather than against each other.

Key Fact

Geof is queer at a time when homosexuality was illegal in Britain (it would not be partially decriminalised until 1967). His choice to move in with Jo and care for her is an act of courage and solidarity that the 1958 audience would have understood as dangerous. Examiners reward students who contextualise Geof beyond a simple “kind friend” reading.

The Boy — sometimes called Jimmie — is a Black sailor on shore leave who has a brief winter affair with Jo. He is one of the earliest sympathetic Black characters in mainstream British theatre, presented without exoticism or stereotype. His relationship with Jo is genuine and tender; the fact that he leaves is structural, not a moral failing. Delaney’s decision to name him simply “the Boy” in the script’s first appearance is sometimes discussed by directors as a deliberate anonymising gesture — he is shaped by the plot’s requirements, not allowed to be fully realised. A performer playing the Boy must resist underplaying him: the brief scenes by the canal carry the weight of Jo’s entire subsequent pregnancy.

A lighting designer might use the canal scenes as the one moment when the flat’s interior logic is softened — a lighting wash of cool blue fading at the edges to evoke the outdoors and winter water, with the performers lit from a lower angle to suggest evening rather than the flat’s harsh practical lights. This visual warmth-within-cold mirrors the emotional quality of the relationship: the most genuine warmth in the play exists in the coldest season.

Designing a World Built on Fear

Before a single word of The Crucible is spoken, the audience reads the world through the design. Salem in 1692 was a Puritan settlement: austere, ordered, suspicious of colour, pleasure and anything that could not be explained by scripture. A production that forgets this context will feel generic; a production that embeds it in every design choice will make Miller’s political allegory feel inevitable. As a designer for this play, your task is to use set design, lighting design, sound design and costume design to make the suffocation visible before the hysteria begins.

Set Design: Wood, Austerity and Thresholds

The most effective set designs for The Crucible tend towards minimalism. A bare wooden floor, rough-hewn timber walls or posts, and a limited number of significant pieces of furniture communicate Puritan austerity instantly. A solid door — centre stage or upstage centre — becomes one of the most important props as symbols in the production: every entrance through it is an intrusion, every exit a flight or an arrest. The door’s weight and sound communicate authority.

For the courtroom scene in Act 3, consider replacing the domestic furniture entirely with a single raised table or platform upstage centre for Danforth — placing the judge at a higher level than everyone else immediately communicates his power through spatial means alone. The accused might be placed downstage, trapped between the judge above and the audience in front, creating a visual and physical sense of enclosure. If you are working in a thrust configuration, the audience on three sides can feel themselves drawn into the courtroom, almost as if they too must submit to its jurisdiction.

Key Fact

Set design for The Crucible should communicate austerity and entrapment. Bare wood, minimal furniture, a symbolically weighted door, and a raised platform for Danforth in the courtroom scene are all design choices that carry meaning — not just decoration. Every object should earn its place by communicating character, power or theme.

Lighting Design: From Candlelight to Interrogation

Lighting can carry the emotional arc of the play on its own. In the domestic scenes — the Proctor household in Act 2 — a warm amber lighting wash from a low angle, suggesting candlelight or firelight, would establish the intimacy and warmth that John and Elizabeth’s relationship might once have had, while the chill between them is communicated through the performance rather than the light. Contrast this with the courtroom in Act 3: a harsh top light — achieved through profile lanterns rigged above the stage — strips the warmth from the scene. Shadows fall sharply downward. No one looks comfortable. The lighting state communicates judgment, exposure and interrogation.

A lighting special can isolate Proctor in his final moment in Act 4 — a single tight beam holding him downstage centre as the drum sounds outside. The rest of the stage falls to near-blackout, so the audience’s entire attention is on his face and his stillness. A gobo projecting a lattice or bar pattern onto the stage floor during the jail scene can suggest both physical imprisonment and the shadow of the gallows without a single line of dialogue.

In the moment in Act 4 when Proctor tears his signed confession, consider the following lighting sequence. As Proctor holds the paper, the general lighting state is a cold, desaturated blue-grey wash — the grey light of early morning in a jail, suggesting hopelessness and institutional bleakness. A warm amber gobo (a flame or lattice pattern from a profile lantern, rigged at 45 degrees from the front-of-house position) catches only Proctor’s hands and the paper, isolating the physical object of his choice.

At the moment of tearing, a sudden white lighting special from directly above cuts through the blue wash — not a dramatic flash, but a steady, unsparing reveal, as if a courtroom spotlight has finally illuminated the truth. The white light holds as Proctor stands motionless. Then, as the drum sounds off-stage, the special fades slowly to a single candle-warm fresnel isolating Elizabeth at downstage right. Her stillness in warm light against his cold exposure makes the audience feel the tenderness and the tragedy simultaneously.

Sound Design: The Forest, the Congregation, the Drum

A soundscape can establish the world of Salem before the set is even visible. The forest sounds heard at the very opening — wind through trees, the distant crack of a branch, perhaps the faint echo of girls’ voices — could play over a dark stage as the audience settles, establishing Salem as a community on the edge of something wild and incomprehensible. This is non-diegetic sound used as atmospheric framing.

During the courtroom scene, you might use underscore very carefully — or not at all. The absence of music in Act 3 can be more powerful than its presence: the audience hears only voices, the scrape of a chair, the bang of a gavel. Real silence makes the audience hyperaware of breath, pause and the moment before a character speaks. The sound of a drum beating off-stage in Act 4 as the hangings begin is one of the play’s most devastating devices: you never see the executions, you only hear the rhythm of their approach.

Key Fact

Sound design for The Crucible should contrast the wild, organic world outside Salem’s walls (forest soundscape, wind, distance) with the silence and severity of interior spaces. The off-stage drum in Act 4 is a design masterstroke: the audience’s imagination fills in what the stage does not show.

Costume Design: Black, White and the Exception

Puritan costume is defined by restraint: dark fabrics — charcoal, black, deep brown — plain cuts, high necklines, little to no ornamentation. For a production of The Crucible, a black and white palette communicates the Puritan worldview with visual clarity: the community has reduced the moral universe to absolutes, and the costume palette reflects this. A designer might dress all the Salem townsfolk in variations of grey and white linen, with only the judges wearing black — authority encoded in the colour of cloth.

Abigail Williams is a particularly interesting costume challenge. She must look like she belongs within the Puritan community — she is not visually marked out as dangerous — but a designer might introduce a tiny detail: a dress cut slightly too well-fitted for a servant, or a single red thread in her collar that catches the light when she moves. In the final acts, if Abigail has fled and we return to the jail, the costumes of the condemned might be deliberately un-corseted, loosened from the community’s tight moral structure, suggesting that what the court tried to bind has broken free.

The most common error in designer questions is writing “I would use period costume to show it is set in 1692.” This tells the examiner nothing about intention or effect. A strong answer names fabric, silhouette, colour, fitting and the meaning generated by each choice. For example: “I would dress Danforth in a heavy black woollen doublet with a stiff white collar, the weight of the fabric communicating institutional authority while the rigid white at the throat suggests a man who has used religion to suppress human complexity. The contrast with Proctor’s rougher, earth-toned linen would signal immediately that one man belongs to the apparatus of power and the other to the soil.”

What the Play Asks Us to Believe

Things I Know to Be True draws its title from a phrase that challenges certainty. The things we know to be true about our families — their loyalty, their stability, their love — are exactly what the play systematically tests. Andrew Bovell structures the play's themes around the tension between what the Price family projects outwardly (a settled suburban life, parental pride, sibling solidarity) and what is actually concealed beneath that surface. For a dramatist, this gap between appearance and reality is a rich seam of dramatic irony.

Family: Conditional and Unconditional Love

The dominant theme of the play is family itself: what it can absorb, what it cannot, and who pays the cost of loyalty. Bovell explores two competing models of parental love through Bob and Fran. Fran's love is fierce and vocal; Bob's is quieter and harder to read. The play tests whether parental love is truly unconditional — offered regardless of what a child does or who they are — or whether it carries conditions that only a revelation can expose.

In staging this theme, a director working with the proxemics of the family group can communicate volumes before dialogue begins. When all six characters occupy the stage together, the distances between them — who stands near whom, who gravitates towards a parent, who is physically at the margin of the group — form an instant visual map of the family's emotional geography. A production using a proscenium arch configuration might arrange the family in a tableau that places Bob and Fran at the apex, with the four children arranged at varying distances, so that the staging enacts the theme of parental expectation as a gravitational force.

Key Fact

The central question of the play is whether the family's love is truly unconditional. Each of the four children's revelations tests this question from a different direction: departure, identity, criminality and grief.

Identity: Gender, Self-Determination and the Family's Gaze

The theme of identity runs through every character arc. For Mark, identity is the most explicit subject: the summer season stages the journey of a character coming forward with a truth about who they are in gender terms. Bovell handles this arc with dramatic care, showing the parents' different responses and the sibling dynamics around the revelation. For a performer, the challenge is to play the specific mixture of assertion and vulnerability that characterises a moment of authentic self-disclosure.

Frantic Assembly's movement sequences are structurally significant here. Contact improvisation and the round-by-through-under vocabulary can express the bodily dimension of identity — the sense of inhabiting a self more fully — in a way that pure dialogue cannot. A designer working on this section of the play might use cross-fading between lighting states to mark the transition between the family's before-and-after relationship with Mark / Mia, rather than a single sudden shift.

For Pip, identity is about self-determination: leaving a marriage and a city is an act of individual will that the family reads as abandonment. For Rosie, identity is the most existential: she is the character who must find meaning after heartbreak and who speaks from the play's narrative edge. Identity is also a theme for the parents themselves: Bob's late-revealed secret reframes who he is in the audience's understanding, retroactively altering the identity they believed they had witnessed across the whole play.

Examiners award marks for responses that treat this arc with specificity and respect for the character. Vague generalisations or language that editorialises about the subject matter earn no credit. Strong answers describe what a performer or director actually does on stage: specific vocal choices, specific physical choices, specific lighting and costume decisions that serve the character's journey at each stage of the arc.

A lighting designer might use a warm but precise lighting special on Mark / Mia during the revelation scene, isolating them from the family group while the family is lit in a broader, cooler wash. This separation in the lighting state communicates the character's position: fully present with the family yet briefly occupying a different emotional space. As Mia is accepted back into the family warmth, the isolated special can gradually fade into the shared wash, a visual enactment of inclusion.

Truth, Secrets and the Things We Don't Know

Alongside the children's revelations, the play harbours two parental secrets: Bob's concealed infidelity and the late-play shock that reframes his character. These secrets introduce the theme of truth itself as a complex, unstable thing. What the family has built together — their shared history, their mutual understanding — turns out to rest on partial information. Bovell suggests that all families are, to some degree, fictions that each member maintains for the others.

The rose garden carries this theme in physical form. A prop as symbol, the roses represent the beauty Bob cultivates and the concealment required to maintain it: a garden needs tending, work, constant management, just as a long marriage does. As a set designer, using the garden's seasonal change — spring blossom, summer fullness, autumn decay, bare winter stems — to mirror the play's structural arc makes the theme of concealed truth visible across the whole production.

Money, Ageing and Australian Suburbia

Ben's arc introduces the theme of financial wrongdoing and the gap between a child's projected success and their private reality. The theme here is the pressure of family expectation: the child who is supposed to have succeeded and has not. A performer playing Ben must communicate the layered quality of this shame — personal guilt, dread of a father's disappointment, awareness that his crime will affect the whole family.

Bovell also explores the theme of ageing parents and the moment when adult children see their parents as fallible. The Price parents are settled into late middle age when the play begins; by its end, they are irrevocably changed. The Australian suburban setting — a comfortable home, a tended garden, the domestic certainties of middle-class life in contemporary Adelaide — provides the context against which every destabilising revelation lands. The ordinariness of the setting is the point: the play insists that its themes are universal.

Students sometimes treat the play's themes as separate compartments — one child's arc = one theme. Bovell's work is more integrated than this. Identity runs through every character, not just Mark / Mia. Truth and concealment are as relevant to Bob's infidelity as to Ben's embezzlement. Family love is tested by Pip's departure just as much as by Ben's arrest. Strong exam answers draw thematic connections across the play rather than treating each season in isolation.

Key Fact

The rose garden embodies the play's central theme: the beauty that is cultivated outwardly and the concealment that sustains it. Designing the garden to change across the four seasons makes the theme of truth and hidden lives visible throughout the production.

Two Lenses, One Play

The Crucible is unusual among the set plays because it sits comfortably at the intersection of two major theatrical traditions. On the one hand, its domestic scenes — the Proctor household, the linen scene, the tense silences between John and Elizabeth — call for the psychological depth and emotional truth associated with Stanislavskian naturalism. On the other hand, the courtroom scenes, the political allegory, the audience’s knowledge that the accusations are lies — all of this calls for a Brechtian awareness of the play as a political argument, not just a human story.

A sophisticated drama student — and a sophisticated director — does not have to choose one and abandon the other. The most interesting productions use Stanislavskian intimacy in the private scenes and Brechtian distancing in the public courtroom, so that the audience experiences both the emotional cost of what is happening and the political consciousness of why it is happening. Understanding when and why to apply each lens is exactly what the practitioner questions reward.

Brecht and The Crucible: The Audience as Jury

Brecht believed that theatre should make audiences think rather than merely feel. His concept of the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) is designed to interrupt emotional absorption and remind the audience that they are watching a constructed performance — that what they see is not inevitable but is the result of choices made by a society, and that societies can change.

The Crucible is already Brechtian in one crucial respect: dramatic irony makes the audience a jury. We know, from very early in the play, that the accusations are false. We sit through scene after scene watching an institution of supposed justice destroy people we know to be innocent. Brecht would recognise this structure immediately — it is his didactic model applied to American political life: the audience cannot simply empathise and forget; they must leave the theatre asking how societies allow this to happen.

Brecht’s concept of gestus is particularly useful for staging Judge Danforth. Danforth is not primarily a psychologically complex individual — he is the representative of an institution that has decided it cannot be wrong, because to admit error would be to admit that it has killed innocent people. A Brechtian staging would make this social function legible through gestus: Danforth’s gavel, the pointed finger of accusation, the upstage position at a raised table that places him literally above everyone in the room.

A performer using Brechtian gestus for Danforth might cultivate a very small physical vocabulary — a limited set of gestures that become recognisable and almost mechanical, suggesting that this is a man who has automated his own moral responses. The gavel does not come down with judicial consideration; it comes down reflexively, the way a machine operates. This makes Danforth’s authority more frightening precisely because it has no doubt in it.

Key Fact

Gestus is a Brechtian concept — a physical attitude or pose that defines a character’s social function rather than their individual psychology. Danforth’s repeated gavel, his pointed finger, his upstage position at a raised platform — these are gestus: the body of institutional authority made physical. The audience reads the social type, not just the man.

Stanislavski and Proctor: Given Circumstances and Emotional Truth

Stanislavski’s system offers the opposite approach. Rather than showing the audience a social type, it asks the actor to inhabit the full psychological life of the character. Stanislavski’s concept of given circumstances is particularly useful for Proctor: a performer approaching John through Stanislavski would build a detailed account of everything that has shaped him before Act 1 begins. His affair with Abigail, his guilt towards Elizabeth, his position in Salem as a man who privately questions the church — all of these given circumstances shape every word and movement in every scene.

Stanislavski’s concept of emotion memory might help a performer access the specific quality of Proctor’s guilt in the domestic scenes. The linen scene is not about witchcraft at all — it is about two people trying to find a way back to each other after a betrayal, in a culture that does not permit direct emotional expression. A Stanislavskian performer would spend time in rehearsal understanding the exact quality of that guilt — its texture, its weight, when it flares up and when it goes quiet — so that the restraint in the scene feels real rather than performed.

A practical guide for a director or performer approaching the whole play:

Stanislavski lens — the linen scene (Act 2) between John and Elizabeth, the moment Proctor confesses his affair in court, the Act 4 jail scene between John and Elizabeth before the execution. These are moments of private psychological truth where emotional authenticity is the primary dramatic currency. The audience needs to feel the interior life to understand the cost of the final choice.

Brechtian lens — the courtroom in Act 3 (particularly Danforth and the girls’ ensemble), Reverend Parris’s early scenes of status-anxiety, Hale’s arrival in Salem. These are moments where the social machinery is most visible. Using gestus, deliberate staging configurations and blocking that makes the audience aware of who holds power and who does not will communicate Miller’s political argument more effectively than trying to find individual psychological truth for institutional characters like Danforth.

Miller’s Didactic Intent and the Modern Stage

Miller wrote The Crucible as what Brecht would have called a teaching play — not to entertain but to argue. Its allegory for McCarthyism means that every production choice is also a political statement about how societies collapse into hysteria and how individuals survive or do not. A director who emphasises the Brechtian framework is saying to the audience: “Watch this and ask whether you would have done differently.” A director who emphasises the Stanislavskian framework is saying: “Feel this, and understand what it costs.” The best productions hold both simultaneously.

For your exam responses on Miller’s intentions, this is the insight that distinguishes a Mastering-band answer: not just knowing that Brecht and Stanislavski are relevant, but being able to argue which approach serves which scene and why — and doing so with reference to specific performance or design choices rather than biographical summaries of the practitioners.

Key Fact

The examiner is not impressed by a paragraph about Brecht’s life or Stanislavski’s background. What earns marks is applying the technique to a specific moment: “Using Brechtian gestus for Danforth — a mechanically repeated gavel motion, a pointed finger, an upstage platform — communicates his social function as the machinery of institutional denial made flesh.”

Performing the Contradictions

Every character in A Taste of Honey is, in some sense, a performance: Helen performs her identity as a good-time girl who needs nobody; Jo performs bravado; Peter performs authority; Geof alone performs only himself, with a gentleness the play earns its right to. For an actor approaching any of these roles, the central challenge is not to iron out the contradictions but to hold them simultaneously — to be both things at once. A good performer playing Helen does not choose between her comedy and her vulnerability; they keep both in play.

Performer skills in drama are divided into vocal and physical categories. Vocal skills include accent, volume, pace, pitch, intonation and pause. Physical skills include posture, gesture, facial expression, stillness and proxemics. For this play, both sets of skills must be calibrated to the Salford, 1958 world the characters inhabit — and to the specific moment being performed.

Key Fact

Examiners expect performers to name specific skills with specific effects. “I would say it angrily” scores no marks. “I would drop my volume to near-silence, slow my pace to a single beat between words, and hold eye contact with the audience rather than the other character” describes a performable choice that the examiner can visualise and evaluate.

Playing Jo: Wit on Top of Fear

Jo is 17. She has grown up in a world of instability, and she has learned to use comedy as a survival mechanism. A performer playing Jo must resist two tempting errors: making her entirely tragic (this flattens the comedy) or making her entirely sharp and funny (this loses the vulnerability). The ideal is a character whose quick-fire Salford wit lands and is genuinely funny, but where the audience can see, in the slight hesitation before a quip or the briefly unguarded face when a line is delivered to the audience rather than to another character, that the confidence is constructed.

Vocally, Jo’s accent is Salford — working-class northern English, flattened vowels, quick pace. A performer should resist softening this towards a generic northern accent; the specificity of Salford matters to the play. In her exchanges with Helen, pace is rapid: neither woman allows the other many long pauses. But a smart performer will find the moments where Jo stops — where her wit runs dry for a second, where the pace drops — and use those moments to reveal what the comedy usually covers.

Physically, Jo occupies space differently at different points in the play. In early scenes, she circles the flat, rarely still, using the space between herself and Helen as a negotiated proxemic territory: close when seeking something, further away when defending against it. By the final scene, her physical world has contracted: the pregnancy, Geof’s departure, Helen’s return — and her gestus (her whole physical attitude) has shifted. A performer might choose a more inward, contained posture in the closing scenes, the energy turned inward.

Helen is the most dangerous character to play in a moralistic register. A performer who signals to the audience “this woman is a bad mother” has already failed: examiners reward students who play her as a fully human woman shaped by limited choices, not a villain. Helen’s swagger — her large gestures, her habit of filling space, her laugh that is slightly too loud for some rooms — is her version of the fur coat: performative armour over a woman who has survived partly by not looking too hard at the consequences of her choices.

A performer playing Helen might choose a broad, open posture — chest open, weight forward, arms wide — that communicates confidence and takes up space in the flat. Her pace and pitch are generally high-energy: she brings the city inside with her. But a smart performer finds the places where the energy drops: a moment of genuine tiredness that slips through before Helen reassembles her performance of herself. These moments, brief and unannounced, are where the audience sees the cost of Helen’s choices.

Geof and the Lullaby Moment

Geof is the play’s moral centre. He is a young queer art student who moves in with Jo as an act of care, building a makeshift domestic world with her in the second act. A performer playing Geof must communicate his gentleness without reducing him to sainthood: he has his own discomforts, his own frustrations, his own longing for something the play does not quite grant him. His physicality should feel considered and still compared to Helen’s expansiveness: quieter gestures, a habit of being near without imposing, an attention to Jo that Helen rarely offers.

The lullaby moment — when Geof sings to Jo’s unborn child while Jo watches — is one of the play’s most tender theatrical passages. A director staging this must decide how much stillness to allow: a complete tableau around Geof while he sings communicates the fragility of this moment, the sense that any movement might shatter it. The lighting state could shift imperceptibly warmer; the jazz musicians, if present, might be silent for the first time, their absence suddenly audible.

Key Fact

The final scene — Helen and Jo alone after Geof has left — closes on a deliberate ambiguity. A director choosing a final tableau that echoes the play’s opening can signal the cyclical nature of Jo’s situation: she is becoming Helen. The staging choice of whether Jo and Helen are close or far apart in this final image is itself an interpretive statement about the play’s ending.

The Final Scene: Two Women, One Flat

Helen’s return in the final scenes displaces Geof and brings the play’s central dynamic back to the mother-daughter relationship. A director must make choices about the blocking of this scene carefully: does Helen immediately take the space back, re-occupying centre stage while Jo retreats? Or does Jo hold the flat for a moment, the proxemic balance temporarily shifted by her months of independent life with Geof?

Vocally, the final exchanges between Jo and Helen should carry a layered sub-text: surface comedy in the banter, but beneath it the knowledge that Jo is on her own again, facing an uncertain future. A performer playing Jo in this scene might choose a slightly flatter delivery than earlier in the play — the wit still present, but the energy reduced, the pace slightly slower — suggesting exhaustion underneath the resilience. Helen’s return to her familiar rhythms might be played with just a hint of false brightness, a performer’s choice that lets the audience sense both women’s awareness of what they are not saying.

Delaney does not provide a neat resolution. A production that ends with Jo and Helen in a warm physical closeness — centre stage, the lighting soft — leans into a comforting reading of maternal reunion. A production that ends with distance — the two women in the flat but not touching, the lighting the same flat, functional wash as the opening — emphasises the cyclical trap: Jo is where Helen was, and nothing has changed. The director and performers must decide which of these (or which point between them) they are making, and ensure every closing choice — proxemics, lighting, sound, the final beats of the jazz — supports that decision consistently.

Design Is Not Decoration

A common misconception is that set, lighting, sound and costume are the “backdrop” to the real action of the performers. In any well-made production, design is as much a language as speech. A single lighting choice — a green wash sliding in at the moment a character tells their first lie — can communicate to the audience something the dialogue never says. Your job in the exam is to decode that language.

The principle is the same as for performers: name the specific design choice, explain how it was executed technically, and evaluate its effect on the audience. The vocabulary is different — you are now working in lantern types, gobos, underscore, set materials — but the analytical method is identical.

Key Fact

Design vocabulary the examiner rewards: Fresnel (soft-edged wash), profile (hard-edged beam), flood (wide area wash), moving light, gobo (patterned effect), gel (colour filter), lighting special (a single focused lantern on one area), blackout, cross-fade, lighting state.

Lighting: Four Questions to Ask

When you observe a lighting moment in a production, run through four questions:

  1. Direction: where is the light coming from? Front lighting is naturalistic; side lighting gives a dramatic split-face effect and implies conflict or duality; top lighting isolates and can suggest divine or oppressive power; back lighting creates silhouette, suggesting mystery or the loss of individual identity.
  2. Colour: what gel or filter is being used? Cool blues and greens signal isolation, threat or the supernatural; warm ambers and yellows signal domestic warmth, nostalgia or golden-age memory; deep red can signal passion, danger or violence. The specific combination matters — a blue wash with a single warm special on one character separates them from the world around them.
  3. Intensity: what is the brightness? A fade to near-darkness before a final moment creates dread; a sudden full-white wash can feel clinical, exposing, accusatory. The rate of the fade or the snap of the change is also a choice — a snap blackout shocks; a slow two-minute fade mourns.
  4. Equipment and effect: if a gobo projects bars across the stage, does that suggest imprisonment? If a lighting special follows a character across the stage, does that suggest they are watched, celebrated or exposed? Note the effect, not just the equipment.

Imagine you saw a fictional production of a thriller at a hypothetical studio theatre in 2025. In the penultimate scene, the villain revealed their true identity to the protagonist. Consider how a strong analysis might read:

Weak version: “The lighting was dark and dramatic, which suited the tense mood.”

Strong version: “As the villain turned to face the protagonist, the stage lighting cross-faded from a warm amber general wash to a single cold tungsten profile focused tightly on the villain’s face from a steeply raked angle above and stage left. The cross-fade took approximately four seconds, so by the time the speech began the protagonist’s face had vanished into shadow while the villain’s was fully lit — a visual metaphor for the shift in power within the scene. The bar gobo projected across the downstage area suggested confinement; the protagonist was already, in lighting terms, trapped before a word had been spoken. The effect on the audience was palpable: the laughter from earlier scenes disappeared completely, replaced by a sustained, uncomfortable silence.”

Notice: lantern type (profile), direction (steeply raked, stage left), colour (cold tungsten), a gobo type (bar), the rate of the change (four seconds), the metaphorical meaning and a specific audience reaction. All from one lighting cue.

Sound: Diegetic, Non-Diegetic and Soundscape

Diegetic sound is sound the characters can hear; non-diegetic sound is heard only by the audience. A creaking door is diegetic; the unsettling low-frequency drone beneath a scene of domestic abuse is non-diegetic underscore. Both can be analysed for meaning.

When analysing sound, note: the texture of the sound (is it crisp and close, or distant and reverberant?), its placement (coming from specific speakers — stage left, from above, or surrounding the audience?), its relationship to the action (does it start before the scene begins, establishing mood before the performers enter?), and any sudden change (a silence that was filled with underscore is often more powerful than the music itself).

A soundscape is a layered sonic environment rather than a single cue: the simultaneous combination of rain, distant thunder, traffic and an indistinct crowd for an opening city scene, for instance. Note how many layers you can identify and what the cumulative effect was.

Set and Costume: Symbol and Material

Set designers make choices about material, colour, scale, level and symbolic meaning. A single chair on an otherwise bare stage can communicate isolation, power or waiting. A set that rotates during the performance communicates flux, the relentlessness of time, or the character’s inability to escape their world. When analysing set, note: what objects are present and what they symbolise; whether the set changed during the performance and what the change communicated; the relationship between the set’s scale and the performer’s body (a small figure dwarfed by an enormous set reads as the individual overwhelmed by forces beyond their control).

For costume, examiners want specific fabric, colour and silhouette analysis, not just era or genre. A costume that is visually impeccable but slightly too large for the performer communicates something very different from one that fits perfectly. Note colour against the set and against other characters’ costumes — if every character wears grey and one wears deep scarlet, that contrast is a design intention, not an accident.

Students frequently write design analysis at a level of generality that earns little credit: “the lighting was atmospheric,” “the costumes were period-appropriate,” “there was dramatic music.” These sentences do not tell the examiner anything analytical.

Compare “the costumes were period-appropriate” with “the lead character’s costume was a knee-length coat in heavyweight charcoal wool with a silhouette that was structured at the shoulders and narrowed at the waist, giving the performer the physical presence of authority even when standing still.” Both sentences are about costume. Only one demonstrates that you understand how design communicates meaning.

The rule is simple: if you cannot say which lantern, what colour, which fabric and what effect, your note-taking in the theatre was not specific enough. Build the habit of technical precision at the performance itself.

Key Fact

Design disciplines to cover in your review: lighting (lantern type, direction, colour, intensity, gobo, lighting state), sound (diegetic / non-diegetic, texture, placement, underscore, soundscape), set (material, level, scale, symbolic props), costume (colour, fabric, silhouette, fit).

Themes as Staging Choices

In A Taste of Honey, Shelagh Delaney’s themes are not stated — they are embodied in concrete physical and social realities: the damp flat, the cheap ring, the absence of fathers, the illegality of Geof’s identity. A director and designer do not need to signal “this play is about class” with a placard; the themes live in the texture of every design choice. Understanding how each theme operates — and how it shapes the stage picture — is essential to high-level analysis. The term gestus is useful here: a single physical gesture or attitude that makes visible a social condition rather than just a personal emotion. Helen’s sweeping entrance that displaces Jo from the centre of the flat is gestus for the power dynamic between mother and daughter.

Class and Poverty

The flat is the play’s primary argument about class. It is damp, rented, inadequate — and Helen and Jo move there because they have no better option. Working-class life in 1950s Salford meant housing with no central heating, shared bathrooms, and a constant precarity about where next month’s rent would come from. A set design that makes this precarity specific — a peeling damp patch on the back wall, a wobbly table propped with a book, a gas ring rather than a fitted kitchen — communicates class more powerfully than any explicit statement.

Class intersects with the movement of characters on stage. Peter occupies space differently from Helen or Jo — his physicality is that of someone who expects the world to accommodate him. A director might contrast his blocking (expansive, unhurried, centre stage) with Jo’s (peripheral, near the walls, close to exits) to make the class and gender power differential physical and visible. When Peter leaves the stage, a director might allow Jo to physically expand into the space he was occupying — a breath of released tension the audience will feel even if they cannot name it.

Key Fact

Class in A Taste of Honey is communicated through material detail: the condition of the flat, the quality of clothing, the absence of comfort. A designer who renders this poverty specifically — not generically — makes the class theme legible without a word of dialogue.

Motherhood and the Cycle of Neglect

The play’s central relationship is between Jo and Helen, and at its heart is a question Delaney refuses to answer simply: what does it mean to be a mother when you are barely surviving yourself? Helen is not a bad mother in any cartoonish sense — she is a woman who had a child young, in poverty, without support, and who has built survival strategies that do not prioritise Jo. The play asks the audience to hold both truths simultaneously: that Jo has been badly let down, and that Helen is not simply a villain.

The structural irony of the play — Jo at the end alone with Helen, pregnant herself, apparently on the same path — is Delaney’s darkest observation. Jo risks becoming Helen. A performer playing Jo in the final moments might make that realisation physical: a posture shift, a look in the mirror (literal or implied), a vocal quality that echoes Helen’s earlier in the play. A staging echo — the same position at the same window, the same low winter light — can make the cycle argument without a single additional word.

Jo’s relationship with the Boy — a Black sailor — is written and staged as a genuine, tender winter love affair. In 1958 Britain, an interracial relationship was not illegal but was socially transgressive. The Notting Hill race riots took place later that year, in late August and early September. Delaney presents the relationship without sensationalism, exoticism or condemnation. This was a deliberate political act: staging Black and white love as ordinary, real and worthy of sympathy at a moment of significant racial tension in Britain.

For a 21st-century production, a director must present the relationship in its historical context while resisting any framing that positions the Boy as exotic or other. The staging of the canal scenes should communicate warmth and equality: similar levels, shared focus, lighting that does not privilege one performer over the other. A lighting state that treats both performers identically is itself a directorial statement about the equality of the relationship. The Boy’s departure is structural, not moral — he sails because his ship leaves, not because of any failure of feeling.

Sexuality and Queer Friendship

Geof’s queer identity is presented with the same matter-of-fact sympathy that Delaney extends to the interracial relationship. Homosexuality was a criminal offence in England in 1958 — the Wolfenden Report had recommended decriminalisation in 1957 but the law would not change until 1967. Geof moves in with Jo knowing that his domestic arrangement with a woman is both his protection from suspicion and his genuine love for a friend. Delaney asks the audience to understand Geof’s situation without moralising or sensationalising it.

The scenes between Jo and Geof — making a home, arguing, caring for each other — are the play’s most tender. A director staging the found-family dynamic between them might use close proxemics and warm, low-key gel tones to create a visual warmth that contrasts with every other relationship in the play. When Helen returns and begins to push Geof out, a director might track the gradual increase in distance between Geof and Jo across these scenes — a physical embodiment of something being broken that should not be.

Key Fact

In 1958, A Taste of Honey staged three subjects rarely seen sympathetically on the British stage: an interracial love affair, a queer friendship, and a single teenage mother. Delaney presents all three without condemnation — a political act as significant as any staging choice.

A common error is to treat these themes as moral lessons — to write about the interracial relationship as “controversial” or Geof’s identity as “brave and unusual” in a way that implies they should be less central to the play. Examiners reward students who present these themes in their historical context (1958 Britain, specific social realities) and then discuss staging choices that make them legible for a contemporary audience without anachronism or moralising. The play’s point is not that these things are transgressive — it is that they are human, and that the world that makes them transgressive is the problem.

How Character Works in The Empress

Tanika Gupta builds her characters on two axes: historical ground (some are real people; some are imaginative reconstructions of documented communities) and dramatic function (each character serves a specific structural and thematic purpose). As a performer or designer approaching this play, your task is to translate character motivation into concrete, physical choices: how does Rani hold her body the moment the English family leaves the docks without her? How does Abdul Karim’s physical bearing change between his early months of nervous service and his later confidence as Victoria’s munshi?

Rani: The Invented Protagonist

Rani is the play’s moral centre. She has no historical name because the ayahs whose lives Gupta draws on largely went unrecorded, but the research behind her is real. Her character arc moves from abandonment and isolation through community — the Lascar sailors, the Ayahs’ Home — to a moment of solidarity that gives the play its emotional resolution. As a performer playing Rani, you might consider how her proxemics shift across the play: isolated at the docks, downstage centre and physically contracted; in the Ayahs’ Home, beginning to expand into shared space with other women.

In terms of vocal choices, Rani’s language moves between formal English — the register she has learned in service — and her own Bengali identity. A performer might use a careful, slightly flattened English accent when addressing English characters, shifting in pitch and pace when she speaks to Lascar Mr Das or in moments of private emotion. This code-switching is itself a character choice: it tells the audience that Rani has learned to perform a certain identity for English employers, and the release from that performance is where her true character lives.

Key Fact

Rani is an invented protagonist grounded in the real history of ayahs stranded in Victorian London. Her character journey moves from isolation to community to solidarity. Examiners reward performers who can specify her vocal register shift and physical transformation across the play.

Abdul Karim: History on Stage

Abdul Karim is a historical figure and Gupta stays close to the documented record: he arrived at Windsor in 1887, became Victoria’s Indian secretary, taught her Hindustani, was resented by the court and had his papers burned by the royal household after her death. As a dramatic character, his arc is one of extraordinary ascent and ultimate erasure. A performer playing Abdul must hold these two things simultaneously: the personal warmth and intelligence of the man, and the knowledge that his story was deliberately destroyed after Victoria died.

In the court scenes, Abdul’s physical choices should communicate his dual status: the formal upright posture and deliberate, measured movements of a man who understands he is under constant scrutiny; and underneath that, the private dignity of someone with a strong sense of his own worth. Gestus is a useful concept here. Abdul’s gestus in the court scenes might be understood as a controlled stillness — the conscious management of self-presentation under an oppressive gaze.

Queen Victoria: Warmth within the System

Gupta’s Victoria is one of the play’s most nuanced characters. She is genuinely fond of Abdul, genuinely curious about India, and uses what power she has to protect him. But she is also the Empress of India — the figurehead of the system that abandons Rani at Tilbury and burns Abdul’s papers. A director must resist letting the audience simply like Victoria. The most interesting staging of Victoria keeps both of these truths visible at once. One design approach: a golden-yellow gobo pattern suggesting the rays of empire in her scenes at court, beautiful but also inescapable — the very light that flatters her power casts shadows on those around her.

Hari Mohan Lal is a dramatic composite figure inspired by the real Dadabhai Naoroji, who was elected Liberal MP for Finsbury Central in 1892 — the first South Asian MP in British parliamentary history. Gupta draws on that real political history without making Hari identical to Naoroji. Examiners reward students who understand this as a dramaturgical choice: Gupta uses Hari to represent the emerging South Asian political voice in Britain without the legal and narrative constraints of a purely biographical depiction. This is the same technique she uses with Rani.

Hari Mohan Lal: The Political Voice

Hari represents the nascent South Asian political presence in Westminster — the first generation of Indian-born men attempting to use the tools of British democracy to argue for Indian rights. As a dramatic character he occupies a different register from Rani or Abdul: more formal in language, more conscious of being observed and judged by a hostile political world. His scenes offer the play’s most direct engagement with political argument, as opposed to personal experience. For a costume designer, Hari’s dress is a significant choice: Western tailoring that signals his assimilation into the political world, versus any remaining South Asian detail in fabric or accessory that suggests his retained identity.

Lascar Mr Das and the East End Community

The Lascar sailor characters — Mr Das and others — represent a community that was physically present in Victorian East London for generations. They are among the most settled of the play’s Indian figures: they have lodging houses, community rituals and networks of mutual support. A designer staging the Lascar lodgings might choose a set made from found maritime objects — rope, canvas, battered sea-chests — to communicate both the nautical origin of this community and the resourcefulness of people who have built a home from whatever they could carry. Warm, low-level lighting specials could suggest lamplight and enclosure: a hidden world behind the docks.

The English Antagonists: Lord Salisbury, Bertie and Mrs Wormwood

The English antagonist figures are not cartoons of villainy. Lord Salisbury and the Prince of Wales are motivated by a genuine belief in hierarchical order: for them, Abdul’s elevation is not merely an affront to taste but a threat to the system that underpins their world. Mrs Wormwood, the English mistress who pays Rani off at the docks, may not even understand herself as doing harm. A director might use proxemics to communicate these power dynamics spatially: in the docks scene, Mrs Wormwood placed upstage, elevated on a trunk or step, with Rani standing downstage left, physically smaller in the frame, reinforces the power asymmetry before a word is spoken.

Key Fact

The English antagonists — Lord Salisbury, Bertie, Mrs Wormwood — are more effective dramatically when staged as people defending a system they believe in, rather than as simple villains. This makes the play’s argument about Empire more unsettling and more honest.

The most sophisticated performer approach to Abdul Karim holds two traditions in tension. Stanislavski’s method asks: what is Abdul’s specific inner life at each moment? What does he want from Victoria in their Hindustani lessons? What does he feel when the court conspires against him? This psychological specificity keeps him real and sympathetic. Brecht’s method asks: what is Abdul’s social gestus? What does his physical presence tell the audience about the relationship between an Indian man and an Imperial court? Both questions matter. A great performance of Abdul does not choose between them: it lets the intimate Stanislavskian truth carry the Brechtian political argument without forcing it.

What Performance Interpretation Means in This Play

Every character in The Empress navigates the same central tension: how to maintain dignity while navigating the structures of British imperial power. As a performer, your task is not to choose whether your character is “angry” or “sad” — it is to find the precise vocal quality and physical shape that communicates what a specific character guards under pressure. Vocal interpretation and physical interpretation are the two instruments available. In Drama, naming the emotion is not enough — you must translate the emotion into a concrete, observable choice.

The four key characters for performance analysis are: Rani, whose journey is from abandoned vulnerability to quiet defiance; Abdul Karim, whose arc moves from nervous deference to grounded confidence; Hari Mohan Lal, who carries the political voice of educated Indian ambition; and Queen Victoria, whose private warmth exists in ironic tension with the Empire she represents.

Rani: Quiet Defiance

The most important performance principle for Rani is that her resistance is almost never loud. When Mrs Wormwood pays her off at Tilbury Docks, a performer who plays Rani’s response as overt anger will lose the scene’s power. The more interesting choice is stillness: Rani holds her ground physically — feet planted, proxemics held at exactly the distance of a servant who refuses to back away — while her vocal volume drops rather than rises. A lower, measured voice, slower pace, distinct pauses before each reply. The pauses are doing the work: they say “I am choosing not to perform the gratitude you expect.”

In the Ayahs’ Home scenes and the Lascar lodging-house scenes, the same performer can open the physical and vocal register completely. Here Rani’s posture is relaxed, her gestures broader, her pitch warmer and more variable. The contrast between these registers tells the audience the full story of what the docks scene cost her. A director might stage these community scenes with Rani downstage, drawing the audience into her community, while the English characters always occupy the upstage area — a spatial argument about whose world this is.

Key Fact

A common error in performance questions is describing what the character feels rather than what the performer does. “Rani feels hurt and betrayed” is interior analysis. “The performer drops vocal volume, slows pace, holds eye contact with Mrs Wormwood for three full beats before turning away with a controlled exhale” is performance interpretation. Write the second kind of answer.

Abdul Karim: Growing Confidence

Abdul arrives at Windsor Castle as a servant who speaks English and is acutely aware of his visible difference. The performer’s opening physical choices should communicate this: shoulders slightly forward, head inclined, movements precise and measured — the body of someone who does not want to take up too much space. A performer could begin with English that is over-articulated, effortful and pitched upward slightly as though each sentence is a question. As his relationship with Victoria develops, these choices can shift: he stands taller, occupies the centre of the stage space more readily, his voice finding a lower, steadier register.

The moment the court conspires against Abdul is a key performance opportunity. The performer playing Abdul in those scenes might use tableau-quality stillness — standing entirely motionless while the English characters move and scheme around him — as a way of communicating his dignity under threat. The stillness is more powerful than movement here: the audience reads it as refusal to perform the panic the court wants to provoke. A lighting designer can heighten this by keeping Abdul in a steady warm lighting state while the scheming courtiers are cast in cooler, more fragmented light.

Consider the scene when Abdul first teaches Victoria a Hindustani word. A Stanislavskian approach asks both performers to find the specific, small truth of the moment: Victoria’s genuine delight and Abdul’s carefully restrained pleasure at being valued rather than dismissed. The performer playing Victoria might lean forward slightly, her posture losing its regal formality for just a moment — a physical signal of private warmth. The performer playing Abdul might allow a brief, controlled smile: eyes warm, a slight release of the permanent slight tension in his shoulders, but the smile does not break into a full grin, because he has learned not to display joy openly in this house. These small, specific choices communicate the relationship’s complexity to the audience more effectively than a larger emotional display.

Queen Victoria: Public and Private

Victoria is one of the most demanding performance challenges in the play because examiners specifically reward students who can hold two contradictory truths about her simultaneously: her genuine warmth towards Abdul is real, and her role as the symbolic head of an Empire that brutalises Rani’s community is equally real. A performer who plays her as a simple imperial villain misses the play’s argument; a performer who plays her as a warm grandmother ignores the structural critique. The key is to show the difference between her public and private registers.

In public court scenes, the performer might use a formal physical posture — upright, hands folded, gaze fixed, deliberate formal diction with full consonants — the performance of imperial authority. In private scenes with Abdul, the same performer can soften: a slight forward lean, a lower vocal register (warmer, less projected), eye contact that admits rather than commands. The transition between these registers, managed precisely and consistently, communicates the play’s central argument about how power works: Victoria can be kind and still be the Empress of India.

Hari Mohan Lal: The Political Voice

Hari carries the explicitly political argument of the play: that Indian people belong in British public life not as servants or curiosities but as citizens and legislators. The performer playing Hari must navigate a different version of the code-switching challenge: Hari speaks entirely in formal Victorian English register, and the risk is that this makes him sound like a British establishment figure rather than an Indian one. The choice might be to maintain a clearly Indian accent throughout, refusing to assimilate vocally even when the words are entirely correct. His physicality might be erect and formal — the body of someone who has studied the gestus of parliamentary authority — but with a stillness and groundedness that is distinctly different from the restless energy of the English political figures around him.

Key Fact

For performance questions in the exam, always anchor your choices to a specific named moment. “Throughout the play” is too vague to score Mastering. “In the moment Abdul is confronted by Lord Salisbury after Victoria’s first lesson, I would drop vocal volume to near-inaudible and stand completely still at centre stage” is the level of specificity the mark scheme rewards.

Students sometimes try to resolve Victoria’s complexity by choosing a single reading: either she is a kind old woman and the Empire is just context, or she is a hypocrite whose warmth to Abdul is meaningless given the system she heads. Gupta’s writing holds both truths in tension and examiners reward students who can maintain that tension in their performance analysis. The challenge is not to resolve the contradiction but to perform it: Victoria’s genuine warmth is what makes the structural critique more devastating, not less. A performer who can show both is doing justice to the play’s argument.

A Cast Built Around Contrast

Blood Brothers is a play built on pairing. Every major character exists in relationship to their opposite: Mickey, the working-class twin, placed beside Edward, his middle-class brother; Mrs Johnstone’s warm, exhausted love beside Mrs Lyons’s anxious, controlling longing. Understanding how to perform these characters is inseparable from understanding what they represent. When a performer makes gestus choices for Mickey and Edward, they are simultaneously making arguments about class.

Mickey Johnstone

Mickey is the emotional heart of the play. As a child, he is quick, curious, foul-mouthed and funny — a working-class boy who has learned to find pleasure in the limited world of his street. As a teenager, he is awkward and infatuated with Linda. As an adult, he is unemployed, depressed and eventually imprisoned. The arc is from joyful energy to crushed stillness, and a performer must make that arc legible through specific choices at each stage.

Physically, the child Mickey should have a loose, impulsive quality: quick direction changes, a low centre of gravity, hands constantly busy. By the depression scenes of Act Two, that same body should feel heavy and constricted — slow movements, sunken posture, a voice that has lost its colour and pace. On stage, the transition is achieved not through a costume change alone but through physical characterisation. The adult Mickey’s proxemics relative to Linda and Edward in the final confrontation should communicate isolation: if Edward is central and commanding, Mickey is peripheral and cornered.

Key Fact

Mickey’s arc is from working-class vitality to social entrapment. The physical journey — loose, energetic child to slow, heavy adult — communicates Russell’s argument that the class system, not personal weakness, is responsible for Mickey’s destruction.

Edward Lyons

Edward is the same biology as Mickey but a different upbringing entirely. Raised in a large house with books and educational opportunity, he speaks in RP (Received Pronunciation), uses formal vocabulary and carries the easy confidence of someone who has never been told their prospects are limited. As a performer, the key challenge with Edward is to make him genuinely warm and likeable rather than simply a symbol of privilege, or the friendship between the brothers will feel implausible. His physical posture should be upright, open and unhurried — not stiff or snobbish, but belonging to someone with no reason to be guarded.

The contrast between Mickey’s Liverpudlian dialect and Edward’s RP is a central theatrical language. A sound designer should consider whether a soundscape or underscore in the childhood scenes reinforces the warmth of the friendship across that divide, or whether the contrast should feel more pronounced and uncomfortable by Act Two.

Mrs Johnstone

Mrs Johnstone is the play’s moral centre. She is a single mother of seven — later nine — exhausted, behind with the hire purchase, still humming Marilyn Monroe songs because she holds onto the idea that life could be beautiful. Russell asks the audience to love and pity her simultaneously. When she gives up one twin, she does so out of desperation, not cruelty, and the audience must feel that gap between her intent and the consequences.

As a performer, Mrs Johnstone requires extraordinary vocal range. She sings through some of her most painful moments; the songs are not relief from grief but a way of bearing it. In the scenes where she makes the deal with Mrs Lyons, a performer might choose a low, quiet vocal register — someone speaking who doesn’t quite believe her own words. Her proxemics relative to Mrs Lyons in this scene should show social submission: she may be physically smaller on stage, seated while Mrs Lyons stands, positioned towards the edge of the acting space while Mrs Lyons occupies centre.

A costume designer working on Mrs Johnstone might use the visual vocabulary of 1960s Liverpudlian working-class life: worn fabrics, faded floral prints, practical but not fashionable. The fit of the clothes might suggest she has little money for new ones; alterations and visible repairs become design language. This contrasts directly with Mrs Lyons, whose costume should communicate affluence through fabric quality (wool, structured tailoring), clean lines and the absence of visible wear. The two women standing together should read as a class map even before they speak.

Mrs Lyons

Mrs Lyons is a more complicated figure than a simple villain. She cannot have children and she wants one desperately. When she persuades Mrs Johnstone to give up a twin, she is acting from real longing, not purely from selfishness. However, her means are manipulative: she exploits Mrs Johnstone’s superstition about the shoes-on-the-table curse, turning a folk belief into a weapon of social control. As she grows more anxious about the truth being revealed, she becomes increasingly unstable — eventually violent.

A performer playing Mrs Lyons must find the genuine pain underneath the control. Her proxemics should change over the course of the play: early on she is composed, her posture upright and assured; by the later scenes, her movements might become tighter, more restless, with sudden bursts of physicality that signal the loss of control underneath the bourgeois surface. Vocally, she begins measured and persuasive; by Act Two, her pitch rises and her pace becomes erratic.

Key Fact

Mrs Lyons uses Mrs Johnstone’s belief in a local superstition to coerce her silence. This moment is central to the play’s exploration of how the powerful manipulate the powerless — and a director should treat it as a key staging moment, not a throwaway exchange.

A common student error is to describe Mickey as “representing the working class” and Edward as “representing the middle class” and leave it there. This is insufficient for an 8 or 12-mark question. The examiner wants to see how you would perform or design these characters as specific people in specific moments — not as walking symbols. Mickey’s depression in Act Two is not just “what happens to working-class people”; it is a specific person in a specific physical and emotional state. Describe the vocal pitch, the pace, the posture, the proxemics for that named moment. Then, and only then, link it to the theme.
